en: Obeisance to Śrī Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
The Śrīmad Bhāgavata Purāṇa. The Eleventh Skandha.
The Uddhava-gītā. Now begins the first chapter.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Having accomplished the slaughter of the Daityas, Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by the Yadus,
swiftly brought about the Kali age, thereby producing for the earth a burden as if it were a new incarnation.
The Lord, having used as a pretext those sons of Pāṇḍu who had been greatly provoked by their rivals through the foul game of dice, insults, the seizing of hair, and so forth—
having caused them to assemble from here and there and having slain them, he removed the burden of the earth.
Having cast off the burden of the earth—the royal armies—by means of the Yadus whom he protected with his own arms, the immeasurable one reflected:
"I think that although the burden has indeed departed from the earth, it has not truly gone, for alas, the Yādava clan remains unbearable. (3)
May there never be any humiliation for him who takes refuge in me, nor any loss of his power or pride;
having brought about internal strife within the Yadu clan, I shall enter my own abode, like a fire that has extinguished a bamboo thicket. (4)
Having thus resolved, O King, the Lord, whose will is truth,
withdrew his own lineage under the pretext of a curse from the brahmins, he who is all-pervading.
By her own form, which was the very essence of the world's beauty, she captivated the eyes of men;
by her songs, the hearts of those who remembered them; and by her footsteps, the actions of those who beheld them.

Having truly and swiftly stripped away their widespread and glorious fame, the Lord has departed to His own abode, thinking, "They shall cross over this darkness by means of [their] misconduct. || 7 ||
The king said: How did the curse of the Brahmins come to pass upon the Vṛṣṇis—who were devoted to the Brahmins, generous, ever-attending upon their elders, and whose hearts were fixed on Kṛṣṇa? (8)
O best of the twice-born, tell me all this: what was the cause of that curse, and of what nature it was; and how did division arise among those who are of one essence? 9.
Śrī Śuka said:
Bearing a form of perfect and beautiful proportions, performing auspicious deeds upon the earth with all desires fulfilled,
and delighting in his own abode, he of noble fame— having completed his remaining duties— desired to withdraw his lineage.

Having performed auspicious deeds that bring a multitude of merits and remove the impurities of the world’s sins, while the Lord dwelt there in his own form within the abode of Yadu’s descendant, the sages were sent forth and arrived at Piṇḍāraka. 11.
Viśvāmitra, Asita, Kaṇva, Durvāsas, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Kaśyapa, Vāmadeva, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, and others. ||12||
While playing, the princes, the delights of the Yadu clan, approached them; having touched their feet in greeting, though they were ill-behaved, they questioned them as if they were well-disciplined.
Having dressed Samba, the son of Jambavati, in female attire, she said: "O Brahmins, this woman with downcast eyes, who is pregnant, asks you a question. (14)
She is ashamed to ask you in person; please speak, O you of unfailing vision:
will those who desire sons give birth, and what indeed will she bring forth?
Having been thus mocked, O King, the sages spoke to them in anger:
"O fools, he shall produce for you a club that will bring about the destruction of your lineage. (16)
Hearing that, they were utterly terrified; suddenly releasing Sāmba’s belly, they indeed beheld within it an iron mace.
"What have we, of such meager fortune, done? What will people say of us?"—thus distressed, they took their pestles and went to their homes. (18)
Having brought him into the assembly, they reported him—his facial splendor faded—to the king in the presence of all the Yādavas. (19)
Having heard that the Brahmin’s curse was infallible and having seen the club, O King, the inhabitants of Dvārakā were struck with wonder and became terrified with fear. ||20||
Having crushed that pestle, King Āhuka, the descendant of Yadu,
cast it into the waters of the ocean, along with whatever iron remained of it.
A certain fish swallowed some iron filings along with the waves;
then, as they were being carried to the shore, they became stuck there, it is said, and turned into irika stones.
A fish was caught by fishermen with a net along with others in the ocean;
the hunter placed iron within its belly for the sake of the arrowhead. ||23||
The Blessed One, who knows all things and is the Lord, did not wish to alter that curse; rather, appearing in the form of Time, he acquiesced to it. ||24||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Curse of the Brahmins," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the collection concerning the state of the Paramahaṃsas.
Now begins the second chapter.
Śrī Śuka said:
O best of the Kurus, while Dvārakā was protected by the arms of Govinda...
Nārada dwelt there constantly, longing for the service of Kṛṣṇa. ||1||

O King, who indeed that possesses sense-control would not worship the lotus feet of Mukunda, which are to be venerated from all sides by the best of the immortals, yet are themselves subject to death? ||2||
Once, when that celestial sage had come to his house, Vasudeva,
having honored him and seen him seated comfortably, saluted him and spoke as follows.
Vasudeva said:

O Blessed One, your journey is for the welfare of all embodied beings, just as it is for the wretched who follow the path of the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka), even as it is for their own parents. 4.
The conduct of the gods toward living beings leads to both suffering and happiness;
but for the virtuous like you, O Acyuta, whose very selves are devoted to the Supreme, it leads only to happiness.
Just as people worship the gods, so too do the gods honor them;
for the virtuous, who are compassionate toward the distressed, follow their actions like shadows.
O Brahmin, nevertheless we ask you about the Bhāgavata duties, hearing which with faith a mortal is liberated from all fear. (7)

Indeed, in the past, for the sake of my subjects, I worshipped the infinite Lord who bestows liberation upon the earth; yet, deluded by the divine illusion (māyā), I did not worship Him for the sake of my own liberation. ||8||
O you of noble vows, instruct us truly and directly in such a way that we may be swiftly liberated from all sides by you from this manifold calamity and fear. 9.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having been thus questioned by the wise Vasudeva,
the celestial sage was pleased and, being reminded of the qualities of Hari, spoke to him.
Nārada said:
"O bull among the Sātvatas, you have rightly resolved this, in that you inquire about the Bhāgavata duties which bring welfare to the entire world. (11)
Whether heard, recited, meditated upon, honored, or even rejoiced in, the True Dharma instantly purifies even those who harbor malice toward the gods and all beings. 12.
By you, the most auspicious Lord Nārāyaṇa, whose merit consists in being heard of and glorified, has been reminded to me today. 13.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history:
the conversation between the sons of Ṛṣabha and the high-souled King of Videha.
The son of Svāyambhuva Manu was named Priyavrata;
his son was Agnīdhra, from whom Nābhi was born, and Ṛṣabha is recorded as the son of that [Nābhi]. ||15||
They say that he was an incarnation of Vāsudeva with the desire to proclaim the dharma of liberation;
he had a hundred sons who had mastered the Vedas.
Among them, Bharata was indeed the eldest and was devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
it is after his name that this wonderful land is celebrated as Bhārata-varṣa. 17.
Having abandoned this world after its enjoyments were exhausted, he departed; worshipping Hari through austerity, he indeed attained His state within three births. ||18||
Of them, there were nine lords of the nine islands on all sides of this [continent], eighty-one twice-born ones who were the originators of the systems of action. ||19||
There were nine highly fortunate sages who proclaimed the ultimate truth;
they were ascetics, subsisting on air, and experts in the knowledge of the Self. ||20||
Kavi, Hari, Antarikṣa, Prabuddha, Pippalāyana, Āvirhotra, Drumila, Camasa, and Karabhājana. ||21||
Indeed, beholding this entire universe, consisting of the existent and the non-existent, as the form of the Blessed One and as non-different from the Self, they wandered over the earth. 22.

O Lord of Munis, Cāraṇas, Bhūtas, and Vidyādharas, those who are liberated wander at will through the worlds of the gods, Siddhas, Sādhyas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Kinnaras, and Nāgas, their desired paths being unimpeded, as well as through the realms of the twice-born and the cows. 23.
Once, by chance, they arrived at the sacrifice of the high-souled Nimi, which was being performed by sages at Ajanābha. ||24||
Seeing those illustrious ones who resembled the sun, the king, while performing the sacrifice, approached them all—both the sacrificial fires and the brahmins. ||25||
Videha, perceiving them to be devoted to Nārāyaṇa,
was pleased and honored them as they sat upon their seats, according to their merit.
The king, exceedingly pleased and bowing with humility, questioned those nine who were shining with their own luster and resembling the sons of Brahmā.
Videha said:
I consider you to be the direct associates of the Blessed One, the enemy of Madhu;
for as manifestations of Viṣṇu, you wander about for the purification of the worlds. 28.
For embodied beings, a human body is difficult to obtain and is momentary;
even within that, I consider the sight of the beloved of Vaikuṇṭha to be most difficult to attain. (29)
Therefore, O sinless ones, we ask you about ultimate happiness:
in this cycle of worldly existence, even half a moment’s association with the virtuous is a treasure for human beings. (30)
Declare those teachings of the Lord if they are fit for our hearing—those by which the Unborn One, being pleased, will grant even his own self to one who has sought refuge in him. (31)
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus questioned by Nimi, those most exalted of the Vasudevas, having honored him in return, spoke with affection to the king and his assembly of priests. (32)
The poet said:
I consider that for one who constantly worships the lotus feet of Acyuta here, there is no fear from any quarter;
for him whose mind is agitated by the nature of the unreal, fear ceases where the Universal Self resides. 33.
Know that those very means which were proclaimed by the Blessed One for the sake of attaining the Self are indeed the Bhāgavata ways for men who lack knowledge. 34.
O King, by relying upon these, a man would never be negligent;
even while running with his eyes closed, he would not stumble or fall here in this world. (35)
Whatever one performs—whether by body, speech, mind, senses, intellect, or self—all that should be dedicated to the Supreme Nārāyaṇa, as it follows His own nature. 36.
Fear arises from attachment to a second [entity]; for one who has departed from the Lord, there is the error of non-remembrance.
Therefore, the wise man, regarding the Guru, the Deity, and his own self as one, should worship that sole Lord with devotion through His illusory power (māyā). 37.
For even though it does not exist, it appears as a duality through the intellect of the meditator, just like dreams and mental fantasies.
Therefore, the wise person should restrain that mind characterized by action, resolve, and conceptualization; from that, fearlessness shall arise.

Hearing the auspicious accounts of the birth and deeds of the Discus-wielder as they exist in the world, and singing the names that correspond to their meanings, one should wander about free from shame and unattached. (39)

Thus observing his vow, with a heart melted by intense love born from the chanting of his beloved’s name, he laughs aloud, weeps, cries out, sings, and dances like one mad, standing outside the world. (40)

One should bow down, without any other thought, to the ether, wind, fire, water, and earth; to the luminaries, living beings, and the quarters; to the trees and so forth, the rivers, and the oceans—to whatever exists as the body of Hari. 41.

Devotion to the Supreme Lord, spiritual realization, and detachment from everything else—these three occur simultaneously for one who takes refuge, just as satisfaction, nourishment, and the cessation of hunger occur with every morsel for one who eats. 42.
"O King, for one who thus worships the feet of Acyuta with devoted service, devotion, detachment, and realization of the Lord arise;
thereafter, that devotee of the Lord attains supreme peace directly. (43)
The King said:
Now, tell me of the Bhāgavata—what his duty toward men is like, how he conducts himself, what he speaks, and by what characteristics one who is dear to the Blessed Lord is known. (44)
Hari said:
He who perceives the nature of the Blessed One in all beings, and perceives all beings within the Blessed One as his own self—he is the best of devotees. 45.
He who practices love, friendliness, compassion, and equanimity toward the Lord, those dependent on Him, the ignorant, and the hostile is a middling [devotee]. (46)
He who strives with faith to worship Hari only in an image, and not toward other devotees, is considered a common, materialistic devotee. ||47||

Even when perceiving objects through the senses, he who neither feels aversion nor rejoices, seeing this as the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu—he indeed is the best among the devotees of the Lord. 48.

He who is not deluded by the worldly conditions of birth, decay, hunger, thirst, fear, and distress affecting the body, senses, vital breath, mind, and intellect, but remains mindful of Hari, is the foremost among the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavata). 49.
He in whose mind there is no arising of the seeds of desire and action, who has Vāsudeva as his sole refuge—he indeed is the most excellent devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata). 50.
He for whom the sense of "I" does not cling to this body—neither because of its birth or deeds, nor because of caste, stage of life, or lineage—he indeed is dear to Hari. 51.

He for whom there is no distinction between "self" and "other" regarding possessions or even his own body, who is equal toward all beings and tranquil—he is indeed the best among the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavata). 52.

He whose memory remains unimpaired even for the sake of the sovereignty of the three worlds, and who does not waver for even half a moment from the lotus feet of the Blessed One—which are sought after by the unconquered self, the gods, and others—is indeed the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas. (53)

When the heat has been dispelled from the heart by the moonlight of the jewel-like nails on the toes of the Blessed One’s feet of wide-striding power, how could that [heat] prevail again, like the sun's scorching heat when the moon has risen? (54)

He whose heart Hari does not directly enter—even though Hari, the destroyer of the flood of sins, has been addressed [by him] involuntarily—and who holds the lotus feet [of the Lord] with a love that supersedes hunger, he is declared to be the foremost among the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavata-pradhāna). ||55||

Thus ends the second chapter, in the dialogue between Nimi and Jājali, in the eleventh book of the glorious Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the great Purāṇa, in the collection concerning the state of the Paramahaṃsas. ||2||

Now begins the third chapter. We desire to know the deluding power (māyā) of the supreme Viṣṇu, the Lord, which even confounds those called masters of illusion (māyins); may the venerable ones speak to us. (1)
I am not satiated by enjoying your words, which are the nectar of stories concerning Hari;
for a mortal scorched by the fevers of saṃsāra, they are the remedy for that suffering. 2.
Antarikṣa said:
O mighty-armed one, by means of these great elements, the primordial Soul of all beings created higher and lower creatures for the sake of establishing his own measure.
Having thus entered the created beings by means of the five elements, he,
dividing himself into one and ten ways, enjoys the qualities.
The Lord, experiencing the qualities through the qualities manifested by his own self, and considering himself as the creator of this world, becomes attached here. ||5||
Performing actions with their causes through various deeds, the embodied soul,
receiving the fruit of each respective action, wanders here in this world between happiness and its opposite.
Thus, proceeding through the courses of karma that bring much misfortune, a person, being powerless, undergoes creation and dissolution until the final dissolution of all beings. (7)
When the dissolution of the elements is imminent, that which consists of the unmanifest substance and its qualities becomes manifest;
for Time, which is without beginning or end, draws all things toward the unmanifest.
For a hundred years, a terrible drought shall occur upon the earth;
at that time, the sun, intensified by heat, will scorch the three worlds.
Starting from the depths of the netherworld (pātāla), the fire from the mouth of Saṅkarṣaṇa, burning with upward-pointing flames, spreads in all directions, fanned by the wind. ||10||
The host of clouds known as Sāṃvartaka rained for a hundred years;
with torrents like the trunks of elephants, the Virāj dissolved into the water.
Then, O King, having abandoned Virāj, the Puruṣa born of Virāj enters the unmanifest and subtle, like a fire without fuel. ||12||
The earth, its fragrance removed by the wind, is transformed into the state of water;
that water, its flavor held fast, is prepared for the state of light. 13.
Light, its form taken away by darkness, dissolves into the wind;
the wind, its touch taken away by space, dissolves into the ether;
and the ether, its quality taken away by Time, dissolves into the Self. (14)

O King, the senses, the mind, and the intellect, together with the products of the *vaikārika* [sattva], enter into the *ahaṅkāra*, which, along with its own qualities, enters into the Self (*ātman*). 15.
This Māyā of the Blessed One, which brings about creation, maintenance, and destruction, has been described by us as having three colors; what more do you wish to hear? ||16||
The King said:
"O Great Sages, please explain how those of dull intellect may easily cross over this divine illusion, which is so difficult for those of unrefined souls to transcend. (17)
Prabuddha said:
One should observe the reversal of results for men who, moving in pairs, undertake actions for the sake of happiness and the destruction of suffering. ||18||

What joy can there be in wealth that brings constant suffering and is difficult to obtain, or in one's own life which is as fragile as death; or in a home, children, kinsmen, and cattle—all of which are unstable, even when acquired? (19)
Thus one should know the next world to be perishable and fashioned by karma, subject to equality, excellence, and destruction, just like that of earthly sovereigns. (20)

Therefore, one who desires to know the highest good should take refuge in a teacher who is thoroughly proficient in both the word of scripture and the supreme Brahman, and who is established in tranquility. 21.

There, regarding the teacher as his very self and deity, he should learn the duties of a devotee with sincerity and devoted service—those by which Hari, the Self and giver of the self, may be pleased. 22.
First, one should practice non-attachment of the mind toward everything, and attachment toward the virtuous;
as well as compassion, friendliness, and humility toward all beings, truly and as is appropriate.
Purity, austerity, forbearance, silence, self-study, uprightness, celibacy, non-violence, and equanimity toward the pairs of opposites. (24)
Everywhere [he should cultivate] the contemplation of the Self and the Lord, solitude, homelessness, clothing made of rags from a secluded place, and contentment with whatever comes by chance. ||25||
Faith in the scripture of the Lord and freedom from censure toward others; the restraint of mind, speech, and action; truthfulness; and also tranquility and self-control. (26)
Hearing and chanting about Hari, whose deeds are wonderful, as well as reflecting upon His births, activities, and qualities, and performing every action for His sake. (27)

Whatever has been sacrificed, given, performed as austerity, recited, or whatever virtuous conduct is dear to oneself—offering all this, including one's wife, sons, home, and very life, to another; ||28||
Thus, one should cultivate friendship toward those whose souls are devoted to Kṛṣṇa and toward men as well; and one should offer service to both types of great and virtuous persons. 29.
The mutual recounting of the purifying glory of the Blessed One brings about mutual delight, mutual satisfaction, and mutual cessation from worldly attachment for the self. (30)
Remembering and causing one another to remember Hari, who removes the flood of sins, they bear their bodies with horripilation through the devotion that has been born within them. 31.
In some places they weep with thoughts of Acyuta; in other places these extraordinary ones laugh, rejoice, and speak.
They dance, sing, and practice the discipline of the Unborn; then, having attained the Supreme, they become silent and are fully satisfied. 32.

Thus, training himself in the duties of the devotees of the Lord through the devotion arising therefrom, this person, intent upon Nārāyaṇa, easily crosses over the insurmountable [stream of worldly existence]. 33.
The king said:
"You ought to tell us of the final state of the Supreme Self, the Brahman designated as Nārāyaṇa; for you are the most eminent among those who know Brahman. (34)
Pippalāyana said:

Know that to be the Supreme, O lord of men, which is the cause of the stability, emergence, and dissolution of this world, yet is itself without cause; which exists within the states of dreaming, waking, and deep sleep, and also externally; and by which the body, senses, life-breaths, and the heart move, being animated. 35.
Neither the mind, nor speech, nor sight, nor the self, nor the vital breaths and senses enter into this [Self], just as flames do not enter their own fire.
Even sound, by way of negating its perceivers, declares the Self to be its root; for without that [Self], the establishment of negation is impossible. ||36||
In the beginning, that which was one became threefold as sattva, rajas, and tamas; they call it the Sūtra, the Mahat, the Ahaṃkāra, and the Jīva.
Through its powers in the form of knowledge, action, and the fruit of objects, Brahman alone shines as both the existent and the non-existent, being that which transcends both. ||37||
The Self was never born, nor will it die; it does not increase, nor does it waste away, for it is the knower of the sacrifice.

Indeed, among those who deviate from the truth, it is everywhere, eternal, and imperishable—the mere consciousness that is the vital breath (prāṇa), which appears differentiated according to the power of the senses. ||38||
In eggs, in embryos, and in trees—where life is not yet determined—the vital breath indeed pursues the living soul here and there.
When the collection of senses has subsided and the ego is fast asleep, that which remains as the immutable witness, apart from the latent impressions, is our memory. (39)

For he who, through exclusive devotion to the two feet of the Lotus-navelled Lord, would dispel the impurities of the mind born of the modes and their activities—within him, purified, the reality of the Self is perceived directly, just as the light of the sun is seen by one with clear vision. (40)
Speak to us of the yoga of action, by which a person, once refined, quickly shakes off all actions here and attains the supreme state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya). 41.
Thus I previously asked this question of the sages in the presence of my father;
the sons of Brahmā did not answer—let the reason for that be told.
Āvirhotra said:
"Action, inaction, and mis-action—this is the teaching of the Vedas, not of the world.
Because the Veda has the Lord as its very soul, even the wise are bewildered by it. (43)
The Veda speaks in an indirect manner; this is an instruction for the immature.
Indeed, it prescribes ritual actions for the sake of liberation from action, just as one prescribes medicine [to cure a disease]. 44.

But he who, being himself ignorant and having his senses unsubdued, does not practice what is declared in the Veda, indeed goes from death to death by means of improper action and unrighteousness. 45.

Performing only that which is enjoined by the Veda, free from attachment and offering it to the Lord, one attains the perfection of actionlessness; the scriptural mention of rewards is for the purpose of encouragement.
He who desires to quickly sever the knot of the heart regarding the Supreme Self should worship the Lord Keśava according to the ritual prescribed in the Tantra. 47.
Having received grace from the teacher and having been shown the traditional scripture by him, one should worship the Great Being (Mahāpuruṣa) through whichever form is personally preferred. 48.

Pure, seated facing the east, having purified the *piṇḍa* through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other means, and having performed protection through the rite of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), he should worship Hari. 49.

In the case of an image and so forth, as well as in the heart, having prepared the substances, the site, and the self-signs using whatever ritual offerings are available, and having sprinkled the seat; ||50||
Having prepared the water for washing the feet and the other offerings, and having placed them nearby with a concentrated mind,
one who has performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the heart and other limbs should worship with the root mantra.
One should worship each respective form, together with its limbs, secondary limbs, and retinue, by means of its own mantra,
using water for the feet, the respectful offering, water for sipping, and so forth, as well as bathing materials, garments, and ornaments.

Having worshipped Hari along with his limbs according to the rules with perfumes, garlands, unbroken grains, wreaths, incense, lamps, and offerings, and having praised him with hymns, one should bow down. 53.
Meditating on his own self as being identical with that [divinity], he should worship the form of Hari;
then, having placed the remainder upon his head and having respectfully bid farewell to the deity in its own abode, he should dismiss it.
Thus, he who worships the Lord as the Self within the fire, the sun, water, and so forth, as well as in the guest and in his own heart, is indeed liberated without delay. 55.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Exposition of Māyā, Karma, and Brahman," in the dialogue between Nimi and Jājali, within the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the collection known as Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||3||
Now begins the fourth chapter.
The King said:
"Whatever actions there are here [to be performed] by those who have taken births according to their own will,"
Let them declare to us whether Hari is the wheel, the act of turning, or the agent. ||1||
Drumila said:
He who would attempt to enumerate the infinite qualities of the Infinite One is indeed of childish intellect;
one might somehow count the particles of dust of the earth over time, but never those of the Abode of All-Power.

When Nārāyaṇa, the primordial God, having fashioned the radiant city (Virāj) by means of the five elements created by Himself, entered it with a portion of His own self and assumed the name Puruṣa. ||3||
This body is the arrangement of the three worlds; by its senses, the embodied beings possess both types of sense organs.

Knowledge arises from itself, strength from the breath, vigor from effort, and through the qualities such as *sattva*, there is the maintenance, dissolution, and emergence [of the world], for it is the primordial creator. ||4||

In the beginning, at the creation of this world, there was Śatadhṛti (Brahmā) in the realm of passion (rajas); Viṣṇu was in the maintenance of the world; and Rudra, the lord of sacrifice and the bridge of dharma for the twice-born, was in the realm of darkness (tamas).
That primordial Person (Puruṣa) is indeed he; thus, the origination, maintenance, and dissolution of all beings occur perpetually through him.
From Dharma, through his form as Nārāyaṇa, was born Nara, the most excellent of sages, who is profoundly tranquil;
he taught the nature of actionlessness while yet performing action, and even today he remains with his feet served by the best of seers. (6)
Thinking, "Indra seeks to seize my abode," he directed his desire toward the one known as Badarī along with his attendants.
Having gone there, that knower of the great [truth] pierced him with the arrows of women's glances, accompanied by hosts of Apsarases, spring, and gentle breezes. ||7||
Perceiving the assault perpetrated by Śakra, the Primal God, free from astonishment, laughed and spoke to those who were trembling:
"Do not fear, O Madana, Māruta, and celestial nymphs! Accept our tribute and keep this place from being empty. (8)
When Abhayadeva had spoken thus, O Naradeva, the gods, their heads bowed with shame, spoke to him with compassion:
"O Lord, this is not surprising in you, who are supreme and unchanging, whose mind is fixed on its own garden, and whose lotus feet are bowed to by the crowns of the gods. (9)
For those who serve you, many obstacles created by the gods arise as they cross their own abodes to reach your supreme state;
yet for no one else who offers oblations on the sacrificial grass as their own portion does he grant a place, unless you, as the protector, place your foot upon the head of the obstacle. 10.

Having crossed over these shoreless oceans—hunger, thirst, the three times, the qualities, the vital breaths, and the cold of winter—some fall under the sway of fruitless anger; they sink into the pit of a cow's hoofprint and cast away their well-performed austerities in vain. (11)
To them who were thus praising him, the powerful Lord revealed women of most wonderful appearance, who were performing service while being well-adorned. ||12||

Seeing those women, who were like the goddess Śrī incarnate, those celestial attendants were bewildered by their fragrance; their own splendor was eclipsed by the beauty and nobility of those women. 13.
To them, as they bowed down, the Lord, the God of gods, said as if smiling:
"Choose one of these women—of equal complexion and the ornament of heaven."
Having received the command "Om," those who are praised by the gods bowed to him and departed for heaven, placing Urvaśī, the best of the Apsarases, at their head. ||15||
Having bowed to Indra in the assembly while the inhabitants of the triple heaven were listening, they spoke of Nārāyaṇa’s power; Śakra stood there, struck with wonder. ||16||

In the form of a swan, the infallible Lord spoke of self-yoga; our father, the blessed Dattātreya, the foremost of sages, is Viṣṇu descended by a portion for the welfare of the worlds; by him, the slayer of Madhu, the Vedas were recovered from the horse-headed one. 17.
In the Fish incarnation, though hidden away, Manu, Ilā, and the medicinal herbs were protected by You as You raised the earth from the waters, having slain the son of Diti;

in the Tortoise incarnation, the mountain was supported upon Your own back during the churning for nectar; and in the Boar incarnation, You released the distressed king of elephants who had sought refuge from the crocodile.

To the sages and seers who were praising him after his crossing of the ocean, and to Śakra who had entered the darkness following the slaying of Vṛtra, and to the helpless celestial women imprisoned in the house of the Asuras—he, the Lion among Men, slew the lord of the Asuras for the sake of the fearlessness of the virtuous. ||19||
Having slain the lords of the Daityas in the war between the gods and the asuras for the sake of the deities, he established the worlds within the intermediate spaces by means of his portions;
then, having become a dwarf, he took away this earth from Bali under the pretext of a request and gave it to the sons of Aditi.
Rāma, the fire of the Bhṛgu lineage, thrice seven times rendered the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas, including the Haihaya clan;
he bound the ocean, slew the ten-faced Rāvaṇa along with Laṅkā, and as the husband of Sītā, he—whose fame is invincible—triumphs over the world. 21.
To relieve the burden of the earth, the Unborn shall be born among the Yadus and perform deeds difficult even for the gods to achieve;
he shall delude with his arguments those unworthy performers of sacrifices, and at the end of the Kali age, he shall slay the Śūdra kings.
O mighty-armed one, such deeds and births of the Lord of the World,
who possesses abundant glory, have been described at great length.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nimi and Jājali," in the eleventh book of the glorious Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, within the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||4||
Now begins the fifth chapter.
The King said:
"Those who consider themselves the best knowers of the Self generally do not worship the Blessed Lord Hari."
What is the end for those whose desires are unappeased and who have not conquered themselves?
Camasa said:
From the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet of Puruṣa, along with the stages of life (āśramas), the four castes—beginning with the Brahmins—were born separately according to their qualities. ||2||
Those who do not worship this Lord, who is the manifest source of these beings and their own Self, and who instead despise Him, fall downward, deprived of their station. (3)
Those for whom stories of Hari are far away, and for whom the chanting of Acyuta’s names is distant—even women, Śūdras, and others like them—are objects of compassion for those such as you. 4.

Even the Brahmin, the Kshatriya, and the Vaishya who have reached the presence of Hari, though they are proponents of the Vedic scriptures, may still be deluded regarding their birth according to the revealed texts. ||5||
Unskilled in action, stubborn, foolish, yet imagining themselves to be wise,
these deluded men speak with flattering words, eager for that speech which is as sweet as honey.
Those of foul resolve due to passion, lustful, full of pride, hypocritical, and sinful, mock those who are dear to Acyuta. 7.
In their homes, they address one another with benedictions while attending to women and the pleasures of sexual union;
for the sake of their livelihood, those ignorant of the truth sacrifice animals that have not been consecrated, lack the prescribed rites, and are devoid of sacrificial fees. ||8||
On account of their fortune, prosperity, noble lineage, learning, renunciation, beauty, strength, and virtuous deeds, the wicked show contempt for the beloveds of Hari. 9.

The ignorant do not hear that the Lord, who is eternally present within the bodies of all beings as their own desired Self, is celebrated in the Vedas; instead, they speak only of the rumors of their own desires. 10.

In the world, sexual intercourse and the consumption of meat are constant for living beings; indeed, there is no scriptural injunction regarding them. However, their regulation is established through marriage, sacrifice, and the drinking of wine; it is desired that one desist from these [in ordinary circumstances]. (11)

Since wealth indeed has dharma as its sole fruit, they apply themselves to knowledge along with realized wisdom and ultimate peace within their homes; yet they do not perceive death, whose power is irresistible, lurking within the body. 12.

That the consumption of liquor was ordained as smelling it, and that the immolation of an animal is not violence; likewise, that sexual union is for the sake of progeny and not for pleasure—they do not know this pure self-dharma. 13.
But those who are ignorant of this, being wicked, arrogant, and conceited, who confidently injure animals—they devour them after death. 14.
Those who hate Hari, the Lord, within their own bodies, yet are bound by affection for this corpse along with its attachments, fall downward. 15.

Those who have not attained isolation (kaivalya), and those who have passed beyond the state of ignorance—those devoted to the three aims of life (traivargika), being transient, truly bring about their own destruction. ||16||
These self-destroyers, restless and imagining they possess knowledge when they are ignorant, truly perish with their purposes unfulfilled, their desires destroyed by time. 17.
Having abandoned their horses, chariots, houses, children, friends, and wealth, those who have turned their backs on Vāsudeva enter into darkness against their own will. 18.
The king said:
At what time is that Blessed One worshipped by men, what is his color, and of what nature is he?
By what name or by what ritual is he honored? Let that be told here. (19)
Karabhājana said:
"In the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages, O Keśava, you are worshipped according to various rites, with various colors, names, and forms. (20)
In the Kṛta age, he is white, four-armed, with matted hair and clad in bark garments;
he bears a black antelope skin, a sacred thread, prayer beads, a staff, and a water-pot.
But at that time, humans were peaceful, free from enmity, friendly, and impartial;
they worshiped the Divine through austerity, tranquility, and self-restraint. ||22||
He is celebrated as Haṃsa, Suparṇa, Vaikuṇṭha, Dharma, Yogeśvara, Amala, Īśvara, Puruṣa, Avyakta, and Paramātman. ||23||
In the Tretā age, he is red in color, four-armed, and wears three girdles;
he has golden hair, is the embodiment of the triple Veda, and is characterized by the sacrificial ladle (sruk), the dipping-spoon (sruva), and other such implements. ||24||
Then those most righteous men, the exponents of the Veda, worship that god Hari—who embodies all the gods—with the threefold knowledge. 25.
Viṣṇu, Yajña, Pṛṣṇigarbha, Sarvadeva, Urukrama, Vṛṣākapi, Jayanta, and Urugāya—thus he is praised. ||26||
In the Dvāpara age, the Blessed One is dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments, bearing his own weapons, and distinguished by the Śrīvatsa and other such marks and characteristics. ||27||
O Great King, O Ruler, mortals who desire to know the Supreme then worship that Puruṣa through the Vedas and the Tantras as the supreme sign. 28.
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva; salutations to Saṅkarṣaṇa as well;
salutations to you, the Blessed One, Pradyumna and Aniruddha. 29.
Salutation to Nārāyaṇa, the seer, the Puruṣa, the Great Self; to the Lord of the Universe, the Universe itself, whose self is all beings. 30.
Thus, O lord of the earth, they praise the Lord of the Universe during the Dvāpara age;
now hear how they do so even in the Kali age through various ritual systems. 31.

The wise indeed worship Him who is dark-complexioned, yet black by His own luster, together with His limbs, secondary limbs, weapons, and attendants, primarily through sacrifices consisting of congregational chanting. 32.

I bow to Your lotus feet, O Great Person—the object of constant meditation, the destroyer of humiliation, the granter of desired fruits, the abode of sacred pilgrimage sites, praised by Śiva and Viriñci, the worthy refuge, the remover of the suffering of servants, the protector of those who seek shelter, and the boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence. 33.

I bow to your lotus feet, O Great Being, who—being most righteous—departed for the forest at the word of his elder brother, renouncing the royal splendor so difficult to abandon and so ardently desired; and who pursued the illusory deer sought after by his beloved wife. 34.
In this way, O King, Hari, the Lord of all blessings, is worshipped by men living in their respective ages according to the requirements of those ages, even though he is the Blessed One.
The noble ones, who recognize virtue and partake of its essence, honor Kali, for by his mere glorification every personal goal is attained. (36)
Indeed, for embodied beings wandering here, there is no gain higher than this, from which one may find supreme peace and the cycle of worldly existence ceases. 37.
O King, in the Kṛta and other ages, people desire birth;
indeed, in the Kali age, they shall be solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
In various places, O Great King, and especially in abundance among the Dravidas,
there are the river Tāmraparṇī, the Kṛtamālā, and the Payasvinī.
O lord of men, those humans who drink the water of the highly meritorious Kāverī and the great river Pratīcī are generally devotees of the Blessed Vāsudeva, possessing pure intentions. 40.

O King, he who has with his whole being gone for refuge to Mukunda, the worthy refuge, is neither a servant nor a debtor to the gods, sages, spirits, men, or ancestors; indeed, he is free from all such obligations. 41.

For the beloved devotee who has abandoned all other attachments and takes refuge at the soles of His feet, Hari, the Supreme Lord, dwelling within his heart, shakes off every ill deed that may have arisen by any means whatsoever. ||42||
Nārada said:
Having thus heard these Bhāgavata duties, the Lord of Mithilā, together with his preceptor, was delighted and honored those sages and Jājali. 43.
Then, while all the world looked on, the perfected ones (siddhas) vanished;
the king, adhering to his duties, attained the supreme goal. 44.
You too, O highly fortunate one, by abiding in these Bhāgavata duties which you have heard, endowed with faith and free from attachment, shall go to the Supreme. 45.
Indeed, the entire world has been filled with the glory of you two, husband and wife, since the Blessed Lord Hari became your son. (46)

O Kṛṣṇā, by means of seeing, embracing, and conversing, as well as by sharing beds, seats, and meals, your very selves have been purified while you were manifesting maternal affection toward your sons.

Even kings such as Śiśupāla, Pauṇḍraka, Śālva, and others, who harbored enmity toward Him, attained His likeness by meditating on His gait, graceful movements, glances, and so forth while lying down, sitting, and the like—those whose minds were fixed on Him; what then need be said of those whose hearts are full of love? 48.

Do not conceive the thought that Kṛṣṇa is merely your offspring; he is the Supreme Lord, the Self of all, the supreme and imperishable one whose divine sovereignty is concealed by his appearance as a human through his power of illusion. 49.

For the sake of removing the earth's burden, for the destruction of wicked kings, for the protection of the virtuous, and for the liberation of one who has descended [to earth], his fame is spread throughout the world. 50.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard this, the highly fortunate Vasudeva was greatly amazed, and the highly fortunate Devakī likewise abandoned her delusion. 51.
Whoever, with a concentrated mind, should preserve this meritorious history, having shaken off all impurity in this world, becomes fit for union with Brahman. 52.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Vasudeva and Nārada," in the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, within the collection known as Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||5||
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Śrī Śuka said:
Then Brahmā, surrounded by his sons, the gods, and the lords of progeny, approached.
And Bhava, the lord of the past and the future, departed, surrounded by hosts of spirits.
Indra with the Maruts, the blessed Ādityas, the Vasus, the two Aśvins, the Ṛbhus, the Aṅgirases, the Rudras, the Viśvedevas, and the Sādhyas are the deities. ||2||
Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Guhyakas, as well as Ṛṣis, Pitṛs, Vidyādharas, and Kinnaras. ||3||
Desirous of beholding Kṛṣṇa and the others, they all approached Dvārakā—
that very form by which the Blessed One, who delights the world of men,
spread his fame throughout the worlds as the remover of the impurities of all people. (4)
While that city was shining and prosperous through great supernatural powers,
they gazed upon Kṛṣṇa of wondrous appearance with eyes that could not be satiated.
Covering the best of the Yadus with garlands brought from the celestial gardens,
they praised the Lord of the World with hymns of wondrous words and meanings.
The gods said:

O Lord, we bow with our intellect, senses, vital breaths, mind, and speech at Your lotus feet, which are meditated upon within the heart by those seeking liberation who are endowed with devotion, as the means to escape the heavy fetters born of karma. (7)

Through Your illusory power consisting of the three qualities, You create, maintain, and dissolve the manifest universe within Yourself—something difficult to conceive—even while remaining established in those qualities.
Yet, O Unconquered One, You are not tainted by these actions, for You are blameless and delight in Your own unimpeded bliss.

O Bull among men, O worshipful one, the purification of those with evil intentions does not come through learning, sacred revelation, study, charity, or the performance of austerities in the same way that it occurs for those whose souls are pure, when their goodness increases through faith in Your glory, which has been gathered by hearing [of it]. 9.

May Your foot be our comet of destruction for those of inauspicious intent—that foot which is carried by sages with hearts full of compassion for the sake of their welfare, and which is worshipped at every sacrifice by self-realized Sātvatas of equal opulence for the purpose of transcending the celestial realms. 10.
O Lord, You are meditated upon by those with purified hands who, having taken the oblation, offer it into the sacrificial fire according to the ritual prescribed in the three Vedas;
and You are sought after through spiritual yoga by the most devoted bhaktas, the practitioners of yoga who desire to know Your own illusory power (māyā).
O Lord, this divine Śrī, like a rival wife, vies with your faded forest garland;
may the foot of him who accepts the well-prepared worship offered by her always be a comet for those of impure intent. 12.

O Lord, may that foot of Yours—which is endowed with the three strides, which has three lines and a banner, and which brings fear to the armies of the demons and gods while granting fearlessness to the virtuous—purify our sin for the sake of heaven; indeed, O All-pervading One, let it purify the feet of those who worship You. 13.

May the foot of You, the Supreme Person, the Time who stands beyond both primordial nature (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa), grant us peace—You under whose control Brahmā and the other gods remain like oxen led by the nose, being repeatedly tormented and crushed. 14.
You are the cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of this universe, as well as of the unmanifest, the individual soul, and the Great Principle (Mahat); they call You Time.
This very Time, with its three naves, set in motion for the total destruction of all things, possesses a profound current; You are that Supreme Person. 15.
Having obtained from you that [power] by which a man of unfailing potency conceives a great embryo as it were, he, followed by her, emitted his own golden egg, endowed with external coverings. ||16||

You are the sovereign lord of both that which stands still and that which moves; for although you enjoy the objects brought forth by the transformations of the qualities arising from Your own Māyā, O Lord of the senses, You remain untainted—unlike others who fear even those things they have naturally cast off. ||17||

Yet his sixteen thousand wives, expert in the erotic arts through the casting of amorous spells by their arching brows—bewitching with expressions revealed even in a fleeting glance—were unable to disturb his senses with their manifold charms, for they were like the arrows of the bodiless god of love. (18)
O Lord who dwells in purity, the rivers of the three worlds—flowing from Your feet and carrying Your all-pervading nectarine stories—descend to destroy the impurities of the universe.

Those who dwell in the sacred waters touch these two holy sites: the one flowing from Your feet through their ears by hearing the revealed scriptures, and the other from Your body through physical contact. 19.
Bādarāyaṇi said:
Having thus praised Hari along with Īśa, Śatadhṛti, stationed in the sky, bowed down to Govinda and addressed him. 20.
Brahmā said:
O Lord, O Soul of all, you were previously requested by us for the purpose of removing the earth's burden; that has now been accomplished exactly as intended.
And by you, who are true to your promise, dharma has indeed been established among the virtuous, and your fame, which removes the impurity of all the worlds, has been spread in every direction. 22.
Having descended into the lineage of Yadu and assuming a form of unsurpassed beauty, you performed deeds of unrestrained power for the welfare of the world. 23.
O Lord, those virtuous men in the Kali age who hear and proclaim your deeds shall easily cross over the darkness. 24.
O Puruṣottama, O Lord, one hundred and twenty-five autumns have passed since You descended into the Yadu lineage.
Now there remains no further task for you, the support of all, to accomplish for the sake of the gods;
moreover, this lineage has become almost entirely ruined by the curse of the brahmins. (26)
Therefore, enter your own supreme abode if you so desire;
protect us, the world-protectors of Vaikuṇṭha, along with our respective worlds. ||27||
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Lord of the gods, I have understood what you have said;
your entire task has been accomplished, and the burden of the earth has been removed."
This very Yadava clan, exalted by the glory of its prowess and heroism, desiring to seize the world, is held back by me as the great ocean is restrained by the shore. (29)
If I depart without having subdued this vast clan of the haughty Yadus, this world will perish because of their overflowing arrogance. (30)
"Now the destruction of my lineage has begun due to the curse of the twice-born;
O sinless Brahmin, I shall go to my own abode, for this [lineage] will not endure until your end. (31)
Śrī Śuka said:
Having been addressed thus by the Lord of the World, the self-born Brahmā, the god, prostrated before Him and, together with the hosts of deities, returned to his own abode. 32.
Then, having observed those great portents that had arisen in Dvāravatī,
the Blessed One spoke to the assembled elders of the Yadu clan.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Indeed, these very great portents are arising here on all sides;
moreover, there was an inescapable curse upon our lineage from the Brahmins. (34)
"Noble sirs, we who wish to live must not remain here;
let us go this very day to the exceedingly great and meritorious Prabhāsa, without delay. (35)
Having bathed there, the lord of stars (the Moon), who had been seized by consumption due to Dakṣa’s curse, was instantly liberated from that taint and regained his full splendor once more. ||36||
And we, having bathed therein and gratified the ancestors and the gods,
fed the learned Brahmins with various kinds of excellent food.
Having sown great gifts with faith into these worthy recipients, we shall indeed cross over our sins by means of those gifts, just as one crosses the ocean by means of boats. (38)
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus instructed by the Blessed One, O delighter of the clan, the Yādavas set their minds on departing for the sacred ford and harnessed their chariots. 39.
Having observed that, O King, and having heard what was spoken by the Blessed One, Uddhava—who was ever devoted to Kṛṣṇa—beheld those terrible portents. ||40||
Having approached the Lord of the lords of the worlds in solitude, he bowed his head at the feet of the Master and, with palms joined in reverence, addressed him. (41)
Uddhava said:
O Lord of the gods of gods, O Lord of yoga, whose hearing and glorification are meritorious!
Having surely withdrawn this lineage, you will surely abandon the world.
Even if the Lord were capable, he did not counteract the Brahmin’s curse. ||42||
O Keśava, O Lord, I do not have the heart to abandon the lotus of your feet even for half a moment;
lead me as well to your own abode. 43.
O Kṛṣṇa, having tasted the nectar for the ears of Your divine play, which is the supreme auspiciousness for men, people abandon all longing for anything else. 44.
In lying down, sitting, walking, standing, bathing, playing, eating, and so forth—how could we, your devotees, ever abandon you, our beloved self? (45)
May we conquer your illusion—you whose servants eat your leftovers and are adorned with the garlands, perfumes, garments, and ornaments you have used. 46.
Those sages who subsist on air, the ascetics who churn the upper regions, those peaceful renunciants free from impurity—they attain the abode known as Brahman. 47.
But we here, O Great Yogin, wandering upon the paths of karma, shall cross over the darkness difficult to traverse by means of your news and those who belong to you. 48.
Remembering and proclaiming his deeds and his words—his gait, smiles, glances, and playful jests—which were a mere imitation of the ways of the world of men; 49.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus addressed, O King, the Blessed Lord, the son of Devakī, spoke to His dear servant Uddhava, who was solely devoted to Him. 50.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Devotion of the Gods and the Submission of Uddhava," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
O highly fortunate one, that which you have spoken to me is indeed what I desire to do.
Brahmā, Bhava, and the world-protectors desire heaven-dwelling for me.
Indeed, I have here completely accomplished the work of the gods for which purpose I descended with a portion [of my essence], as requested by Brahmā. ||2||
"The family, consumed by the curse, shall perish through mutual strife;
on the seventh day, the ocean will submerge both this city and them."
For this world which has been abandoned by me,
O virtuous one, will soon become devoid of all auspiciousness and will be cast out by the Kali age.
"You must not dwell here on this earth once it has been abandoned by me;
O gentle one, in the Kali age, people will take delight in unrighteousness. (5)
But you, having renounced all affection for your kinsmen and relatives,
and having properly fixed your mind on me, wander the earth with an even eye.
Know that whatever is perceived by the mind, by speech, by the eyes, by hearing, and so forth— all that which is perishable— is composed of illusion and the mind.
For a man who is not disciplined, there is delusion regarding the manifold objects of the senses; he partakes in both virtue and vice.
The distinctions between "action," "inaction," and "mis-action" arise from the perception of virtue and vice. 8.
Therefore, with the group of senses restrained and the mind composed, behold this world within yourself, and behold yourself within me, the Supreme Lord. 9.
Endowed with both knowledge and discernment, you have become the very self of all embodied beings;
with a self satisfied by the experience of the Self, you are not obstructed by obstacles. 10.

Perceiving both as defects, he transcends them; through negation he does not turn back from the world, yet through perceiving it as a quality he does not perform what is prescribed, just like a child.
A friend to all beings, tranquil, and certain in his knowledge and realization, he who perceives the entire universe as consisting of me shall never again fall into calamity. 12.
Śrī Śuka said: Thus instructed by the Blessed One, O King, Uddhava, the great devotee, desiring to know the truth, prostrated himself and spoke to Acyuta.
Uddhava said:
O Lord of Yoga, O Knower of the yoga of renunciation, O Soul of Yoga, O Source of Yoga!
For my ultimate liberation, you have explained renunciation characterized by total relinquishment. (14)
O Infinite One, this renunciation of desires is difficult for those whose selves are attached to sense objects;
it is even more difficult for those who lack devotion to You, the Soul of all—this is my conviction. 15.
Thus, with a deluded mind deeply immersed by Your Māyā in this self and its adjuncts—which are fashioned by You—I think "this is I" and "I am mine.
O Blessed One, please instruct Your servant as to how I may correctly accomplish that which has been succinctly described by You.
O Lord, among even the wise, I do not see anyone other than Yourself—who are Truth, self-perceiving, and the Self—capable of describing You.
All these embodied beings, from Brahmā downwards, have their intellects deluded by Your Māyā; they perceive external objects as having real existence.

Therefore, with a weary mind and scorched by the afflictions of worldly existence, I take refuge in You—Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nara, the blameless one, infinite and boundless, the omniscient Lord whose abode is unimpeded and inviolable. ||18||
The Blessed Lord said:
Generally, those men in the world who are discerning of the true nature of the world uplift themselves by their own selves from an inauspicious disposition. (19)
For a person, especially, the self alone is its own teacher, since it attains what is beneficial through direct perception and inference. (20)
And in my form as the Puruṣa, the wise, who are experts in Sāṅkhya and Yoga, behold me most clearly, augmented by all powers. 21.
There are many cities created with one, two, three, four, or many feet, as well as those that are footless; among them, my city Pauruṣī is the most dear to me. ||22||
Here, those who are diligent truly seek me, the Lord, by means of logical reasons—inferring through perceivable qualities and signs that which cannot be grasped by direct perception. (23)
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history:
the conversation between Avadhūta and Yadu of immeasurable splendor.
Having observed a certain young Avadhūta, a twice-born sage wandering about fearless from any quarter, Yadu, who was conversant with dharma, questioned that seer.
Yadu said:
O Brahmana, from where has this highly proficient intellect come to you, who are yourself a non-doer, having attained which you, though a learned man, move through the world like a child? (26)
Generally, human beings strive for virtue, wealth, pleasure, and the desire for knowledge, as well as for longevity, fame, and prosperity, solely by means of a specific cause. 27.
But you are wise, learned, skillful, fortunate, and a speaker of immortal truths;
yet you do nothing and desire nothing, like one who is dull-witted, insane, or a ghost. ||28||
While people are being consumed by the forest fire of desire and greed,
you do not feel the heat, like an elephant standing in the waters of the Ganges, released from the fire.
O Brahmin, please tell us who inquire of you the cause of bliss within the self—bliss belonging to you, the absolute Self, which is devoid of touch. 30.
The Blessed Lord said:
Thus questioned and honored by the highly fortunate Yadu, who was devoted to Brahman and possessed of great wisdom, the twice-born sage spoke to him as he stood bowed in humility. (31)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O King, I have many teachers whom I have taken refuge in through my intellect;
having acquired wisdom from them, I wander here as one liberated. Listen to them. (32)
Earth, wind, space, water, fire, the moon, the sun, the pigeon, the python, the ocean, the moth, the honeybee, and the elephant. (33)
The honey-thief, the deer, the fish, the tawny one, the osprey, the child, the maiden, the reed-maker, the serpent, the spider, and the weaver of fine cloth. ||34||
O King, these twenty-four who have resorted to me are my gurus; from them I have here learned for myself the teachings and modes of conduct. ||35||
Therefore, O tiger among men, listen as I tell you exactly what I am teaching and how, O son of Nahuṣa. (36)
Even when assailed by elemental beings who follow the power of destiny, the wise man, knowing this, should not deviate from his path; such was the vow I learned from the Earth.

Ever intent on the welfare of others in all endeavors, with the sole possibility of acting for the sake of others, the virtuous man, like a mountain-pupil of the king, should train himself in identifying with others as his own self. 38.
The sage should be content with the mere function of sustaining life, and never with the objects dear to the senses;
he should act so that his knowledge does not perish, nor do his speech and mind become scattered. (39)
Entering into various objects and manifold phenomena from all sides, the yogi whose self is free from qualities and defects should not become attached, like the wind. 40.
Having entered here into earthly bodies, the yogi who perceives the Self is supported by those qualities yet is not joined with them, just as the wind is not joined with odors. ||41||

The sage should contemplate the nature of the pervasive sky-like Self—immanent within all moving and stationary beings through its identity with Brahman and its universal connection—as being free from limitations and unattached. 42.

Just as the sky is not touched by the entities consisting of fire, water, and earth—such as clouds and the like—when impelled by the wind, so too the person (puruṣa) is not touched by the qualities (guṇas) created by time. 43.
Pure by nature, gentle, sweet, and a source of sanctity for men, the sage—who is a friend of the waters—purifies through his sight, touch, and praise. 44.
Radiant and blazing with ascetic power, that invincible vessel of the stomach,
though consuming all things, remains self-disciplined and does not take on impurity, just like fire.
In some places he is hidden and in others manifest; he is to be worshipped by those desiring the highest good.
He partakes everywhere of the offerings of his givers, burning away their prior and subsequent misfortune. 46.

The all-pervading Lord, having entered this universe created by His own Māyā—which is characterized by both the existent and the non-existent—is perceived in various forms, like fire within fuel. ||47||
The states beginning with emission and ending with the cremation ground belong to the body, not to the self,
just as the phases of the moon occur through time by its unmanifest path.

For indeed, by the force of the current of time, even the origin and destruction of beings are not perceived as eternal, just as the flames of a fire are not seen [as permanent] by the fire itself. ||49||
The yogi takes up the qualities through the qualities and relinquishes them at the proper time;
he does not become attached to them, just as the lord of cows is not bound by the cows. ||50||
Established in manifestation as if residing therein, it is perceived by those of gross intellect through its own differentiation; yet the Self remains like the sun. //51//
One should not form excessive attachment or intimacy with anyone anywhere;
by doing so, one incurs suffering like the foolish-minded pigeon. 52.
A certain pigeon, having built a nest in a tree in the forest, lived there for several years together with his wife, a female pigeon. ||53||
The two pigeons, their hearts overflowing with affection as householders, bound themselves together—eye with eye, limb with limb, and mind with mind. (54)
Having become a couple, they moved with confidence through the forest groves, engaged in lying down, sitting, walking, standing, conversation, play, eating, and other such activities. (55)
O King, whatever she desired, being moved by compassion, she fulfilled that very wish for him, even though he had not conquered his senses and did so with great difficulty. (56)
When the proper time had arrived, the female dove conceived her first pregnancy;
being faithful to her husband, she laid her eggs in the nest in his presence.
At those times, they were born with the limbs of Hari already formed,
their delicate bodies and hair produced by his inconceivable powers.
The couple, affectionate toward their children, reared their offspring with joy;
they were filled with delight as they listened to their warbling, soothed by those sweet, soft-voiced utterances.
Through their soft-feeling wings, their warbling, their charming movements,
and their welcoming advances, those noble birds brought joy to their parents.
With their hearts bound by affection for one another, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu,
those two of feeble intellect nurtured their children and progeny.
Once, those two householders went out for the sake of food for them;
seeking alms, they wandered for a long time throughout that forest. (62)
Then, by chance, a certain forest-dwelling hunter saw them as they were moving about near their own dwelling after having spread out their net, and he seized it. (63)
The male pigeon and the female pigeon, ever eager to nourish their offspring, went out to gather food and returned to their own nest. (64)
Seeing her own young offspring ensnared in the net, the female pigeon, crying out as they cried out, ran toward them in great distress. (65)

Repeatedly overcome by affection and with a distressed mind, she was herself bound by the snare of her own delusion; though seeing those who were already bound, she remained devoid of right mindfulness.
And the dove, distressed and deeply afflicted by grief, lamented for his sons— who were dearer to him than himself and had been bound— as well as for his wife, who was equal to himself.
Alas! Behold my downfall, I who am of little merit and evil intellect;
unsatiated and with my purpose unfulfilled, my home—its threefold aims destroyed—is ruined. (68)
My wife, who was so worthy and devoted to her husband as a deity, has abandoned me in this empty house and ascended to heaven along with her virtuous sons. (69)
Such as I am, wretched in an empty house, with my wife dead and my children dead—why should I wish to live, separated from all and leading a life of misery? (70)
Seeing them thus enveloped by the snakes, seized by death, and writhing, the ignorant man himself, though wretched and seeking instruction, fell down. ||71||
Having obtained that householder pigeon— the male pigeon, the female pigeon, and the young pigeons— the cruel hunter,
his purpose accomplished, departed for home.
Thus, the householder whose self is unpeaceful and who delights in dualities falls like the three [who fell];
nurturing his family, he, being wretched and bound by attachments, comes to ruin. ||73||
He who, having attained the human world— the open gateway to liberation—
is attached to household life like a bird in a cage, is known as one who has fallen after having ascended.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Legend of Yadu’s Daughter-in-law," within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava, in the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, the compendium of the Paramahaṃsas.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
O King, the pleasure derived from the senses, as well as heaven and even hell, are all forms of suffering for the embodied soul; therefore, the wise do not desire them. (1)
Whether it be well-prepared or tasteless, large or even small, let the one who is like a python, free from action, swallow whatever morsel falls to him by chance. (2)
He should lie for many days without food and without exertion;
if a morsel of food does not come to him, let him remain like a great serpent, subsisting on destiny alone.
Even one possessed of the senses, though endowed with vigor, stamina, and strength, would not desire to maintain a body free from activity while lying down and devoid of sleep. ||4||
The Sage is serene and profound, difficult to fathom and difficult to surpass;
indeed, he is infinite and boundless, as unshakeable as an ocean with still waters. ||5||
Whether his desires are fulfilled or diminished, the sage who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa neither swells nor withers, just as the ocean is not affected by rivers.
Having seen a woman who is a divine illusion, one whose senses are unsubdued and who is enticed by her charms falls into blinding darkness like a moth into a fire. (7)
A fool, deluded by women, gold ornaments, garments, and other objects created by illusion, his mind enticed by the thought of enjoyment, perishes like a moth, his vision destroyed. (8)
The sage should swallow his food bit by bit, just enough to sustain the body; he should dwell in houses without causing injury and adopt the "bee-like" mode of livelihood. 9.
A skillful man should extract the essence from all treatises, whether they be small or great, just as a bee gathers honey from flowers. ||10||
He should not accumulate alms for the evening or for the morrow;
having his hand as his bowl and his belly as his vessel, he should not hoard like a fly.
A mendicant should not store provisions for the evening or for the morrow;
by storing them like flies, he perishes along with them. 12.
A monk should not touch even a young woman made of wood;
by touching her, he would be bound like an elephant that has come into physical contact with a female elephant. ||13||
A wise man should never approach a woman, for he might meet his own death;
he could be slain by those superior in strength, just as one elephant is slain by other elephants. 14.
That which has been accumulated with difficulty by the greedy should neither be given away nor enjoyed;
yet even that, another enjoys—just as one who knows the value of wealth consumes the honey, while the honey-maker [perishes]. 15.
While those who hope for household blessings enjoy wealth acquired through pleasure and pain, the ascetic indeed eats before them, like a honeybee. 16.
A forest-dwelling ascetic should never listen to vulgar songs; otherwise, he might be caught like the deer who was ensnared by the hunter’s song. 17.
Delighting in the dances, instrumental music, and songs of village women, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, the son of a deer, became their plaything and remained under their control. ||18||
Deluded by taste through the tongue that causes excessive agitation, a person of unwholesome intellect meets death, just as a fish is caught by hooks. ||19||
Wise men who abstain from food quickly conquer the senses;
however, with the exception of the tongue, those [senses] increase in one who is without food. ||20||
A man cannot be said to have conquered his senses until he has mastered the sense of taste;
for when taste is conquered, everything is conquered. (21)
In former times, there was a courtesan named Piṅgalā in the city of Videha;
O prince, learn from me that which I have learned from her. 22.
One day, that wanton woman, intending to bring her lover to the rendezvous,
appeared at the outer gate at the appointed time, wearing a most excellent form.
Seeing those wealthy and handsome men coming along the road, O bull among men, she regarded them as seekers of wealth who had paid their toll.
As they arrived and departed, she who lived by assignations thought:
"Perhaps some other wealthy man, a liberal giver, will come to me. (25)
Thus, with her hopes shattered and deprived of sleep, she remained leaning against the door;
going out and coming in, the night passed away for her.
As her face withered from the desire for wealth and her mind became dejected, a supreme sense of world-weariness arose within her— a source of anxiety that yet brought her peace.
Listen to the song of her whose heart was filled with world-weariness, just as it was mine;
for world-weariness is like a sword to a man for severing the bonds of hope. (28)

For one who has not developed detachment toward the constituents of existence does not seek to abandon the bondage of the body, just as a man devoid of wisdom, O King, clings to the sense of "mine. 29.
Piṅgalā said:
"Alas! Behold the expansion of my delusion, I who have not conquered myself;
for like a fool, I desire passion from an unreal lover. (30)

Forsaking this peaceful one who dwells nearby—He who is delightful, the bestower of joy, and the eternal giver of wealth—I, ignorant, worship that which is trivial, devoid of desire, and the source of suffering, fear, grief, and delusion. (31)
Alas! I have needlessly tormented myself with a life of conventional social conduct and highly censurable pursuits;
I am pitiable, craving wealth from men who are themselves slaves to women, and seeking my own pleasure through that which has been purchased. 32.

What other house could I resort to than this one, constructed with bones as its rafters and beams, bound together by skin, hair, and nails, possessing nine leaking doors, and filled with feces and urine? 33.
Indeed, in this city of the Videhas, I alone am of deluded intellect,
for I desire from another— though he is not real— the fulfillment of my desires from that Imperishable One who bestows his very self.
He is the dearest friend, the Lord, and the very self of all embodied beings;
having sold Him by means of my own self, I shall delight with Him as Lakṣmī does.

How much do those desires that grant objects of longing truly delight you—desires that, like gods or human beings, have both a beginning and an end, and are driven away by Time, even as they were once held by one's wife? (36)
Surely the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is pleased with me for some deed;
for this disillusionment with my wicked desires has arisen within me, bringing me happiness. (37)
Let not such afflictions, which cause despondency, befall this unfortunate woman;
for by casting off the continuity of worldly existence, a person attains peace. (38)
Taking to heart the favor he has bestowed, and casting off all base attachments and evil desires, I go for refuge to that Supreme Lord. (39)
Contented and placing my faith in this, I live according to whatever comes to me; indeed, I dwell with this very Self as my companion. 40.
Who else is capable of rescuing this self, fallen into the well of saṃsāra, its vision stolen by sense-objects, and seized by the serpent of Time? (41)
For the self alone is the protector of the self; one should become weary of everything when, being vigilant, one perceives this world devoured by the serpent of time. 42.
The Brahmin said:
With her mind thus resolved, she cut through that wicked hope born of her longing for her husband and, taking refuge in tranquility, sat down upon her bed. 43.
For hope is the supreme suffering, and freedom from hope is the supreme happiness;
just as Piṅgalā, having utterly severed her hope for her beloved, slept in peace. 44.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Piṅgalā," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the great Purāṇa, in the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||8||
Now begins the ninth chapter.
The Brahmin said:
"Indeed, whatever is most dear to men, that very thing leads to suffering when it is acquired."
But that wise man who possesses nothing attains infinite happiness. ||1||
The powerful birds, being free from desire for meat, slew the osprey who was possessed by it;
having abandoned that meat, he attained happiness. ||2||
I have neither pride nor humiliation, nor do I have the anxieties of those who possess homes and children;
sporting in the self and delighting in the self, I wander here like a child. ||3||
Only two are liberated from anxiety and immersed in supreme bliss:
he who is deluded, inert, and childish, and he who has gone beyond the qualities (guṇas). ||4||
In some places, when her kinsmen had departed, a maiden herself received those who had come to her house seeking her hand in marriage and honored them.
O King, as she was pounding rice grains in secret for their consumption,
the conch shells resting on her forearms produced a loud sound.
Considering that act loathsome, she was then greatly ashamed;
she broke the conch shells one by one, leaving only two remaining in each hand. ||7||
A sound indeed arose from both as she struck the two conchs;
yet there, one was pierced, and from the other no sound emerged. ||8||
O subduer of enemies, while wandering through these worlds with a desire to know the true nature of the world, I followed this instruction of hers.
Among many there will be strife; even between two there is talk.
Therefore, one should wander alone, like the single bangle of a maiden. (10)
With breath controlled and posture mastered, one should, remaining unwearied, join the mind to a single point through the yoga of dispassion and practice, holding it steady. ||11||

When the mind has found its footing therein and gradually sheds the dust of karma, it—having shaken off passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas) through the growth of goodness (sattva)—attains the fuel-less state of Nirvana. ||12||
Thus, with his mind absorbed in the Self, he perceived nothing at all, whether external or internal;
just as the arrow-maker, whose soul was fixed on the arrow, did not see the king passing by his side. ||13||
He should dwell alone in a hermitage, vigilant, dwelling in a cave;
unobserved in his conduct, a silent sage, speaking but little. 14.
The undertaking of building a house leads to extreme suffering and is fruitless for one whose self is impermanent;
yet a snake, having entered a dwelling made by another, prospers in happiness. ||15||
At the end of the kalpa, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the sole deity, having withdrawn by means of his own māyā this previously created universe through the movement of time, [remains alone]. ||16||
He alone existed without a second, self-supported and the refuge of all;
when his powers—sattva and the others—had been brought to equilibrium by time through his own power, he became the Puruṣa, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa. ||17||
He who is designated as Kaivalya (isolation) dwells as the supreme among the high and the low;
he is a mass of the bliss of absolute experience, free from all limiting conditions. 18.
O subduer of enemies, at the beginning, by the power of his own pure self, agitating his own māyā which consists of the three guṇas, he creates through it the *sūtra*. 19.
They call her the manifestation of the three qualities, creating [the world] with faces on all sides;
that in which this entire universe is woven and by which the person transmigrates. 20.
Just as a spider, having extended a thread from its heart and from its mouth, sports with it and then swallows it again, so too does Maheśvara. 21.
Wherever the embodied soul holds the mind fixed with its intellect—whether out of affection, hatred, or even fear—it attains the very form of that object. 22.
O King, a worm that enters a wall made by a weaver while meditating upon it attains the very nature of that wall, without abandoning its former form. 23.
Thus has this wisdom been learned by me from these gurus;
O Lord, hear me as I speak of the understanding I have cultivated within my own self. 24.

This body of mine is heavy, yet it is the cause of my detachment and discernment; though it constantly bears the sun of intense suffering and brings about the destruction of its own essence, I contemplate the principles of reality through it in whatever way possible, and having resolved that it belongs to others, I wander free from attachment. (25)
He nourishes his wife, children, wealth, cattle, servants, home, and circle of kinsmen by extending himself, desiring to do what is pleasing to them.
Having accumulated wealth with great effort within his heart, that body, having produced its seed, perishes according to the nature of a tree. ||26||
The tongue drags one way; thirst and the genitals another; the skin, the belly, and the ear from here and there;
the nose from yet another direction; and the fickle eye and the power of action elsewhere—like many co-wives, they tear at the master of the house. (27)
