Having formerly created various cities by means of his own power, Aja, with trees, reptiles, beasts, birds, gadflies, and fish,
the god Brahmā, his heart not yet satisfied by them, fashioned Puruṣa— whose intellect is directed toward the vision of Brahman— and thereby attained joy.

Having obtained this human birth—which is extremely difficult to attain at the end of many existences, though it is impermanent even here—the wise man should strive quickly before death overtakes him; for as long as one has the capacity, one must indeed apply oneself in every way toward the supreme good. (29)
Thus, having become free from passion, with the light of discernment within myself, I wander this earth, liberated from attachment and devoid of egoism. (30)
For knowledge cannot be firmly established or fully perfected from a single teacher;
this non-dual Brahman is indeed proclaimed in many ways by the seers. ||31||
The Blessed Lord said:
Having spoken thus and taking leave of Yadu, that sage of profound intellect,
saluted and entreated by the king, departed contentedly as he had come.
Having heard the words of Avadhūta, that ancestor of ours, our forefather, became liberated from all attachments and possessed a mind of equanimity. ||33||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Uddhava," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the great Purāṇa, within the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||9||
Now begins the tenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"One who is attentive to their own duties as declared by Me, and who takes refuge in Me,"
One whose mind is free from desire should practice the conduct appropriate to one's caste, stage of life, and family.
With a purified soul, he should investigate through meditation on reality the failure of all undertakings among embodied beings whose minds are fixed on sense objects. ||2||

Just as the perception of objects by one who is asleep, or the mental construction of one who is meditating, is fruitless because it lacks manifoldness, so too is the cognition of the Self as differentiated through the qualities (guṇas). ||3||
One who is devoted to Me should abandon active worldly action and practice renounced action;
one who has set out in the pursuit of knowledge should not heed the injunctions to perform ritual action. 4.
One who is devoted to Me should occasionally practice the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) repeatedly;
he should attend upon a peaceful guru who knows Me and whose very self is Me. ||5||

Free from pride and envy, skillful, devoid of possessiveness, firm in friendship, unhurried, desirous of knowing the truth, free from malice, and one whose word is never in vain—[he should be such a person]. (6)
Remaining indifferent toward wife, children, home, fields, kinsmen, wealth, and so forth,
he looks upon all things with equanimity as if they were his own self-interest.
The Self, the seer and self-luminous, is distinct from the gross and subtle body;
it is like fire, which is distinct from the wood that is to be burned, being both the burner and the illuminator. ||8||
Having entered within, the Supreme One bestows upon the body its qualities—cessation, origination, minuteness, magnitude, diversity, and those qualities produced by them. 9.
This body, which is indeed composed of the qualities (guṇas), belongs to the person;
this worldly existence (saṃsāra) is its bondage for the man who knows the Self through discernment. 10.
Therefore, through inquiry, having united with the supreme Self abiding within the self, one should gradually eliminate this perception of [the world as] a substantial reality. ||11||
The teacher shall be the lower kindling wood (araṇi), and the pupil the upper kindling wood;
their union is the oral instruction, and the resulting knowledge is the blissful junction. 12.
That wisdom, born of fearlessness and exceedingly pure, shakes off the illusion produced by the qualities (guṇas);
and having consumed the qualities themselves, it becomes extinguished of its own accord, like a fire without fuel. ||13||
Now, [there arises the inquiry] regarding the diversity and the eternity of these selves— the agents of action, the enjoyers of pleasure and pain, and those who come from the world and time.
You think that the configuration of all entities is indeed innate;
yet, according to the distinction of each particular form, the cognition arises and differs accordingly. (15)
Thus, my dear friend, for all embodied beings, by virtue of their connection with a body, states such as birth and so forth occur repeatedly through the divisions of time. (16)
Here too, the lack of independence of the agent of actions is observed;
and for the experiencer of pleasure and pain, what meaningful purpose could there be in one who is subject to helplessness? (17)
Not even for the wise is there any happiness for embodied beings;
likewise, suffering belongs to the deluded, for egoism is utterly in vain. 18.
Even those who know the attainment and the obstruction of pleasure and pain do not truly know Yoga, by which death might have no power over them. ||19||
What is the true meaning [of this]? Does desire bring him happiness, or is death near?
For one being led to the place of execution, it is surely death that awaits him, not satisfaction. ||20||
And what is heard is as flawed as what is seen; it is marred by rivalry, envy, and losses through calamities.
Because desire involves many obstacles, it is as fruitless as farming.
If dharma is well-practiced and remains unimpeded by obstacles, listen now to how one goes to the station conquered by that very practice. ||22||
Having worshipped the deities here with sacrifices, the performer of sacrifice goes to the heavenly world;
there he shall enjoy divine pleasures, earned by his own merit, like a god. (23)
In a bright celestial chariot acquired through his own merit,
he is praised by Gandharvas as he sports in the midst of goddesses, wearing attire that captivates their hearts.
Sporting with women on pleasure-vehicles adorned with networks of tinkling bells, he did not perceive his own downfall, being absorbed in the delights of the celestial groves. ||25||
One rejoices in heaven for as long as one's merit is not exhausted;
when merit is spent, one falls back down, driven by time and even against one's will. (26)

If one is devoted to unrighteousness due to association with the wicked, or if he has no control over his senses, being full of lust, miserable, greedy, addicted to women, and a harmer of living beings; ||27||
Having sacrificed animals according to improper rites and worshipping hosts of spirits and ghosts, a living being goes helplessly to the hells and then enters into blinding darkness. ||28||
Performing actions that result in future suffering, he again assumes a body through them;
in that state, what happiness can there be for one subject to mortality? (29)
The worlds and the world-protectors who live for a kalpa have fear of me;
even Brahmā, whose life lasts for two parārdhas, has fear of me.
The qualities (guṇas) produce actions; the quality follows after the qualities.
But the individual soul (jīva), conjoined with the qualities, experiences the fruits of those actions. 31.
As long as there is an inequality of qualities, so long does the multiplicity of the Self exist;
indeed, as long as there is multiplicity of the Self, so long is there dependence. (32)
As long as there is a lack of independence for him, so long will there be fear of the Lord;
those who worship this [world] become deluded and are overwhelmed by grief. ||33||
"When there is a transformation of the qualities (guṇas), they speak of me in many ways as Time, the Self, the Scripture, the World, Nature, and indeed Dharma. (34)
Uddhava said: O Lord, although the embodied soul exists within the qualities born of the body, it remains unenveloped by them; how then is it bound by the qualities, or why is it bound at all? 35.
How should he conduct himself and dwell? By what characteristics should he be known? What should he eat, or what should he renounce? Should he lie down, sit, or go about? (36)
O Acyuta, best among those who know how to answer questions, tell me this:
is one eternally liberated or eternally bound? This is my confusion. (37)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Uddhava," in the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, within the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||10||
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"The designations 'bound' and 'liberated' are due to my qualities (guṇas), not in reality."
Since the quality (guṇa) is rooted in Māyā, for me there is neither liberation nor bondage. ||1||
Through Māyā, grief and delusion, pleasure and pain, and the assumption of a body appear to the Self like a dream; this cycle of worldly existence is not, however, real. ||2||
"Know, O Uddhava, that knowledge and ignorance are my two primary forms for embodied beings;
they cause liberation and bondage, and are fashioned by my Māyā. (3)
O Mahāmati, for this very soul, which is but a portion of me, bondage is beginningless through ignorance, and likewise, its opposite [liberation] is through knowledge. 4.
Now, O dear one, I shall describe to you the distinction between the bound and the liberated, which possess contradictory attributes while abiding in a single substratum. (5)
These two birds are similar and friends; by chance, they have built their nests upon a tree.
One of them eats the fruit of the *pippala* tree, while the other remains without food, yet he is greater in strength. (6)
The learned Pippalāda knew both himself and the other, but not so did Pippalāda.
He who is joined with ignorance is eternally bound; he who consists of knowledge is eternally liberated. (7)
Though situated in the body, the wise man is not situated in the body, like one who has awakened from a dream;
though not situated in the body, the person of dull intellect is situated in the body, like a dreamer. 8.
When the senses are engaged with their objects, and the qualities with the qualities, the wise man who is changeless should not form the notion of "I. ||9||
While this body is dependent on destiny, the ignorant person, acting through action which is itself a product of the gunas, becomes bound by the thought, "I am the doer. (10)
Thus detached, he remains indifferent toward lying down, sitting, walking, and bathing, as well as toward seeing, touching, smelling, eating, hearing, and so forth. (11)

The wise man, though engaged with the qualities in their various manifestations, is not bound in that way, for he remains unattached even while situated in nature, like the sky, the sun, and the wind. 12.
Through the vision of fearlessness and the sharpness of non-attachment, with all doubts severed, he turns away from manifoldness like one awakened from a dream. (13)

He whose functions of the vital breath, the senses, the mind, and the intellect are free from all volitional constructs is indeed liberated from those qualities, even while remaining within the body. ||14||
For the wise man is not disturbed by whatever is harmed or honored toward his self by others through violence or by chance in any circumstance. ||15||
A sage who possesses equanimity and is free from both merit and fault neither praises nor blames one who performs either good or evil deeds, nor one who speaks of them. 16.
He should do nothing, say nothing, and think neither of what is good nor of what is bad;
delighting in the Self through this mode of conduct, the sage should move about like one who is dull-witted. 17.
If one who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound does not dive into the Supreme, his labor bears fruit only as labor, like that of one who guards a barren cow. 18.

O dear one, he who protects a cow that yields no milk, an unfaithful wife, a body dependent on others, worthless offspring, wealth that has not been offered at sacred fords, and speech devoid of me, suffers misery upon misery. (19)

O dear one, that age in which my purifying activity—consisting of the maintenance, creation, and cessation of this world, or my birth through desired incarnations—is not found, a wise man would not bear such barren speech. ||20||
Thus, having dispelled the delusion of manifoldness within the self through inquiry, one should bring the stainless mind to rest by offering it to Me, who am all-pervading. 21.
If you are unable to hold the mind steady upon Brahman,
then perform all actions for Me, free from desire for their fruits.
Full of faith, listening to my stories which are auspicious and purify the worlds, he sang, recollected my deeds, and repeatedly enacted them. ||23||
O Uddhava, one who, relying on Me, practices virtue, pleasure, and wealth for My sake, attains unwavering devotion to Me, the eternal. 24.
Worshipping Me with devotion acquired through the company of the virtuous, he indeed attains directly that state which has been revealed by the wise. ||25||
Uddhava said:
O Lord, O You of excellent renown, what kind of person is considered virtuous by You?
And what kind of devotion toward You is practiced and honored by the righteous? (26)
O Overseer of Men, O Overseer of the World, O Lord of the Universe—let this be told to me, who am bowed down, devoted, and have sought refuge in you. (27)
You are the Supreme Brahman, the infinite ether, the Puruṣa beyond primordial nature;
O Blessed One, you have descended, having assumed a distinct form by your own will. (28)
The Blessed One said:
He is compassionate, free from malice toward others, patient with all embodied beings, whose essence is truth, whose nature is irreproachable, equanimous, and a benefactor to all. (29)

One whose intellect is unassailed by desires, self-controlled, gentle, pure, possessing nothing, free from worldly effort, moderate in diet, tranquil, steadfast, and a sage who has taken refuge in Me—[such a one attains peace]. ||30||
He was vigilant, profound in soul, steadfast, and had conquered the six internal enemies; he was free from pride yet bestower of honor, disciplined, friendly, compassionate, and wise.
Having thus understood both the virtues and the faults, he who, even after abandoning all the duties prescribed by me for himself, should worship me—he is the most excellent of beings. (32)
Whether they know Me or do not know Me, those who worship Me with undivided devotion—however great I am, and who I am, and of what nature—I consider them to be My most devoted. 33.
Beholding, touching, and worshipping the Linga of Malli;
serving it, praising it, and proclaiming its humble qualities and deeds. (34)
O Uddhava, faith in hearing My stories, meditation upon Me, the offering of all gains, and the surrender of oneself through service—these constitute devotion. (35)
The narration of the story of my birth and deeds, the celebration of my festival, and festivals in my home with songs, tāṇḍava dances, musical instruments, and assemblies [are my worship]. 36.
Pilgrimages and the performance of bali offerings during all annual festivals, Vedic and Tantric initiation, and the observance of my vows; ||37||
I have faith in the establishment of my worship, and I shall exert myself by uniting with others in the work of building gardens, groves, pleasure-grounds, cities, and palaces. (38)
Serving my household with sincerity, like a slave, by means of sweeping, smearing, sprinkling water, and drawing decorative circles. (39)
Humility, freedom from hypocrisy, and not proclaiming one's own deeds;
he would not even use the light of a lamp offered to him. 40.
Whatever is most desired in the world, and whatever is exceedingly dear to oneself—that one should offer to Me; that conduces to infinity.
The Sun, Agni, the Brāhmaṇa, the cows, Vaiṣṇava, the ether, the Maruts, water, the earth, the Self, and all beings—may these be the objects of my auspicious worship. 42.
One should worship me in the sun with the threefold Vidyā, and in the fire with oblations;
likewise, O dear one, the foremost of Brahmins [should worship me] in cows with hospitality consisting of grass and other fodder. 43.

In Vaiṣṇava, [the worship is performed] by honoring kinsmen; in the heart, by steadfastness in meditation; in space, by the primary intellect; in air, by means of substances preceded by water; and in water, by substances preceded by water. ||44||
On the sacrificial ground, with the essences of the mantras and with offerings, one should worship me—the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)—within oneself and within all beings through equanimity. 45.
Meditating upon my form within these sacred seats—four-armed, peaceful, and endowed with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus—one should worship with a concentrated mind. 46.
He who, being composed, worships me alone through his sacrifices and meritorious works, attains true devotion to me and mindfulness of me through service to the virtuous. 47.
O Uddhava, generally there exists no effective means other than the yoga of devotion and the company of the virtuous; for I am the ultimate goal of the righteous. 48.
Now, O delighter of the Yadus, I shall speak this supreme secret to you as you listen; though it is most to be guarded, I shall tell it because you are my servant, friend, and companion. 49.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Elevenfold Mode of Worship," in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava within the Eleventh Book of the glorious Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the collection known as Pāramahaṃsyā Saṃhitā. ||11||
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
Neither yoga, nor sāṅkhya, nor even dharma restrains Me.
Neither Vedic recitation, austerity, renunciation, nor sacrifices, charitable works, or ritual fees [avail him]. ||1||
Vows, sacrifices, Vedic meters, sacred fords, observances, and restraints—association with the virtuous indeed surpasses them all, for it removes attachment to everything, including myself. ||2||
For by association with the virtuous, the Daityas, Yātudhānas, beasts, birds, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Guhyakas [attain excellence]. ||3||
O sinless one, among humans, the Vidyādharas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, women, and those of low birth are of the nature of rajas and tamas in their respective ages. 4.
Many have attained my state, such as Tvaṣṭraka, Kāyādha, and others;
Vṛṣaparvan, Bali, Bāṇa, Maya, and also Vibhīṣaṇa. ||5||
Sugrīva, Hanumān, the bear, the elephant, the vulture, the merchant, the hunter, Kubjā, the cowherd girls in Vraja, the wives of the sacrificers, and others as well. ||6||
They have not studied the multitude of scriptures, nor have they served the greatest of beings;
yet, having neither observed vows nor performed austerities, they have come to me through my grace. ||7||

Indeed, by their pure devotion alone, the cowherd women, the cows, the trees, the deer, and others—beings of dull intellect, serpents, and even perfected beings (siddhas)—have easily attained Me. ||8||
That which one might not attain even through effort by means of yoga, Sāṅkhya, charity, vows, austerity, sacrifices, explanations, Vedic study, or renunciation—[that state is attained here]. ||9||

When I was led to Mathurā along with Rāma by the son of Śvaphalka, those whose hearts were devoted to me, through their deep affection, could find no other source of happiness than the intense longing caused by separation from me. (10)

Those various nights, spent with my most beloved while wandering in Vṛndāvana, passed for them like half a moment; yet, O dear one, when deprived of him, those same nights through Māyā became equal to kalpas. 11.

Those women, their minds bound by attachment to me, did not perceive their own selves, nor that [Supreme Self], nor this world, just as sages in deep meditation do not perceive name and form, or as rivers have entered the waters of the ocean. ||12||
Desirous of me, those women—unaware of my true nature—attained me, the Supreme Brahman, through their attachment to me as a lover and a paramour, by the hundreds of thousands. 13.

Therefore, O Uddhava, casting aside both injunction and counter-injunction, as well as the path of engagement and withdrawal, and both what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard—[abide in Me]. (14)
Come to Me alone as the sole refuge, the Self of all embodied beings; with your whole being, take shelter in Me, and through Me you shall indeed be free from fear from every quarter. 15.
Uddhava said:
O Lord, Master of Yoga, this doubt that arises while hearing Your words does not depart even though it is rooted in the Self, and by it my mind is bewildered. (16)
The Blessed Lord said:

This very living soul (jīva), born from the cavity, having entered the cave by means of the resonance of breath, assumes a subtle form consisting of mind; yet it becomes most gross as measure (mātrā), accent (svara), and phoneme (varṇa). ||17||
Just as fire, the companion of the wind in the sky, though minute when first produced from wood being vigorously churned, is kindled by oblations; even so is this manifestation, my voice. 18.
Thus, speech, the faculty of action, excretion, smell, taste, sight, touch, and hearing;
volition, discernment, and then self-identification—these are the transformations of the thread-like qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas. ||19||
For this living soul (jīva) is threefold, born from the lotus, unmanifest, one, and primordial in age;
yet, with its powers differentiated, it appears as many, just as seeds do when they reach the womb of the earth. ||20||
In whom all this is woven without exception, like a cloth resting upon an expanse of threads;
he is this ancient tree of worldly existence, whose nature is action, which brings forth flowers and fruit. (21)
This tree has two seeds, a hundred roots, three stalks, five trunks, and produces five flavors;
it has ten branches, one single stem, two nests for birds, three bark-layers, and two fruits, and it has entered into the sun. ||22||
Village-dwelling vultures eat one of its fruits, and forest-dwelling vultures eat another;
he who knows that one which is manifold in form, consisting of sacrificial rites and composed of illusion, he truly knows the Veda. 23.
Thus, by serving the guru with single-minded devotion, the wise and vigilant man, having cut through the seat of the individual soul with the sharpened axe of knowledge,
and having realized the Self, should then cast away the weapon.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the great Purāṇa, within the collection known as the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||12||
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are the qualities of the intellect (buddhi), and not of the self (ātman).
One should destroy one of the two beings by means of the other being, for indeed, one being is to be destroyed by means of the very same being.
From sattva, dharma characterized by devotion to Me arises from the matured person;
through sattvic worship, sattva is attained, and from that, dharma proceeds. ||2||
Dharma, which is the supreme increase of sattva, destroys rajas and tamas;
for when both are struck down, unrighteousness (adharma), whose root they are, quickly perishes.
Scripture, water, progeny, place, time, action, birth, meditation, mantra, and ritual refinement—these ten are the causes of excellence. ||4||
Whatever among these the elders proclaim as purely sattvic, that is so;
whatever they censure as tāmasa, that is so; and whatever they disregard as rājasa, that is so. ||5||
A person should cultivate only those things that are characterized by *sattva* for the sake of increasing *sattva*;
from that comes righteousness, from that knowledge, until memory reaches the state of dispelling [all impressions]. (6)
Just as the fire born from the friction of bamboo stalks is extinguished after burning that forest,
so too the body produced by those actions is extinguished when it arises from the reversal of its constituent qualities.
Uddhava said:
Mortals generally know that sense-objects are the very path to calamity;
nevertheless, O Kṛṣṇa, they still enjoy them—how is this so, like dogs, donkeys, and goats? (8)
The Blessed Lord said:

Just as the erroneous notion of "I" arises in the heart of the heedless man, from that the terrible passion (rajas) surges forth, and from that the mind becomes subject to transformation (vaikārika). ||9||
The conceptualization of a mind joined with passion is accompanied by mental construction;
from that, through meditation on the qualities [of objects], desire arises, which is indeed unbearable for one of evil intellect. (10)
Under the sway of desire and with his senses unconquered, he performs actions that result in future suffering,
being utterly deluded by the force of passion (rajas).
Even though he is a man of knowledge, when his intellect is distracted by passion and darkness (tamas), [he acts thus].
Unwearied and yoking the mind, one who perceives faults does not become attached. ||12||
Being vigilant, one should practice application, gradually fixing the mind upon Me;
undiscouraged, at the proper time, having conquered the breath and mastered the posture. ||13||
This much alone is the yoga taught by my disciples, Sanaka and the others, so that, having withdrawn the mind from all things, it is truly absorbed in Me. 14.
Uddhava said: O Keśava, I desire to know that form in which You instructed the yoga to Sanaka and the others. ||15||
The Blessed Lord said:
The sons of Hiraṇyagarbha, Sanaka and the others, who were born of his mind, questioned their father regarding the subtle and absolute goal of yoga. (16)
Sanaka and the others said:
O Lord, the mind enters into the modes of nature, and the modes enter into the mind;
how can there be mutual abandonment for one who desires liberation and seeks to cross beyond them? (17)
The Blessed Lord said: Thus questioned, Mahādeva, the self-born creator of all beings,
though reflecting upon the seed of the question, did not find the answer, for his intellect was fixed on ritual action.
That god thought of me with the desire to cross to the further shore of his questions;
I then went into his presence in the form of a swan.
Having seen me, they approached, paid homage at my feet, and placing Brahmā at their head, asked: "Who are you? (20)
O Uddhava, listen to me as I relate what I said at that time to those sages who questioned me, desiring to know the truth. 21.

O Brahmins, if there is no plurality in the substance of the Self, how could such a question of yours be possible? Or rather, what is the basis for either you as questioners or for me as the speaker? (22)
Since the five elements are identical in their essential nature, the question "Who are you? among you is merely a matter of words and is indeed meaningless. (23)
"I am grasped by the mind, by speech, by sight, and even by the other senses;
understand directly that I alone exist and nothing other than me. (24)
The mind enters into the qualities, and the qualities enter into the mind;
both the body and the qualities belong to the individual soul, while the mind belongs to Me, its Self. 25.
The mind repeatedly enters into the qualities through the constant pursuit of those qualities;
yet both the qualities and the mind originate from Me—one who has My nature should abandon both. 26.

Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are the modifications of the intellect according to the qualities; the individual soul (jīva) is determined to be distinct from them by virtue of being their witness. 27.

For this bond of transmigratory existence, which bestows the functioning of the qualities upon the self, ceases when one is established in me, the Fourth; that renunciation is the relinquishing of the mind directed toward those qualities. 28.

Having become disillusioned with the bondage of the self caused by egoism and the resulting perversion of reality, the wise man, having ceased all thought of worldly existence, should remain established in the Fourth State (turya) and renounce it. 29.

As long as the man's cognition of manifold objects does not cease through reasoned arguments, the ignorant one remains awake even while sleeping, just like one who experiences a waking state within a dream. (30)
Because the self does not exist, the distinctions made by it regarding other entities—its destinies and its causes—are false, just like those of one who dreams. (31)

He who, while awake, experiences through all his senses objects that possess the nature of momentary flux, and who, in sleep, withdraws those same [objects] into the heart, and in deep sleep [withdraws them further], is that one Lord of the Senses, the witness of the functions of the three qualities, known through the continuity of memory. 32.

Having thus reflected upon the qualities [of the mind], those who have reached the certainty that "the three states of the mind were created within me by my own *māyā*," severing the mental affliction residing in the heart with the sword of knowledge—sharpened by inference and scriptural testimony—worship me, free from all doubt and mental anguish. (33)
One should regard this as a delusion, a play of the mind—seen and then vanished, exceedingly flickering like a whirling firebrand.
Single consciousness shines forth in many ways; it is an illusion, a dream, a conceptual construction produced by the emission of the three qualities. (34)

Then, having withdrawn the gaze, with craving ceased, one should remain silent, experiencing one's own bliss, free from worldly effort. And if this [world] is seen as unsubstantial, it is abandoned; then, until the fall of the body, there shall be no memory leading to delusion. //35//
The perfected one perceives neither the perishable body as it remains stationary nor as it has arisen, because he has realized his own true nature;
he regards it as a garment, whether cast off by fate or acquired through the power of destiny, just as one blinded by the intoxication of wine views a robe that has been discarded.
Indeed, even the body, subject to destiny, remains alive only so long as it awaits the exhaustion of the karma that initiated its formation.
One who has ascended to the yoga of non-conceptual samādhi and awakened to reality no longer experiences that dream-body again. (37)
O Brahmins, I have told you this secret concerning Sāṅkhya and Yoga;
know that I have come to this sacrifice with the desire to speak of dharma. 38.
O best of the twice-born, I am the supreme goal of Yoga, Sāṅkhya, truth, righteousness, splendor, prosperity, fame, and self-restraint.
All qualities—such as equanimity, non-attachment, and the rest—worship me, who am devoid of qualities, independent, the well-wisher, the beloved, and the Self. (40)
Thus, their doubts severed, the sages headed by Sanaka honored him with supreme devotion and praised him with hymns of praise. 41.
Having been duly honored and praised by those supreme sages,
I returned to my own abode while the Supreme Lord looked on.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Haṃsa-gītā," in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava within the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||13||
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Uddhava said:
O Kṛṣṇa, those who discourse on Brahman speak of many means to the highest good.
Is it that conceptual construction is predominant for them, or rather that it is their sole primary [characteristic]? (1)
O Lord, you have described the yoga of devotion which, when all attachment is cast off in every respect, causes the mind to enter into You. ||2||
The Blessed Lord said: This speech known as the Veda, which was lost in the course of time during the dissolution, was first proclaimed by me to Brahmā; within it, Dharma has me as its very soul.
She was then told by him to his first-born son, Manu;
thereafter, the seven great Brahmanical seers, Bhṛgu and the others, received her.
From those Pitṛs were born their sons: the gods, Dānavas, Guhyakas, humans, Siddhas, Gandharvas, along with the Vidyādharas and Cāraṇas. ||5||
The Kinnaras, Nāgas, Rakṣasas, Kiṃpuruṣas, and others—
many are their varieties, arising from the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas.
By these means beings are distinguished, as are the minds of beings;
indeed, according to their respective natures, the diverse words of all flow forth.
Thus, due to the diversity of innate dispositions, the minds of men differ;
some follow traditional lineages, while others hold heretical views. (8)
O bull among men, those persons whose intellects are deluded by my māyā proclaim various notions of the highest good, according to their karma and according to their own inclinations. 9.
Some speak of dharma, others of fame, some of desire, truth, self-restraint, and tranquility;
others speak of their own interest, or sovereignty, renunciation, and enjoyment; some [speak] of sacrifice, austerity, charity, vows, and observances. (10)
These worlds, fashioned by karma, have indeed both a beginning and an end;
they result in suffering, culminate in darkness, offer only trivial pleasure, and are fraught with grief. ||11||

O assembly members, for one whose mind is offered unto me and who is indifferent toward everything else, that happiness which exists through me as the Self—how could that belong to those whose souls are absorbed in sense objects? 12.
For one who possesses nothing, who is self-controlled, tranquil, and even-minded, whose mind is satisfied with Me—every direction is filled with happiness. 13.

With the self surrendered to Me, he desires nothing other than Me—not the status of Brahmā, nor the abode of Mahendra, nor sovereignty over the whole earth, nor lordship over the waters, nor the perfections of yoga, nor even liberation from rebirth. ||14||
Neither my own source of birth, nor Śaṅkara, nor Saṅkarṣaṇa, nor Śrī, nor even my own self is as dear to me as you are. ||15||
I constantly follow the Sage who is indifferent, serene, free from enmity, and possessed of equal vision, so that I may be purified by the dust of his feet. (16)

Those who possess nothing, whose minds are devoted to me, who are peaceful, great-souled, and compassionate toward all living beings, and whose intellects are untouched by desires—they enjoy that state of detachment which I know to be true happiness. 17.
Even if my devotee is assailed by sense objects and has not yet conquered his senses, he is generally not overcome by those objects due to his mature devotion. 18.
Just as a well-kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Uddhava, so does devotion directed toward Me completely consume all sins. 19.
Neither yoga, nor Sāṅkhya, nor religious duty, O Uddhava, nor Vedic study, nor austerity, nor renunciation accomplishes Me as does my own powerful devotion. 20.
I am to be grasped by exclusive devotion and by faith as the Self, dear to the virtuous.
Devotion centered on Me purifies even dog-cookers from their very birth. 21.
For dharma endowed with truth and compassion, or knowledge accompanied by austerity, does not truly purify a self that is devoid of devotion to Me. ||22||
How could the Destroyer be purified without the bristling of hair, without a melting heart, without tears of joy, and without devotion? 23.
He whose speech is faltering, whose mind melts away, who weeps constantly and sometimes laughs, who sings aloud and dances without shame—he, endowed with devotion to Me, purifies the world. 24.

Just as gold, when smelted by fire, casts off its dross and regains its own natural form, so too the self, having shaken off the latent tendencies of karma through the yoga of devotion to Me, then attains Me. 25.
Just as this self is cleansed by hearing and reciting my meritorious verses, so too does it perceive subtle reality, just like an eye treated with medicinal ointment. (26)
The mind of one who contemplates sense objects becomes attached to those objects;
the mind of one who remembers Me is absorbed in Me alone. 27.
Therefore, abandoning the contemplation of the unreal, such as dreams and mental fantasies, fix your mind on Me, permeated by My being. 28.
Having abandoned from afar the company of women and those who associate with women, the self-possessed man, sitting in a secure and secluded place, should meditate upon Me without weariness. 29.
Affliction and bondage would not befall him through such incidental association in the same way as they do for a man from contact with a woman, or from contact with one who is attached to her. (30)
Uddhava said:
O lotus-eyed one, how, in what manner, or as having what nature one should meditate upon You—this meditation for one desiring liberation, it behooves You to tell me. (31)
The Blessed Lord said:
Sitting on a level seat, with the body held straight and at ease, placing the hands in the lap, one should fix the gaze upon the tip of one's own nose. 32.

One who has conquered the senses should purify the path of the vital breath through inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka); one may also practice these slowly in reverse order.

Having raised the uninterrupted *oṃkāra*— which is like the resonance of a bell or a lotus fiber— from the heart by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one should then cause that sound to dissolve back into it.
Thus, one should practice the breath itself conjoined with the *praṇava* ten times at each of the three daily junctures; within a month, one becomes a conqueror of the vital air (*anila*). ||35||

Having meditated upon the lotus of the heart situated within, with its stalk pointing upward and its face downward, as being turned upward, fully blossomed, eight-petaled, and possessing a pericarp. ||36||
One should place the Sun, Moon, and Fire within the pericarp in successive order;
one should contemplate this form of mine in the center of the fire—this is the auspicious meditation. (37)

He was equanimous, perfectly tranquil, and possessed a beautiful countenance; he had long, lovely, and symmetrical four arms, a most charming and handsome neck, beautiful cheeks, and a pure smile. ||38||
He had shimmering shark-shaped earrings set upon his equal ears;
he was dark as a rain cloud, clothed in golden garments, and bore the Śrīvatsa mark, the abode of beauty.
Adorned with a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, and a forest garland,
his feet shone with anklets, and he was endowed with the radiance of the Kaustubha gem.
Resplendent with a crown, bracelets, armlets, and a girdle, he was beautiful in every limb, heart-pleasing, and possessed a gracious countenance and eyes. 41.
One should meditate upon the Subtle One, fixing the mind upon all its limbs;
having withdrawn the senses from the sense-objects by means of the mind, the wise man should, with the intellect as his charioteer, lead that mind toward Me from every side. 42.
Having drawn that all-pervading mind back, one should hold it in one place;
one should not think of other things further, but should cultivate a face with a gentle smile. 43.

There, having drawn back the mind that has found its footing, one should hold it in space; and having abandoned even that, like one who has mastered the art of riding, one should not think of anything at all. 44.
Thus, with a concentrated mind, one perceives Me alone as the Self within the self;
in Me, who am the Self of all, he beholds the light united with the light. 45.
For the yogi thus engaged in such intense meditation, the mind—along with its delusion regarding substance, knowledge, and activity—will quickly attain Nirvāṇa. 46.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Determining the Secret of Devotion," in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava, within the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||14||
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: For the yogi who has conquered the senses, who is disciplined, and who has mastered his breath—
For one who holds me in their heart, the supernatural powers (siddhis) manifest.
Uddhava said:
By what means of concentration, on what objects, and in what manner is perfection attained, O Acyuta?
How many are these perfections? Pray tell me, for you are the bestower of perfection upon yogis. (2)
The Blessed One said:
Eighteen perfections (siddhis) have been proclaimed by those who have reached the further shore of the yoga of concentration (dhāraṇā).
Of these, eight are presided over by me, while ten are indeed the causes of [worldly] qualities. ||3||
Minuteness, magnitude of the body, lightness, attainment through the senses, the power of irresistible will regarding what has been heard or seen, and sovereignty as the impelling of power; ||4||
Non-attachment to the qualities (guṇas) and mastery such that one attains whatever one desires—these, O gentle one, are considered by me to be the eight innate perfections (siddhis). ||5||
Freedom from the body's waves [of affliction], hearing and seeing from afar, the speed of thought, the ability to assume any form at will, and the power to enter the bodies of others. (6)
Death at one's own will, witnessing the sporting together with the gods, the complete fulfillment of every intention, and movement whose command is unimpeded. (7)

Knowledge of the three times, freedom from the pairs of opposites, supernormal knowledge of the minds of others and so forth, the immobilization of fire, the sun, water, poison, and the like, and invincibility. ||8||
These perfections of yoga-meditation have been declared by way of summary;
learn from me which perfection arises through which meditation, or how it may come to be. 9.
One should fix the mind upon Me, the Self who am the subtle element of the elements;
the worshiper of My subtle element attains the power of atomization (aṇimā). 10.
Placing the mind, according to its respective order, within me—the Great Self who am supreme—he attains the majesty of all beings, each in their distinctness. ||11||
By concentrating his mind upon me as consisting of atoms while delighting in all beings, the yogi attains the power of levity (laghimā), which is the state of having a self subtler than time. ||12||
Fixing his entire mind upon me as the principle of ego (ahaṃtattva) within the vaikārika [mode], he whose mind is fixed on me attains the state of being the self of all the senses. 13.
He who fixes his mind upon Me, the Great Self, the Thread, shall attain from Me—whose birth is unmanifest—the power of irresistible will and the supreme state of Brahmā. 14.
One should fix the mind upon Viṣṇu, the supreme lord of the three, whose form is Time;
he attains sovereignty and the impelling of both the field and the knower of the field. 15.
Fixing his mind upon me, who am Nārāyaṇa, designated as the Fourth State (turīya) and called by the name Bhagavān, the yogi shall attain the state of being fully absorbed in my nature. 16.
Fixing his clear mind upon me, the Brahman devoid of qualities, he attains supreme bliss wherein all desire ceases. 17.
Fixing his mind upon me, the pure Lord of the White Island who consists of Dharma, a man becomes white himself and is freed from the six waves [of worldly existence]. 18.
Bearing the sound with the mind within me—the vital breath whose self is space—that swan, being perceived therein, hears the voices of all beings. 19.
Having joined the eye with Tvaṣṭṛ and Tvaṣṭṛ with the eye, and meditating upon me there with the mind, one of subtle vision beholds the universe. 20.
Having thoroughly fixed the mind upon Me, and thereafter the body by means of the vital air, the self comes to abide where the mind is through the power of concentration on Me. 21.
Whenever, by means of the mind, one desires to become whatever form it may be, that very form of the mind shall come to be, by relying on the power of my yoga. 22.
Entering another's body, the perfected one should contemplate himself therein;
having abandoned the physical body, he should enter it as the vital breath, becoming like the wind, just like a bee. (23)
Having pressed the anus with the heel and having raised the vital breath through the heart, chest, throat, and head,
one should lead it to Brahman through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and cast off the body.
While dwelling in the pleasure-garden of the gods, one should contemplate the being situated within oneself;
celestial women, following the conduct of beings, attend upon him in a celestial chariot. (25)
Whatever a person devoted to Me might conceive with their intellect, or whenever they do so, by fixing the mind upon Me, the Truth, they obtain that very thing. ||26||
Indeed, that man who has attained my state, being a master and a controller, cannot be thwarted by anything; his command shall be just like mine. ||27||

For that yogi who possesses pure being through devotion to Me and who knows the method of concentration, his intellect regarding the three periods of time—enveloped by birth and death—is [liberated]. 28.

This body of the sage, through this yoga, cannot be destroyed by fire and other elements, just as water [cannot harm] one whose mind is weary from my yoga, like [the element of] water [to those born] among aquatic creatures. 29.
Meditating upon my glory, adorned with the Śrīvatsa and weapons,
and provided with a banner, an umbrella, and fans, he shall be unconquered.
O Sage, for a lay follower who maintains this yoga, the previously described accomplishments manifest in their entirety. ||31||

For the sage who has conquered his senses, who is self-controlled, who has mastered his breath, and who maintains the concentration (dhāraṇā) upon Me—what perfection is there that is difficult for him to attain? 32.
"These are said to be obstacles for one engaged in the highest yoga;
they are the causes of delay for one who is attaining perfection through me. (33)
Whatever accomplishments exist here through birth, herbs, austerity, or mantras—one attains them all through yoga; one cannot reach the goal of yoga by other means. (34)
I am the cause, the Lord, and the Master of all perfections;
I am [the goal] of yoga, of Sāṅkhya, of dharma, and of those who discourse on Brahman.
I am the inner Self, external and unenveloped for all embodied beings;
just as the elements exist within and without other elements, so do I myself. 36.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Description of the Siddhas," in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava within the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the collection known as the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||15||
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Uddhava said:
You are the supreme Brahman in its true essence—beginningless, endless, and unveiled.
For all phenomena as well, there is protection, stability, dissolution, and arising. ||1||
Among beings of high and low station, you are difficult to know for those whose selves are unrefined;
yet the Brahmins, O Blessed One, worship you according to reality.
Tell me also those various states of being through which the supreme sages, worshipping you with devotion, attain perfection. (3)
You move hidden as the inner self of beings, O creator of beings;
deluded by you, living creatures do not perceive you even as you behold them.

Whatever manifestations exist on earth, in heaven, or in the netherworld, O Lord of Great Power, tell them to me as they have been experienced by You; I bow to Your lotus feet, which are the source of all sacred pilgrimage sites.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O best among those who know how to inquire, it is even so;
this question was asked by Arjuna, who desired to fight his rivals at the place of destruction."
Having understood that the slaughter of kinsmen—a censurable unrighteousness—is for the sake of a kingdom, the worldly man desists from it, thinking: "I am the slayer; he is the slain. (7)
Then that tiger among men, having been awakened by me through skillful means,
addressed me in this very manner on the front line of battle, just as you have done.
O Uddhava, I am the Self, the well-wishing friend, and the Lord of these beings;
I am all beings, as well as their maintenance, origin, and dissolution. (9)
I am the goal of those who seek a goal; I am time for those who reckon time;
I am the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), and I am the originating quality of the possessor of qualities. 10.
Among those possessing qualities, I am the thread; among the great, I am the greatest.
Among subtle things, I am the life-force (jīva); among those difficult to conquer, I am the mind.
Of the Vedas, I am Hiraṇyagarbha; of sacred hymns, I am the Praṇava; of the threefold chant, I am the Trivṛt; of letters, I am the letter 'A'; and of meters, I am the feet. 12.
Among all the gods, I am Indra; among the Vasus, I am the bearer of oblations (Agni).
Among the Ādityas, I am Viṣṇu; among the Rudras, I am the blue-and-red one (Śiva). 13.
Among the Brahman-sages I am Bhṛgu; among the royal sages I am Manu;
among the divine sages I am Nārada; and among the cows I am the sacrificial vessel. 14.
Among the perfected masters I am Kapila; among winged creatures, I am Garuda;
among the lords of progeny I am Daksha; and among the ancestors, I am Aryaman. 15.
Know me, O Uddhava, to be Prahlāda, the lord of the Daityas and Asuras;
Soma, among the constellations and herbs; and Dhaneśa, among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas. 16.
Among lordly elephants, Airāvata; among aquatic creatures, Varuṇa the sovereign;
among those that scorch with heat, the radiant Sun; and among men, the king. ||17||
Among horses I am Uccaiḥśravas; among metals I am gold;
I am Yama among those who exercise restraint, and among serpents I am Vāsuki. 18.
Among the lords of serpents, I am Ananta; among the beasts of prey with horns and fangs, I am the lion;
among the stages of life, I am the fourth; and among the social orders, O sinless one, I am the first.
Among sacred fords I am the Ganges; among bodies of water, the ocean;
among weapons, I am the bow; and among archers, I am the destroyer of Tripura.
Among the sacrificial hearths I am Meru; among the dense forests I am the Himalayas;
among the lords of the forest I am the Ashvattha; and among herbs I am barley. 21.
Among domestic priests, I am Vasiṣṭha; among those most proficient in the Vedas, I am Bṛhaspati;
among all army commanders, I am Skanda; and among the foremost of the immortals, I am the Lord Aja. 22.
Among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of Vedic study; among vows, I am non-violence.
Among the pure, I am the wind, fire, the sun, water, speech, and the self; indeed, I am the purest of the pure. 23.
Among yogas, I am the restraint of the self; among those desiring victory, I am counsel; among skills in inquiry, I am dialectical analysis; and among proponents of renown, I am fame. 24.
Among women, I am Śatarūpā; among men, I am Svāyambhuva Manu; among sages, I am Nārāyaṇa; and among those who practice celibacy, I am Kumāra. 25.
Among relinquishments, I am the renunciation of all phenomena; among secure states, I am the mind that does not look outward;
among secrets, I am truthful silence; and among couples, I am the Unborn. 26.
I am the year among those who do not blink; I am Madhu and Mādhava among the seasons;
I am Mārgaśīrṣa among the months; and likewise, I am Abhijit among the lunar mansions. 27.
Among the ages, I am the Kṛta; among the wise, Devala; Asita; among the Vyāsas, Dvaipāyana; and among the poets, the self-possessed Kāvya. 28.
Among the Blessed Ones you are Vāsudeva; among the devotees I am [Uddhava]. Among the Kimpuruṣas I am Hanumān; among the Vidyādharas I am Sudarśana. ||29||

Among gems, I am the ruby; among beautiful lotus buds, I am the lotus calyx; among species of kusha grass, I am the kusha; and among sacrificial offerings, I am the clarified butter from cow's milk. (30)
I am the prosperity of those who strive for success; I am the ability to detect deception of gamblers;
I am the endurance of the patient; and I am the courage of the courageous. (31)
Know that I am the action of those Sātvatas who possess vital energy, vigor, and strength;
I am the supreme primordial form of the nine forms of the Sātvatas. 32.
I am Viśvāvasu, the first-born Gandharva among the Apsarases;
I am the stability of the mountains, and I am the mere fragrance of the earth. ||33||
I am the supreme essence of the waters, the most brilliant among luminous bodies,
the radiance of the sun, moon, and stars, and I am the sound that transcends the sky.
Among those devoted to Brahman, I am Bali; among the Virājas, I am Arjuna.
Among beings, I am indeed their stability, their origin, and their dissolution. 35.
I am the characteristic of movement, speech, excretion, grasping, bliss, touch, taste, hearing, and smell; I am the sense-faculty of all the senses. 36.

Earth, wind, ether, water, light, I, the Great One (Mahat), the modification (Vikāra), the Person (Puruṣa), the Unmanifest (Avyakta), passion (Rajas), goodness (Sattva), and darkness (Tamas)—the Supreme (Param). This enumeration is knowledge; it is the determination of reality. 37.
Without me—the Lord, the individual soul, the quality, and the possessor of qualities—even as the all-pervading Self and as everything, no entity whatsoever exists anywhere. (38)
The number of atoms is calculated by me over time,
yet not so [easily] do I create my own manifestations as I produce millions of cosmic eggs.
Wherever there is splendor, beauty, fame, sovereignty, modesty, renunciation, good fortune, prosperity, heroism, forbearance, and wisdom—he is my portion there. (40)
All these manifestations have been described to you in brief;
they are indeed merely modifications of the mind, just as they are expressed by speech. 41.
Restrain your speech, restrain your mind, restrain your vital breaths and your senses;
restrain the self by means of the self, so that you no longer strive upon the path of worldly existence. 42.
Indeed, for that ascetic who does not properly restrain speech within the mind through his intellect, his vow, austerity, and charity flow away like water from an unbaked clay pot. (43)
Therefore, with me as your supreme goal, you should restrain your mind, speech, and vital breath;
through an intellect joined with devotion to me, you will then reach complete perfection. 44.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Manifestations," in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava within the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of the Paramahaṃsas. ||16||
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Uddhava said:
That dharma characterized by devotion to You, which was previously described by You in its entirety—
Of all bipeds as well, who possess the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life.
O lotus-eyed one, you ought to explain that by which devotion to you may arise in men through the performance of their own duty. 2.
O mighty-armed Lord, O Mādhava, that supreme dharma which you formerly spoke to Brahmā while in the form of a swan—[that I wish to hear]. 3.
O crusher of enemies, after such a very long time, he will likely no longer exist in the world of mortals, having already passed away. ||4||
O Acyuta, there is no other on earth who is the speaker, the doer, and the protector of Dharma than you—
even in the assembly of Brahmā, where the creative powers (kalās) exist in embodied form.
O Madhusūdana, O Lord, when you—the creator, protector, and proclaimer—have abandoned the surface of the earth, who will proclaim that which has been lost? (6)
O Knower of all dharmas, tell us the truth regarding dharma, which is characterized by devotion to you;
O Lord, explain to me how it is ordained for each person.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus questioned by his chief servant, the Blessed Lord Hari, being pleased, spoke of the eternal duties for the welfare of mortals. 8.
The Blessed Lord said:
This question of yours is righteous and brings about the supreme good for human beings.
O Uddhava, listen to Me regarding those who observe the conduct prescribed for their social class and stage of life. 9.
In the beginning, in the Kṛta Yuga, the caste of men was known as Haṃsa;
because all subjects were born with their duties already accomplished by nature, they know that age as Kṛta Yuga. 10.
In the beginning, the Veda was indeed the Praṇava; I am Dharma, assuming the form of a bull.
Those whose sins have been cast off worship me as the Haṃsa, established in austerity. 11.
O highly fortunate one, at the beginning of the Tretā age, the triple Vedic knowledge emerged from my heart, which is the source of life;
of that knowledge, I was the threefold sacrifice.

The Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras were born from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet respectively, produced from the Purusha of the Vairaja class, who is characterized by his own conduct. ||13||
The householder's stage of life is at my hips, celibacy is in my heart; dwelling in the forest is in my chest, and renunciation is established in my head. ||14||
The dispositions of men belonging to the various classes and stages of life were according to their place of birth; they were low for the lowly and high for the high. (15)
Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, contentment, forbearance, uprightness, devotion to Me, compassion, and truth—these indeed are the qualities of the nature of Brahman. 16.
Splendor, strength, fortitude, heroism, endurance, magnanimity, exertion, steadfastness, and sovereignty in sacred knowledge—these are the innate qualities of the Kṣatriya. 17.
Faith in the hereafter, dedication to giving, freedom from deceit, service to the Brahmins, and lack of contentment with the accumulation of wealth—these are the natural qualities of Vaiśyas. 18.
Service to the twice-born, cows, and gods without guile, and contentment with what is obtained therein—these are the natural characteristics of Śūdras. 19.
Impurity, falsehood, theft, atheism, and idle quarreling;
lust, anger, and greed—these are the inherent nature of those who dwell at the teacher's feet. (20)
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, freedom from desire, anger, and greed, and the desire for the welfare and happiness of living beings—this is the dharma common to all social classes. 21.
Having attained the second birth in due order, the twice-born man, dwelling in the teacher's house, self-controlled and summoned, shall study the Veda. ||22||
Wearing a girdle, a deerskin, a staff, a rosary, a sacred thread, and a water-pot, with matted hair and unwashed garments, he sat upon an uncolored seat holding kusha grass. (23)
During bathing, eating, and fire-offerings, as well as during recitation and voiding, one should remain silent;
nor should one clip the nails or hair, even that which has grown in the armpits or the private parts. 24.
One who has himself spilled his semen while observing the vow of sacred study shall never again spill it;
having immersed himself in water with restrained senses, he should mutter the Tripadī mantra. 25.
Pure and composed, one should worship the fire, the sun, the teacher, cows, Brahmins, elders, and the gods, remaining silent and reciting prayers at the two twilights. 26.

One should recognize me as the Teacher and never treat me with contempt; one should not regard me with the mindset of a mere mortal or feel resentment toward me, for the Guru embodies all the gods. 27.
Having brought almsfood in the evening and the morning, he should present it to him;
and whatever else is permitted, he should consume it while remaining self-controlled. 28.
Desiring to serve, he should always attend upon his teacher like a servant;
whether moving, lying down, sitting, or standing, he should remain not too far away with palms joined in reverence. 29.
Living in such a manner, free from worldly enjoyments, he should reside in the teacher's household, maintaining his vows without interruption until his learning is completed. (30)
If he intends to ascend to the world of the Vedas, the abode of Brahman, he who is firm in his great vows should offer his body to his teacher for the sake of sacred study. (31)

One should worship Me as the Supreme in the fire, in the teacher, in oneself, and in all beings, with a mind free from differentiation; thus one becomes radiant with the splendor of Brahman and stainless. 32.
A person who is not a householder should avoid from the outset looking at, touching, conversing with, or laughing with women, as well as witnessing living beings engaged in sexual union. (33)

Purity, sipping water for ritual purification, bathing, the twilight devotions, worship, straightforwardness, resorting to sacred fords, recitation of mantras, and the avoidance of those who should not be touched, food that should not be eaten, and those with whom one should not converse. ||34||
O delighter of your lineage, this discipline is prescribed for all stages of life:
maintaining my nature toward all beings through the restraint of mind, speech, and body. (35)
Thus, a Brahmin who maintains great vows, blazing like fire, devoted to me, his latent impressions and karma burnt away by intense austerity, becomes stainless. ||36||
Then, immediately after, having examined the scripture as he had desired to know it,
and having given the teacher his fee, he should bathe with the teacher's permission.
An excellent twice-born man should either dwell in a house or in the forest, or he should renounce the world;
he should proceed from one stage of life to the next, for one devoted to Me should not act otherwise. (38)
One who desires a household should marry a wife who is suitable, blameless, of the same caste, and younger in age, according to the prescribed order. (39)
Sacrificing, studying, and giving are for all twice-born classes;
however, receiving gifts, teaching, and officiating at sacrifices belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone. (40)
Considering the acceptance of gifts to be a destroyer of austerity, splendor, and fame,
one who perceives faults in those two [accepting and giving] should subsist by means of the other two [teaching and officiating at sacrifices], or even by gleaning grains.
For this body of a Brahmin is not intended for trivial desires, but for arduous austerity in this world and for infinite happiness after death. 42.

With a mind fully content through the practice of gleaning ears of grain, enjoying the great and stainless Dharma, and having dedicated his soul to Me, even while remaining in the home, he who is not overly attached attains peace. ||43||
Those who rescue a Brahmin who is sinking while having me as his supreme refuge—I shall rescue them from calamities before long, like a boat from the ocean. 44.
A wise king should rescue all his subjects from calamity, just as a father does for his children, and just as a lordly elephant protects his herd with his own self. 45.
A king of such a kind, having shaken off all his evil deeds here by means of an aerial chariot as swift as the sun, rejoices together with Indra.
A Brahmin who sinks while following the profession of a merchant should overcome his distress by means of his wares alone;
or, if overwhelmed by calamity, he may take up the sword, but never, under any circumstances, the way of a dog.
O King, he who must live by the occupation of a Vaiśya during times of distress may subsist by hunting;
or he may conduct himself in the guise of a Brahmin, but never by the occupation of a dog.
A Vaiśya should adopt the livelihood of a Śūdra, and a Śūdra that which is dear to artisans.
Once released from hardship, one should not seek a livelihood through a despicable occupation. 49.

Every day, one should worship the gods, sages, ancestors, and elemental beings—who are all forms of My own self—with Vedic recitations, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, and offerings of food and other oblations, according to their respective order. 50.
With wealth acquired either by chance or through pure means, he should perform sacrifices according to the law, without causing distress to his dependents. (51)
One should not become attached to families, nor should one be negligent even toward those who belong to one's family.
A wise person should perceive the perishable as if it were imperishable, and see the unseen as if it were seen. (52)
The meeting with sons, wives, kinsmen, and friends is like the meeting of travelers; these depart from one's body at death, just as a dream vanishes upon waking. (53)
Reflecting thus, one who is liberated, dwelling in houses like a guest, is not bound by those homes, being free from possessiveness and free from egoism. (54)

Having performed sacrifices with rites conducive to prosperity for the sake of his household, the devoted man may remain [at home], retire to the forest, or, having obtained offspring, wander forth as a mendicant. ||55||
But he who is attached to his home, afflicted by the desire for sons and wealth, devoted to women, of wretched intellect, and deluded, is bound by the thought "I am [this]" and "this is mine. ||56||
"Alas! My parents are aged, my wife is young, and my children are infants;
how will they live, wretched and miserable, without a protector and deprived of me? (57)
Thus, with his heart drawn away by the desire for home, this man of deluded intellect, dying while still unsatisfied and dwelling upon those things, enters into blind darkness. (58)

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties and Laws of Students and Householders," within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava, in the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||17||
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
Desiring to enter the forest, one should either entrust one's wife to one's sons or go together with her.
One should dwell in the forest, tranquil, during the third part of one's life. ||1||
He should provide his livelihood with pure wild roots, tubers, and fruits;
he should wear bark, grass, leaves, or skins as his clothing.
He should maintain his hair, body hair, nails, and beard in their natural state;
he should not run, he should bathe in water three times a day, and he should sleep on the bare ground.
In summer he should practice penance amidst five fires; during the rains, he should remain in water while enduring the downpour;
and in the cold season, he should perform penance submerged up to his neck—one who conducts himself thus should practice austerity.
He should eat food cooked by fire, or even that ripened by time;
he may be one who grinds with a mortar and stone, or indeed one whose teeth serve as the mortar. ||5||
One who understands place, time, and strength should personally gather everything required for one's own livelihood; one should not accept what has been brought by others at an improper time.

One who dwells in the forest hermitage should offer, as impelled by the proper time, oblations of sacrificial porridge and cakes made of wild grains; however, he should not sacrifice me with an animal according to the Śrauta ritual.
The Agnihotra, the Darśa, and the Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, as previously described, as well as the Cāturmāsya rites, were prescribed for the sage by the followers of the Vedas. ||8||
Having thus practiced such austerity until his veins are visible, the sage, having propitiated me who am composed of ascetic power, comes to me from the world of the seers. ||9||
But what fool other than him would employ this great austerity, performed with such hardship for the sake of a trivial desire? (10)
When he is no longer capable of the observances, trembling with old age, he should, having internally consigned the sacred fires into himself, enter the fire with his mind fixed on Me. ||11||
When detachment arises toward the worlds that are the ripening of karma, and toward one's own self, then, having properly laid down the sacred fire, one should go forth. ||12||

Having performed the sacrifice according to the instructions and having given all his possessions to the officiating priest, he should enter the sacred fires into his own vital breaths and wander forth as a mendicant without attachment. ||13||
Indeed, when a Brahmin intends to renounce, the gods, appearing in the form of wives and other such things, create obstacles, thinking:
"He might advance toward the supreme state by bypassing us. 14.
If the sage should wear a garment, let it be at most a loincloth for covering;
except in times of distress, he should possess nothing other than his staff and alms-bowl. ||15||
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is purified. 16.
Silence, lack of desire, and breath-control are the three staffs of speech, body, and mind;
he who does not possess these, my dear, cannot be a true ascetic merely by means of bamboo staves. 17.
He should wander for alms among the four castes, avoiding those who are censurable; he should be content with whatever is obtained from seven houses that have not been pre-selected. ||18||

Having gone outside to a body of water and performed ritual ablutions there while remaining silent, he should divide the remainder of what was brought; having purified it, he should eat it all without leaving anything behind. ||19||
One should wander this earth alone, free from attachment, with senses restrained, sporting in the Self, delighting in the Self, self-possessed, and possessing equal vision toward all. 20.
Taking solitude as his secure refuge, with a mind purified by my own being, the sage should contemplate the Self as one, inseparable from me. (21)
One should investigate one's own bondage and liberation through steadfastness in knowledge:
bondage is the distraction of the senses, and liberation is their restraint. 22.
Therefore, having restrained the group of six, the sage should live with his being fixed on me;
detached from trivial desires, he attains great bliss within the self. 23.
For the sake of alms, he should wander through cities, villages, cow-pens, and merchant caravans;
he should traverse the earth, which abounds with holy places, rivers, mountains, forests, and hermitages.
In the stages of life of the forest-dweller, he should constantly practice begging for alms;
thus, with his essence purified by roots and fruits, he attains perfection as his delusion quickly subsides.
One should not view this [world] as a real entity, for that which is seen perishes;
with an unattached mind, one should desist from what is desired here and in the hereafter. 26.
Whatever this world is within the self, composed of mind, speech, and breath—all that is illusion; having abandoned it through reasoning, one who is established in the Self should not remember it.

Whether established in knowledge, or dispassionate, or my devotee, or free from expectations—having abandoned the stages of life along with their emblems, he should wander beyond the scope of prescribed rules. ||28||
The wise man should play like a child, the skillful one should move about like one who is dull-witted;
the learned man should speak like a madman, and the follower of the scriptures should conduct himself in the world like a commoner. 29.
One should not be devoted to the mere recitation of the Vedas, nor be a heretic, nor a rationalist;
one should not take recourse to any side in dry disputation or debate. (30)
The wise man should not be agitated by people, nor should he agitate others. He should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone.
For the sake of the body, he should not harbor enmity toward anyone, even as one does toward a beast. (31)
For there is indeed only one supreme Self abiding within the self of all beings;
just as the moon is reflected in various vessels of water, so too all beings possess that single Self. 32.
Not finding food at times, one should not despair; nor, having found it, should one rejoice. One should maintain equanimity toward both, for they are governed by destiny.
One should strive for food only for the sake of sustaining life;
by that, reality is investigated, and having realized it, one is liberated. (34)
Whatever food the sage may obtain by chance, whether it be excellent or otherwise, as well as clothing and bedding, he should accept whatever is obtained as it comes. (35)
The knower of truth should not perform purification, sipping water, or bathing merely because of scriptural injunction; nor should he observe other rules, just as the Lord acts with ease. 36.
Indeed, that which is called his conceptual construction has been destroyed by my vision; therefore, it never again appears to me until the end of the body. 37.
Having become disillusioned with desires that result in suffering, the self-possessed man, desiring to know my dharma, should approach a guru who is a sage. ||38||
One should serve with devotion, faith, and freedom from malice, and with respect for me as the teacher, until one realizes Brahman. 39.
But he who has not restrained the group of six, whose charioteer is his fierce senses,
and who is devoid of knowledge and dispassion, merely lives off the triple staff.
The destroyer of dharma, whose impurities are not yet matured, denies the gods, himself, the Self residing within himself, and me;
therefore, he is deprived of this vital heat. ||41||
The duty of a monk is tranquility, non-violence, austerity, and contemplation;
that of a forest-dweller is the protection of living beings; that of a householder is sacrifice; and that of a twice-born man is service to the teacher. 42.

Celibacy, austerity, purity, contentment, and kindness toward all beings—these, as well as worship of Me, belong to everyone, even for a householder who approaches his wife only during her season. (43)
Thus, he who worships me constantly according to his own duty, being devoted to no other, and who perceives my nature in all beings, soon attains devotion to me. 44.
O Uddhava, by means of unwavering devotion, he approaches Me—the Great Lord of all worlds, the Brahman who is the cause of the origin of everything. ||45||
Thus, one whose being is purified by his own duty, who has discerned My state, and who is endowed with knowledge and realization, attains Me before long. 46.
This dharma, characterized by right conduct, belongs to those who follow the system of social classes and stages of life;
when joined with devotion to Me, it alone brings about the supreme good. 47.
This has been declared to you, O virtuous one, regarding that which you asked me:
how a devotee, united with his own duty, may attain Me, the Supreme. 48.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of Vanaprastha and Sannyāsa," in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava within the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||18||
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
He who is endowed with learning and sacred revelation, who possesses self-mastery, and who does not rely on mere inference;
Having realized that this world is mere illusion, one should surrender all knowledge into Me.
But for the wise, I alone am the desired object, the purpose, and the accepted cause;
both heaven and liberation—no other goal—is dear apart from Me. ||2||
Those perfected in both knowledge (jñāna) and realized wisdom (vijñāna) know my supreme state;
therefore, the man of knowledge is dearest to Me, for by means of knowledge he sustains Me. ||3||
Austerity, sacred pilgrimage sites, recitation of mantras, charity, and other purifying acts are not capable of producing that perfection which is achieved by even a fraction of knowledge. ||4||
Therefore, O Uddhava, having realized your own self together with knowledge, and being perfected in both theoretical and experiential wisdom, worship Me with a spirit of devotion. 5.
Having worshipped Me— the Lord of all sacrifices— within the Self by means of the sacrifice of knowledge and discernment,
the sages have indeed attained perfection.
O Uddhava, whatever threefold modification arises within You, that pertains to the realm of Māyā; it does not exist at the beginning or at the end.
Since these transformations such as birth and so forth belong to You, what could they be for Him? That which is non-existent at the beginning and the end must likewise be non-existent in the middle.
Uddhava said:

O Lord of the Universe, O You whose form is the universe, please declare this ancient, vast, and pure knowledge, which is joined with dispassion and realization, as well as the great yoga of devotion to You that is sought after by all.

O Lord, for me who am struck by the threefold miseries and scorched on this terrible path of worldly existence, I see no other refuge than the pair of Your feet, which are like a parasol raining down nectar. 9.
This person, bitten by the black serpent of worldly existence which yields only meager pleasure, has fallen into this pit;
O noble one, lift him up out of compassion and sprinkle him with words that lead to liberation. 10.
The Blessed Lord said: Thus, in former times, King Ajātaśatru questioned Bhīṣma, the best among the upholders of dharma, while all of us were listening.
When the Bhārata war had ended, he, overwhelmed by the death of his kinsmen,
heard many teachings on dharma and subsequently inquired about the dharma of liberation.
I shall declare those [teachings] to you, as heard from the mouth of Devavrata, augmented by knowledge, dispassion, realization, faith, and devotion. 13.
That by which one indeed perceives nine, eleven, five, and three states within the elements—even if only one among these—is my certain knowledge. 14.
For this very consciousness is not such that, by means of it alone, one might perceive the persistence and origination of entities whose nature consists of the three qualities (triguṇa). //15//
That which persists through the created world at its beginning, its end, and its middle, and which remains when that world has again dissolved—that alone is real. 16.

Scripture, perception, tradition, and inference—this fourfold set [of means of knowledge] is rejected by him because of the instability found among these means of knowledge and because of their conceptual construction. ||17||
Because actions are subject to transformation, everything up to Brahmā is inauspicious;
the wise man should perceive even the unseen as perishable, just like that which is seen. (18)
O sinless one, the yoga of devotion has already been taught to you when you were pleased;
yet I shall speak of it again, for it is the supreme cause of my own devotion. 19.
I have constant faith in the discourse of the nectar of immortality, the perpetual chanting of my names, complete dedication to my worship, and the praising of me with hymns of praise. (20)
Reverence in service, salutation with all one's limbs, worship of My devotees as superior to [the worship of] all beings, and a mind fixed on Me—[these constitute the highest yoga]. 21.
Gesturing with the limbs for my sake, praising my qualities with speech, dedication of the mind to me, and the renunciation of all desires. ||22||
The renunciation of wealth and of enjoyments and pleasures for my sake;
whatever is sacrificed, given, offered in the fire, or muttered in prayer, and whatever vow or austerity is performed for my sake—[all this is done]. 23.
O Uddhava, for those humans who thus offer themselves through these practices, devotion to Me arises; what other goal remains for them? (24)
When the mind is offered into the Self, tranquil and nourished by sattva, it attains virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty. ||25||
That which is projected by the senses runs toward conceptual construction;
