know that the mind, being full of passion (rajas) and established in its seat, is characterized by error. 26.
Dharma is said to be the practice of devotion to Me; knowledge is the vision of the oneness of the Self;
detachment is non-attachment to the qualities (guṇas); and sovereignty consists of the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest. ||27||
Uddhava said:
O crusher of enemies, how many kinds of *yama* (restraint) and *niyama* (observance) are proclaimed?
What, O Kṛṣṇa, is *śama* (tranquility), what is *dama* (self-control), what is *titikṣā* (forbearance), and what is *dhṛti* (fortitude), O Lord? 28.
What is charity, what is austerity, and what is heroism? What is truth, and what is called ṛta?
What is renunciation, what is desired wealth, what is sacrifice, and what is the sacrificial fee? 29.
O illustrious Keśava, what indeed is the strength of a man? What are fortune, power, and gain?
What is knowledge? What is supreme modesty? What is prosperity? And what are happiness and suffering? (30)
Who is wise and who is a fool? What is the right path and what is the wrong path? What is heaven and what is hell? Who indeed is a kinsman, and what is a home? (31)
Who is wealthy, who is poor, who is miserable, and who is a lord?
O Lord of the virtuous, tell me the answers to these questions and their opposites as well. (32)
The Blessed One said:
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, non-attachment, modesty, lack of hoarding, faith, celibacy, silence, steadfastness, forgiveness, and fearlessness. (33)
Purity, recitation, austerity, burnt offerings, faith, hospitality, worship of Me, pilgrimage to sacred fords, striving for the sake of others, contentment, and service to the teacher. (34)
These twelve restraints (yamas) along with the observances (niyamas) are traditionally taught for both [genders];
when practiced by men, O dear one, they indeed yield all desires according to one's wish. ||35||
Tranquility is the steadiness of the intellect; self-control is the restraint of the senses;
endurance is the patient bearing of suffering; and fortitude is the mastery over the tongue and the organ of generation. (36)
The laying down of the staff is the supreme gift; the renunciation of desire is known as austerity;
victory over one's own nature is heroism; and truth is even-mindedness toward all. (37)
Truth and speech that is pleasant and beneficial have been extolled by the seers;
purity consists in non-attachment to actions, while renunciation is said to be relinquishment. (38)
Dharma is the desired wealth of men; I am the sacrifice, the most blessed one;
the instruction of knowledge is the sacrificial fee, and breath control is the supreme strength. 39.
Fortune is my sovereign state; gain is supreme devotion to Me;
knowledge is the absence of delusion regarding the Self; and shame is the aversion toward unrighteous acts. 40.
Fortune consists of qualities such as independence and the like; happiness is the transcendence of both suffering and pleasure;
suffering is the longing for sensual pleasure; and the wise man is one who knows the liberation from bondage. 41.
The fool is one who possesses the notion of "I" regarding the body and so forth; the path is known as my scripture (Nigama);
the wrong path is the distraction of the mind; and heaven is the arising of the quality of goodness (sattva). 42.
O friend, hell is darkness, and I am its kinsman, its elder, and its master;
the human body is the home, for one who is rich in virtues is indeed called "wealthy. (43)
But he who is poor yet discontented, or miserable with senses unsubdued, whose intellect is unattached to virtues—O Lord, such attachment to qualities is the opposite [of liberation]. ||44||
O Uddhava, all these questions of yours have been well resolved. What is the use of much description? The characteristic of both merit and fault is this:
the perception of merit and fault is itself a fault; the true merit, however, is that which is free from both. 45.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Uddhava," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the great Purāṇa, within the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||19||
Now the twentieth chapter.
Uddhava said:
Indeed, both injunction and prohibition are Your command as the Lord.
O lotus-eyed one, he examines both the merit and the fault of actions.
The distinctions of the castes and stages of life, those born of inverse and natural unions,
as well as substances, place, age, time, heaven, and hell.
Without the perception of a distinction between merit and fault, how can your speech—characterized by prohibitions and injunctions—lead to the supreme good for human beings? (3)

O Lord, the Veda is the eye for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings; it is indeed the authority regarding the welfare that is not perceived through other means, as well as concerning the relationship between the goal and its means.
The perception of a distinction between qualities and defects does not arise from you by itself, for it is derived from the Veda;
and that the Veda contains a refutation of such distinction is indeed an error. ||5||
The Blessed Lord said: Three paths of yoga have been proclaimed by Me for the sake of securing the ultimate good of human beings—knowledge, action, and devotion; there is no other means anywhere. (6)
For those who are disillusioned with worldly actions and have renounced them, the yoga of knowledge is prescribed here;
for those whose minds are not disillusioned with such actions and who possess desires, the yoga of action is prescribed.
If a person, having developed faith at the outset through hearing my stories by chance, is neither despondent nor excessively attached, for him the yoga of devotion is the bestower of perfection. 8.
One should perform ritual actions as long as one does not become weary of them, or until faith arises toward such things as listening to my narrations. (9)
O Uddhava, one who remains established in his own duty and performs sacrifices without desire for rewards does not go to heaven or hell, provided he acts otherwise [with detachment]. ||10||
Abiding in this world, established in his own duty, sinless and pure, he attains either purified knowledge or devotion to Me by chance. ||11||
Even those in heaven and likewise those in hell desire this world;
it is effective through both knowledge and devotion, but it is ineffective when lacking both.
A wise man should desire neither the path to heaven nor that of hell;
he should not long for this world either, for one becomes heedless through attachment to the body. 13.
Knowing this, one should strive before death for liberation;
being vigilant and understanding this, even a mortal finds the fulfillment of his purpose. 14.
When a tree that has served as its nesting place is being cut down by these restraints, the bird, abandoning its own home, indeed goes to safety, free from attachment. ||15||
Perceiving that his life-span is being cut away day and night, he trembles with fear;
yet, having realized the Supreme and become free from attachment, he becomes effortless and attains peace.

If a person does not cross the ocean of worldly existence—using this first human body, which is both easily obtained and yet so difficult to find; a well-constructed raft with the Guru as its helmsman; and propelled by the favorable wind that is myself—he is a destroyer of his own self. 17.
When the yogi becomes disenchanted with worldly undertakings, detached, and has his senses restrained, he should, through practice, hold his own mind immovably. 18.
For he who, being vigilant, brings under his own control the mind—which, when not restrained, wanders swiftly and remains unstable—by means of the appropriate path; ||19||
One who has conquered the vital breaths and subdued the senses should not let the course of the mind wander;
with an intellect endowed with purity, one should bring the mind under the control of the self.
This indeed is remembered as the supreme yoga: the steady withdrawal of the mind, like one who repeatedly seeks to understand the heart of a horse yet to be tamed. 21.
By means of Sāṃkhya, one should contemplate the existence and non-existence of all entities in both their reverse and direct orders, until the mind becomes serene. ||22||
The mind of a man who is disillusioned, detached, and who understands what has been taught, abandons its wickedness through constant reflection upon that which has been contemplated. (23)

One should contemplate the mind as being fit for yoga through the paths of Yoga such as Yama and others, through the science of Ānvīkṣikī, or through the worship of My icons, but not by other means. ||24||
If a yogi should, through negligence, perform a censurable act, he should burn away that evil solely by means of yoga; never by any other means. 25.
The steadfastness in one's own respective duty is proclaimed as "guṇa" (virtue).

By this, a restriction has been established for actions that are inherently impure by their very nature, with the intent of causing the abandonment of attachments through the prescription of virtues and defects. 26.
Having developed faith in my teachings and becoming disillusioned with all ritual actions, he understands that desires are essentially suffering, yet remains unable to renounce them. (27)
Then, being pleased, full of faith, and firm in resolve, one should worship Me, while enjoying those desires yet censuring them as having sorrow for their ultimate result. 28.
For the sage who worships me repeatedly through the yoga of devotion as described, all desires of the heart perish when I am established within his heart. 29.
The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are severed, and his karmas are exhausted when I, the indwelling Self of all, am seen. 30.
Therefore, for the yogi who is endowed with devotion to Me and whose self is absorbed in Me, neither knowledge nor detachment is generally considered the highest good in this world. ||31||
Whatever is attained through ritual acts, through austerity, and through knowledge and dispassion;
through yoga, through the duty of charity, and through other auspicious means as well. ||32||
My devotee easily attains everything through the yoga of devotion to me—whether heaven, liberation, or my own abode—if he so desires it. (33)
For those virtuous, steadfast, and single-minded devotees of mine do not desire even liberation from rebirth, though it be offered by me. ||34||
They say that supreme indifference is the great means to the highest good;
therefore, for one who is free from desire, devotion to Me arises. 35.
For those who are single-mindedly devoted to me, for the virtuous who possess equanimity of mind and have reached that which is beyond the intellect, neither virtues nor faults arise within me. (36)
Thus, those who follow the path ordained by me find security;
they attain my station, which the wise know as the supreme Brahman. 37.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Division of the Three Vedas," in the dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Uddhava, within the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the collection known as the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||20||
Now the twenty-first chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
He who, having abandoned these paths of Mine consisting of devotion, knowledge, and action—
Indulging in trivial desires with their flickering lives, they wander through the cycle of rebirth.
That which is steadfastness in one's own respective duty is proclaimed as a quality (guṇa);
conversely, the opposite would be a defect (doṣa). This is the certainty regarding both. ||2||
Purity and impurity are prescribed even for identical objects;
they are the auspicious and inauspicious qualities and defects intended for the discernment of substances. (3)
O sinless one, this conduct has been shown by me, who bear the burden of dharma, for the sake of dharma, for the sake of legal affairs, and for the sake of sustenance. ||4||
Earth, water, fire, air, and ether are the five elements of all beings;
from Brahmā down to the immovable objects, bodies are composed of these and joined with the self. (5)
O Uddhava, by means of their knowledge, these [sages] conceptualize names and forms—even among things that are equal—within the elements for the sake of accomplishing their own purposes. ||6||
O best of men, the merits and defects of things such as place, time, and so forth are established for the purpose of regulating actions.
The black antelope (kṛṣṇasāra) is unfit for sacrifice in regions that are unrighteous and impure;
even the black antelope is unfit in Sauvīra, Kīkaṭa, and in uncultivated wasteland. ||8||

A time that is fit for action and endowed with excellence, whether by virtue of its material circumstances or by its own nature, is such that from which action ceases is known as the fault of non-action (akarmaka). ||9||
The purity and impurity of a substance are determined by the substance itself, by verbal designation, by ritual consecration, by time, or by its magnitude or minuteness. ||10||
Whether by ability or inability, by intelligence or by wealth, people indeed commit sin against themselves according to their place and circumstances. ||11||
Of grains, wood, bone, and fibers; of liquids, luminous bodies, and skins; and of earthen objects, by means of time, wind, fire, earth, and water—whether joined or separated. ||12||
Whatever removes the odor and the stain of what has been smeared with impurity, and returns that object to its natural state—that much is considered its purification. 13.

Through bathing, charity, austerity, stage of life, vigor, purificatory rites, and actions, as well as by the constant remembrance of Me, the twice-born man should perform his duties with self-purification; being thus pure, he should engage in ritual action. 14.
Full knowledge of the mantra, purity of action, and dedication to me—through these six, dharma is accomplished; adharma, however, is the opposite. ||15||
In some cases, even a merit may become a fault, and by rule, even a fault may become a merit;
such a restrictive determination regarding merits and faults subverts their very distinction.
Engaging in the same activities as those who have fallen does not constitute a sin;
association is an innate quality, for one who is merely lying down does not fall downward. ||17||
From whatever [object] one may turn away, from that one shall be liberated;
this is the dharma for men, which brings security and removes sorrow, delusion, and fear. ||18||
From the superimposition of qualities upon sense objects, attachment arises for the person;
from attachment, desire for them arises, and from desire alone comes strife among men. (19)
The wrath of Kali is difficult to endure; it follows after that darkness.
By that darkness, the pervasive consciousness of man is swiftly swallowed up. 20.
O virtuous one, a living being separated from that [mindfulness] is as if empty;
consequently, his own welfare is lost, like one who is unconscious or dead. (21)
Through attachment to sense-objects, one knows neither oneself nor another;
living by the life of a tree while breathing like a bellows, such a person lives in vain. 22.
This proclamation of rewards for men is not the supreme means of making them find delight in the highest good;
it was spoken with the desire to communicate the true welfare, just as one might use a sweetener to make medicine palatable. (23)
For from the very beginning, mortals have their minds attached to sensual pleasures, to vital breaths, and to kinsmen—all of which are causes of harm to the self. (24)
How could a wise man again employ those ignorant ones—who are wandering on the path of misfortune for their own sake and entering into darkness—back into that same state? 25.
Thus, some of evil intellect, failing to understand this settled truth, speak of the scriptural declarations regarding rewards as if they were mere flowers, for they do not truly know the Vedas. (26)
Lusting, wretched, and greedy, with the notion of fruit in flowers, deluded by fire and perishing in smoke, they do not find their own world. 27.
They do not know me who am situated within their very limbs, for they are intent upon this [external world];
indeed, like those who delight in the Soma-pressing, they have eyes only for the mist [of ignorance]. 28.
Not understanding my intention, those who are devoted to sense objects might think that if there were passion for violence, then sacrifice alone would not be a scriptural injunction. (29)

For indeed, those wicked ones who delight in violence, desiring their own pleasure, worship the gods, the ancestors, and the lords of beings with sacrifices using animals they have not rightfully obtained. 30.
Having mentally conceived desires for this world— which is like a dream, non-existent, yet pleasant to hear— they abandon their goals just as a merchant leaves behind his wares.
Those who are devoted to passion, goodness, and darkness, and who delight in passion, goodness, and darkness, worship the gods and others headed by Indra; they do not worship me in that same way.
Having worshipped the deities here with sacrifices and having gone to heaven, we shall rejoice;
at the end of that [merit], may we become great householders of noble lineage in this world. (33)
Thus, for those men whose minds are distracted by flowery speech,
who are conceited and excessively arrogant, even news of me is not pleasing.

These Vedas, which have Brahman and the Self as their subject matter and encompass the three divisions [of ritual, knowledge, and conduct], speak in an indirect manner; for the sages, and for me as well, the indirect mode of expression is dear.
The Brahman of Sound is extremely difficult to comprehend; it consists of vital breath, the senses, and the mind, and like the ocean, it is infinite, shoreless, profound, and hard to fathom. ||36||
Amplified by me through the abundant Brahman of infinite power, it is perceived as sound within all beings, like wool within lotus stalks. (37)
Just as a spider emits its web from its heart and its mouth, so from space arises the resonant vital breath (prāṇa) together with the mind, which has the nature of touch. 38.
Consisting of meter and consisting of nectar, the Lord [revealed] the path of a thousand verses, adorned with the consonants, vowels, sibilants, and semivowels manifested from the syllable Oṃ. ||39||
He himself creates and withdraws the vast Vṛhatī, which is spread across diverse languages and possesses four ever-increasing meters, and is infinite in its limits. 40.
Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, Aticchandas, Atyaṣṭi, Atijagatī, and Virāj. ||41||
"What does it enjoin? What does it describe? And what does it prescribe by way of restatement?"—no one else in this world knows her heart as I do. (42)
It ordains me, it designates me, and having conceptualized me, it negates me;
such is the entire meaning of all the Vedas: the Word, having resorted to me through differentiation, merely reiterates that which is illusion and, having negated it at the end, becomes serene. 43.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Division of the Three Vedas," in the dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Nārada, within the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the collection concerning the state of the Paramahaṃsas. ||21||
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Uddhava said:
O Lord of the Universe, O Master, how many principles (tattvas) have been enumerated by the sages?
Nine, eleven, five, three, and eight—these we have heard from you here. ||1||
Some say there are twenty-six; others, twenty-five;
some seven, nine, or six; some four, while others say eleven;
some say seventeen; some sixteen, and others thirteen. (2)
O long-lived one, you alone among the enumerators are capable of speaking this which the sages sing separately according to their own intentions; it behoves you to tell this to us. (3)
The Blessed Lord said:
"And it is fitting that the Brahmins speak thus everywhere;
for when they take hold of my own Māyā, what indeed is difficult for them to say? (4)
"This is not as you say; it is exactly as I say.
While we thus dispute, my powers, which are difficult to overcome, shall provide the proof. (5)
From the conflict of those [views], the sphere of conceptualization arose for speakers;
yet when tranquility and self-control are attained, speech likewise subsides along with them. (6)
O bull among men, because the principles (tattvas) interpenetrate one another, their enumeration is relative to the speaker's intention regarding priority or posteriority. (7)
Even within a single [principle], all other principles are seen to be fully entered, whether in the preceding or the succeeding principle, in every respect. (8)
Therefore, for those who desire to enumerate these [categories] in their sequential order, we shall grasp whichever face is distinct according to the possibility of logical reasoning. (9)
For a person joined with beginningless ignorance, self-realization is not possible by itself; therefore, another who knows reality must be the giver of that knowledge. (10)
In this regard, there is not even an atom’s worth of difference between the Puruṣa and Īśvara;
therefore, the conception of another [Īśvara] is useless, and knowledge is a quality of Prakṛti. ||11||
Nature (prakṛti) is indeed the equilibrium of the qualities; the qualities do not belong to the Self (ātman).
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the causes of maintenance, origination, and dissolution. ||12||
Sattva is knowledge; rajas is action; tamas is said here to be ignorance.
Time is the intermingling of the qualities (guṇas), as well as inherent nature (svabhāva) and the Sūtra itself. 13.

The Person (Puruṣa), primordial nature (Prakṛti), the manifest (Vyakta), ego (Ahaṃkāra), ether (Nabhas), wind (Anila), light (Jyotis), water (Āpas), and earth (Kṣiti)—these nine principles have been declared by me. 14.
The ear, skin, sight, nose, and tongue are the powers of cognition;
speech, hands, the organ of generation, the anus, and the feet are the organs of action; O dear one, the mind belongs to both. (15)
Sound, touch, taste, smell, and form are the classes of objects;
movement, speech, excretion, and manual arts are the accomplishments of the spheres of action. ||16||

At the beginning of creation, primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of both cause and effect, assumes [the world] through the qualities (guṇas) such as sattva; the unmanifest Puruṣa merely observes. ||17||
The elements, beginning with the manifest, undergoing transformation and having gained potency through the gaze of Puruṣa, together create the cosmic egg by the power of Prakṛti. (18)
There are exactly seven elements; among them, the objects are five, beginning with space (ether).
Consciousness is the self, which is the support for both; from that [arise] the body, the senses, and the vital fluxes. 19.
Regarding the word "six" here as well: there are five elements and the Supreme Person is the sixth.
Having created this [universe] by means of those [elements] produced from himself, he entered into it. 20.
In that case as well, there are only four: fire, water, food, and the self;
from these this world is born, for birth indeed belongs to the whole. ||21||
In the seventeenth enumeration, there are the five subtle elements and the five senses; with the mind as the sixth, the self is traditionally reckoned as the seventeenth.
Similarly, in the enumeration of sixteen, the self (ātman) itself is called the mind (manas);
the five elements and the five senses, together with the mind and the self, constitute thirteen. ||23||
This self consists of eleven: the great elements and the sense organs;
furthermore, there are the eight primordial natures and the Puruṣa as the ninth. ||24||
Thus, various enumerations of the principles have been made by the sages;
since all are logical and reasoned, what among them is not excellent for the wise? (25)
Uddhava said: O Kṛṣṇa, although both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are distinct from the Self, no difference between them is perceived due to their mutual dependence.
For the Self is perceived in Prakṛti, and likewise, Prakṛti is perceived in the Self. ||26||
Thus, O lotus-eyed one, you ought to sever this great doubt in my heart with your words, O omniscient one, through your skill in reasoning. 27.
For from you comes the knowledge of living beings, and by your power, its loss occurs here;
indeed, you alone know the course of your own self-māyā, and no one else. 28.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Nature and Spirit—this is the dualistic conception, O bull among men.
This is the transformational creation, consisting of the interplay of the qualities. (29)
O my dear one, my illusory power (māyā), consisting of the qualities (guṇas), produces manifold conceptual cognitions through those very qualities;
it is threefold as the transformative (vaikārika), namely, the internal (adhyātma), the divine (adhidaiva), and the elemental (adhibhūta). ||30||
The eye [perceives] form, the ear [perceives] sound, the body [perceives] touch—here, in this void of the senses, that which is established by itself through its own nature is the Self.
That which is other than these is the Primordial One, who, by His own self-experience, is the perfection of all perfections.
In this same way, the skin and so forth, the ears and so forth, the eyes, tongue and so forth, and the nose and so forth are joined with the mind. (31)

That modification which arises from the Great Principle (mahat), the root of Pradhāna, caused by the agitation of the qualities (guṇas)—I am that, threefold: the cause of delusion and conceptualization, consisting of the transformative (vaikārika), the dark (tāmasa), and the sensory (aindriya). ||32||

Indeed, this dispute consisting of the non-comprehension of the Self—which is grounded in the distinctions of "it exists" and "it does not exist"—would not cease for those men whose minds have turned away from their own true world, even though it is futile. (33)
Uddhava said:
O Lord, those whose intellects have turned away from You take up and cast off various high and low bodies according to their own performed actions.
Tell me that, O Govinda, which is difficult to be conceived by those who lack self-mastery;
for generally, even the learned in this world are deceived. (35)
The Blessed Lord said:
The mind of men, composed of karma and joined with the five senses, travels from world to world; another, the Self, follows after it. (36)
When the mind meditates upon objects seen or heard, it rises up and sinks down within the machinery of action; thus, mindfulness becomes agitated. ||37||
When, due to attachment to sense objects, one no longer remembers oneself again for some reason, that is death for a living being—the ultimate forgetfulness. (38)
O bestower of abundant wealth, they say that for a person, birth as the self consists of the appropriation of objects through every mode of being, just like a dream or a mental fantasy. (39)
In this way, he does not remember his former dreams or desires;
there he perceives himself as if new, as though never having existed before. ||40||
Through the creation of the movement of the senses, this threefold division appears within the reality;
it is the cause of the distinction between "outer" and "inner," just as an unreal person creates another unreal person. 41.
For indeed, O dear one, beings are constantly coming into existence and ceasing to exist;
because it is subtle, that which occurs through time with its imperceptible speed is not seen.
Just as [the variations] of flames, of streams, or of the fruits of a tree are produced, even so have the stages of life and other conditions been ordained for all beings. 43.

Just as this lamp is nothing other than its flames and this water is nothing other than its currents, so too the speech of men that "this is the person" is false, and their thought regarding living beings is false. 44.
This person is neither born nor does he die through the seed of his own karma;
he appears and disappears through delusion, just as fire manifests when joined with wood. 45.
Conception, gestation, birth, infancy, childhood, youth, middle age, old age, and death—these are the nine stages of the body. 46.
For these various bodies of another, consisting of the products of desire, one assumes through attachment to qualities and at some time another abandons them. (47)
The origin and dissolution of the self are to be inferred from its father and son;
one who possesses the characteristics of duality is not a knower of the reality of origin and dissolution. 48.
Just as one who understands the birth and restraint of a tree through its seed and its fruition is a seer distinct from the tree, so too is the seer separate from the body. 49.
Thus, the ignorant man, failing to distinguish the Self from primordial nature (prakṛti) and being utterly deluded regarding its true nature, enters into the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra). 50.
Driven by attachment to the quality of goodness (sattva), one approaches the sages and gods; by passion (rajas), the asuras and humans;
and by darkness (tamas), one is whirled about by actions and goes to the state of spirits or animals. ||51||
Just as one who observes others dancing or singing imitates them, so too, observing the qualities of the intellect, even one who is free from effort is made to conform to them. (52)
Just as trees appear to move when the water is flowing, so the earth appears to spin when the eye is being whirled around. (53)
O descendant of Daśārha, just as the experience of objects by the mind in a state of desire is false, so too is this worldly existence of the self, like things seen in a dream. 54.
For even when an object does not exist, the cycle of worldly existence does not cease for one who contemplates sense-objects, just as the arrival of misfortune occurs in a dream. ||55||
Therefore, O Uddhava, do not enjoy sense objects with your unrefined senses;
behold the self, which shines forth when free from grasping, as a conceptual delusion. 56.
Whether he has been insulted, humiliated, mocked, or envied by the wicked;
or whether he has been beaten, imprisoned, or deprived of his livelihood. (57)
Thus shaken in many ways—exhausted, drenched with urine, and fallen into distress—he who desires his own welfare should rescue himself by his own effort. 58.
Uddhava said:
O best among speakers, tell us how I may understand this, for I consider this transgression against my own self to be most difficult to endure. (59)
O Soul of the Universe, even for the wise, nature is indeed more powerful;
except for those devoted to Dharma who find their refuge at Your feet, they remain tranquil. 60.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Uddhava," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, within the collection known as Pāramahaṃsyā Saṃhitā. ||22||
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
Bādarāyaṇi said:
Thus addressed by Uddhava, the foremost of the Bhāgavatas, that chief of the Dāśārhas—
Honoring the words of his servant, Mukunda, whose heroic deeds are worthy of being heard, spoke to him.
The Blessed Lord said: O Bṛhaspati, he indeed is not virtuous here who is unable to compose his own self when it has been pierced by the ill-spoken words uttered by the wicked. ||2||
A man pierced by arrows that strike his vital organs does not suffer so much as he is tormented by the harsh shafts of the wicked lodged in his very vitals. (3)
O Uddhava, they relate here a great and meritorious history;
I shall describe that to you—listen with a well-composed mind.
A certain monk, who had been treated with contempt by wicked people, sang while remembering his own past actions and remaining endowed with fortitude. (5)
On this earth there was a certain twice-born man who was most wealthy in prosperity;
yet he lived by the profession of trade, and was miserly, lustful, greedy, and exceedingly wrathful.
His kinsmen and guests were not honored even with mere words;
his empty dwelling and his own self were likewise unhonored by desires at the proper time. ||7||
The sons, kinsmen, wives, daughters, and servants of one who is immoral and miserly become hostile; dejected, they no longer act with affection. 8.
When that Yakṣa-wealth had thus perished from both worlds, being devoid of both dharma and desire, the five sharers [of the sacrificial offerings] became enraged. (9)
O Giver of Abundance, for him whose mass of merit had been dissipated by that neglect,
even his wealth met its end despite much exertion and toil.
O Uddhava, his kinsmen took some [wealth], his horses took some, and by fate or through the king—the lord of men—some was taken from that pseudo-Brahmin. ||11||
Thus, with his wealth lost and deprived of both dharma and desire,
and neglected by his own kinsmen, he fell into an insurmountable state of anxiety.
As that ascetic meditated in this manner for a long time, his wealth lost and his throat choked with tears, a very great world-weariness arose within him. ||13||
And he said: "Alas, what misery! My soul has been tormented in vain;
for neither dharma nor desire is served by such exertion as this for wealth. (14)
Generally, the wealth of misers never leads to happiness;
in this world it results in self-torment, and after death, it leads to hell. (15)
The fame of the famous is pure, as are the praiseworthy virtues of the virtuous;
yet even a slight greed destroys them, just as vitiligo destroys a desired complexion. (16)
In the acquisition, preservation, expenditure, loss, enjoyment, and effort regarding wealth, men experience distress, fear, anxiety, and delusion. (17)
Theft, violence, falsehood, deceit, lust, anger, pride, intoxication, dissension, enmity, lack of trust, rivalry, and vices—[these are the qualities of tamas]. ||18||
These fifteen objects are indeed considered by men to be rooted in wealth;
therefore, one who desires the highest good should avoid from afar that which is called "wealth" when it is actually a source of harm. 19.
Brothers, wives, fathers, and likewise friends—who were once bound by a single bond of affection—are instantly made all enemies for the sake of a single cowrie. (20)
For even for a very small matter, these men become enraged, their minds aflame;
they quickly abandon their rivals and, casting aside friendship, they slay them with violence. 21.

Having obtained a human birth sought after even by the immortals, and having attained that state of being the foremost among the twice-born, those who disregard it and destroy their own true interest go to an inauspicious destination. 22.
Having reached this world, which is the gateway to heaven and liberation, what mortal man would cling to wealth, the abode of misfortune? (23)
One who possesses Yakṣa-like wealth, failing to share with the gods, sages, ancestors, spirits, kinsmen, and relatives, and not even sharing with himself, falls downward. 24.
Wealth is lost through the vain pursuit of objects, and the vigor of youth is wasted by the heedless;
since those who are skillful achieve success through such means, what indeed can an old man accomplish? 25.
Why does the wise man repeatedly become afflicted by this futile pursuit of wealth?
Surely this world has been utterly deluded by the illusion of someone. (26)
What is the use of wealth or those who bestow wealth, or of desires or those who grant desires, for one being swallowed by death, or even by actions that bring about rebirth? (27)
Surely the Blessed One, Hari who embodies all the gods, is pleased with me, since he has led me to this state and provided the raft for my own world-weariness. 28.
Therefore, in this Kali age, I shall completely wither away my own body,
remaining vigilant for the sake of my entire goal, if only I may attain perfection within myself.
May the gods, the lords of the three worlds, favor me therein;
with a single moment, Khaṭvāṅga reached the world of Brahmā.
The Blessed One said:
Having thus reflected in his mind, O best of the twice-born, that sage from Avanti untied the knots of the heart and became a peaceful mendicant. 31.
With his mind, senses, and breath restrained, he wandered this earth;
for the sake of alms, he entered towns and villages, unattached and unrecognized.
Seeing that aged mendicant, who was an ascetic free from worldly attachments, wicked people indeed insulted him, O noble one, with many forms of contempt.
Some took up the triple staff, others a water-pot and a mendicant's bowl; some took a seat, others a rosary, and some took a patched garment and rags.
And having presented them again, they took back those things shown to the sage as he was eating food consisting of alms on the riverbank. ||35||
The most wicked ones urinate upon him, spit on his head, force him to speak while restraining his speech, and beat him if he does not speak. (36)
Others threaten him with words, saying, "This man is a thief! while some bind him with ropes, crying out, "Bind him! Bind him! (37)
Some, despising him, cast him out, saying: "This rogue is a mere pretender to righteousness;
having lost his wealth and been abandoned by his own kin, he has adopted this mode of life. (38)
"Aha! This mountain is of great substance and possesses fortitude;
like a heron, he achieves his purpose through silence, being firm in his resolve. (39)
Thus some laughed at him, while others reviled him;
they bound that bird and confined him like a plaything. (40)
Thus he understood that whatever material suffering—whether caused by fate, the body, or other sources—is ordained for the self, it must be experienced as it arrives. 41.
Though thus insulted by those lowest of men who sought to cast him down from his own dharma, he remained established in sattvic fortitude and sang this verse: 42.
The twice-born said:
"Neither this person, nor the gods, nor the spirits, planets, actions, or time are the cause of my pleasure and pain;
they declare that the mind alone is the supreme cause which causes the wheel of worldly existence to revolve. (43)
The powerful mind indeed creates qualities, and from those arise various actions—white, black, and red; from these, paths of corresponding colors come into being. ||44||
The inactive Self, golden-hued and my friend, looks on with the mind that is striving;
yet that [mind], having grasped its own characteristic marks and enjoying desires, becomes bound through attachment to the qualities (guṇas). ||45||

Charity, one's own duty, observances, restraints, sacred learning, ritual acts, and virtuous vows—all these have their ultimate goal in the control of the mind; for the supreme yoga is the concentration of the mind.
Tell me, what further need has he for generosity and the like whose mind is concentrated and tranquil? And if one's mind is uncontrolled and perishing, what purpose do these other virtues serve? (47)
For other gods have come under the power of the mind, yet the mind does not come under the power of another.
Bhīṣma is indeed a god, more powerful than the powerful; he alone can bring that [mind] under control, for he is the God of Gods. 48.
Without having conquered that invincible enemy of unbearable force who pierces the vital organs, some deluded mortals here engage in improper conflict with friends, neutrals, and enemies alike. 49.

Having grasped this body, which is merely mind, as "this is I" and "this is mine," men of blinded intellect wander in darkness that is shoreless and endless, through the delusion of thinking, "I am this one, and he is another. (50)
If people are the cause of pleasure and pain, then what is the role of the self in this matter?
When one bites one's own tongue with one's teeth while tasting something, at which of those two sensations should one become angry? (51)
If the gods are the cause of suffering, why does that [suffering] affect the self during those two states of transformation?
When one limb is struck by another limb somewhere, at whom within his own body would a person become angry? (52)
If the self were the cause of pleasure and pain, what need would there be for anything else? In that case, it would be its own inherent nature.
For if nothing other than the self exists, then [the experience of] pleasure and pain would be false; why then should one be angry? Why should there be neither pleasure nor pain? (53)
If the planets are the cause of pleasure and pain for people, then how can they affect the unborn Self?
They say that affliction by the planets belongs only to the planet itself; therefore, at whom else should a person be angry? ||54||
If karma is the cause of pleasure and pain, then what is the role of the self? For that [karma] exists whether the self is insentient or sentient.
This body, however, is an unconscious person; to whom could this "fair-winged" one (the self) be angry? For anger is not rooted in karma alone. ||55||
If time is the cause of pleasure and pain, then how can the self be of that nature?
For heat does not belong to fire, nor would cold belong to frost; with whom then could one be angry? Duality belongs to another. (56)

For that which is beyond the beyond, there can never be, anywhere, or in any way, a dualistic affliction caused by another, such as might belong to the "I-sense" which consists of the form of worldly existence;
thus the awakened one does not fear beings. 57.

Having resorted to this state of being established in the Supreme Self, which was practiced by the most ancient great sages, I shall cross over the darkness whose further shore is difficult to reach, solely through service to the feet of Mukunda. 58.
The Blessed Lord said:
Having become disenchanted and lost his wealth, free from weariness, this sage wandered the earth after renouncing the world;
though thus rejected by the wicked, he remained unshaken from his own duty and spoke this verse: ||59||
Nothing other than the delusion regarding the self brings pleasure and pain to a person;
friends, neutrals, and enemies are all created by the darkness of saṃsāra. (60)
Therefore, my dear son, restrain the mind with the intellect in every way by means of it being absorbed in me; this is the entirety of the summary of yoga. 61.
The monk who, being composed, maintains, causes others to hear, or hears this song concerning the culmination of Brahman, is never overcome by the pairs of opposites.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Song of the Mendicant," in the dialogue between the Blessed One and Uddhava within the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the collection concerning the state of the Paramahaṃsas. ||23||
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
Now I shall fully declare to you the Sāṃkhya as determined by the ancients.
Having realized which, a person may immediately abandon the delusion of conceptual construction. ||1||
In the beginning, during the ageless Kṛta Yuga, there was indeed only one undifferentiated reality—both knowledge and its object—for those skilled in discernment. ||2||
That Great Reality, which is beyond speech and mind, being merely non-conceptual in the form of the fruit of Māyā, became twofold. ||3||
Of these two, one principle is Nature (prakṛti), which possesses a dual nature;
the other state is Knowledge (jñāna), which is designated as the Spirit (puruṣa). ||4||
Tamas, rajas, and sattva—these qualities of Prakṛti arose from her as she was being agitated by me with the consent of Puruṣa. (5)
From them arose the Sūtra, which was joined with the Mahat-sūtra;
from that, as it underwent transformation, was born the delusive Ahaṃkāra.
I am threefold— as the Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Tāmasa—
and I am the cause of the subtle elements, the senses, and the mind, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious.

From the *tanmātra* of darkness (*tāmasa*) was born *artha* (the objects of sense), and from the *tanmātra* of passion (*taijasa*) arose the eleven senses; from the modified (*vaikṛta*) [ego] came the deities. ||8||
Impelled by me, all the elements, acting in concert, produced the cosmic egg, my supreme abode. ||9||
I existed within that egg resting upon the waters;
from my navel arose a lotus called Viśva, and there the Self-born (Brahmā) appeared.

Endowed with austerity and through my grace, he, the soul of the universe, created by means of the quality of passion (rajas) the worlds together with their guardians, in three divisions: Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar. ||11||

The world of heaven (svaḥ) was the abode of the gods; the world of the atmosphere (bhuvaḥ) was the station of living beings; the world of earth (bhūḥ) was for mortals and the like; and beyond these three was the realm of the perfected ones (siddhas). ||12||
Below, the Lord created the abode of the Asuras and the Nāgas within the earth;
and in the three worlds, he established all the destinies for those whose selves are composed of the three guṇas according to their actions. ||13||
The stainless goals of yoga, austerity, and renunciation are the realms of Maharloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka; but the goal of the yoga of devotion is My own state. 14.
By me, the Creator whose nature is Time, this world is joined with karma;
in this stream of the qualities (guṇas), it emerges and submerges. ||15||
Whether minute, vast, slender, or gross—whatever state of being is established, it is all joined with both Prakṛti and Puruṣa. 16.
That which is the beginning and the end of something is indeed its middle as well;
modification exists for the sake of conventional usage, just as [the terms] "golden" or "earthen" [are applied to various objects]. ||17||
When a prior state undergoes transformation into another by depending upon something, that which constitutes its beginning and its end is designated as the Truth (satya). ||18||
For Prakṛti is its material cause, the Supreme Puruṣa is its substratum, and Time is the manifestor of that which exists; I am indeed that triad, which is Brahman. 19.

Creation proceeds perpetually in a continuous succession of prior and subsequent stages; it is the great manifestation of the qualities (guṇas), lasting from its inception until its dissolution, as long as the Lord’s gaze endures. (20)
When the Virāt, which brings about the formation and dissolution of the worlds, is reached by me, it leads to the state of fivefold dissolution along with all the worlds. ||21||
Mortal food dissolves into the grain; the grain dissolves into seeds;
the seeds dissolve into the earth; and the earth dissolves into fragrance. ||22||
Smell dissolves into water, and water into its own quality, taste;
taste dissolves into light, and light dissolves into form. (23)
Form dissolves into air, and that [air] dissolves into touch; that too dissolves into space.
Space [dissolves] into the subtle element of sound, and the sense organs [dissolve] into their own sources. (24)
The womb, O gentle one, dissolves into the mind, which is the lord of the Vaikārika [ego];
sound merges into the source of the elements (bhūtādi), and the powerful source of the elements merges into the Mahat. ||25||
That Great One, the most excellent of the possessors of qualities, dissolves into his own qualities;
they dissolve into the Unmanifest, and that Unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable. 26.

Time resides in the living being composed of illusion; the living being resides in the Self; the Self resides in Me, the Unborn; and the Absolute Self resides in itself, characterized by the cessation of all conceptual differentiation. 27.
For one who investigates in this manner, how could a conceptual delusion remain in the heart of the mind? It would be like darkness at the rising of the sun in the sky. ||28||

This method of Sāṃkhya has been declared by me—through both the reverse and the direct orders of creation, and by means of the vision of the higher and the lower—as that which cuts through the knots of doubt. 29.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Sāṅkhya regarding Nature and the Person," in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava within the Eleventh Book of the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the collection concerning the state of the Paramahaṃsas. ||24||
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"By which means a person may become one whose qualities are unmixed..."
Therefore, O best of men, attend to this as I speak it. ||1||

Equanimity, self-control, forbearance, discernment, austerity, truthfulness, compassion, mindfulness, contentment, renunciation, lack of desire, faith, modesty, mercy, and so forth, as well as self-contentment—[these are the qualities]. ||2||
Desire, effort, intoxication, thirst, rigidity, longing, division, pleasure, pride, enthusiasm, fame, affection, laughter, valor, strength, and exertion; ||3||
Anger, greed, falsehood, violence, begging, hypocrisy, exhaustion, strife, grief, delusion, despondency, affliction, sleep, hope, fear, and lack of effort. ||4||
These functions of sattva, rajas, and tamas have been described for the most part according to their respective proportions; now hear of their conjunction. ||5||
But that notion, O Uddhava, which consists of "I" and "mine," is a conjunction;
this conventional usage is a conjunction of the mind alone with the senses and the vital breaths. (6)
When he has reached perfection in virtue, wealth, and pleasure, this accumulation of qualities brings forth faith, which is the bringer of supreme riches. (7)
For that man who finds his final goal in the stage of active life within the householder's order and performs his own duty—that indeed is the assembly of all virtues. (8)
One should infer a person endowed with *sattva* by means of tranquility and other such qualities;
one joined with *rajas* by desire and the like; and one possessed of *tamas* by anger and the like. (9)

When one worships me with devotion, free from expectations regarding one's own actions, whether that person be a man or indeed a woman, one should know them to be of the nature of goodness (sattva). 10.

When one worships me while seeking blessings for oneself through one's own actions, one should know that person to be of the nature of passion (rajas); but when one worships seeking violence, one should know them to be of the nature of darkness (tamas). ||11||
The qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas belong to the individual soul (jīva) and not to Me; they are born of the mind, and by them the soul, becoming attached, is bound. 12.
When the other two [qualities] have been conquered and sattva is radiant, pure, and auspicious, then the person becomes joined with happiness through dharma, knowledge, and the like. ||13||
When tamas conquers sattva—[tamas which is] characterized by attachment, divisiveness, and instability—then one becomes joined with suffering, [worldly] action, fame, and prosperity. (14)
When rajas conquers sattva, one becomes deluded; when tamas conquers them, one experiences stupor and dissolution.
Indeed, one is then joined with grief and delusion, with sleep, violence, and worldly desire. 15.
When the mind becomes serene and the senses find their rest, and there is fearlessness in the body and attachment of the mind [to the Self], know that to be Sattva, which is My state. 16.
Behold passion (rajas) through these: its transformation by action, its lack of steadiness, its lack of tranquility for the mind, the unwellness of the limbs, and the wandering of the intellect. 17.
The mind sinks and dissolves when it is incapable of grasping the object;
know that this loss of mental power, the darkness, and the exhaustion are all forms of tamas. 18.

When the quality of goodness (sattva) increases, the strength of the gods flourishes; when passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas) increase, O Uddhava, the strength of the asuras and the rākṣasas flourishes. 19.
One should know that wakefulness arises from sattva; one should indicate sleep through rajas;
deep slumber belongs to a living being through tamas; and the fourth state is continuous throughout these three.
By means of *sattva*, people ascend higher and higher as far as the world of Brahmā;
by means of *tamas*, they descend lower and lower down to the very bottom; and by means of *rajas*, they move in the intermediate space. ||21||

Those merged in *sattva* go to their own [heavenly] state; those merged in *rajas* go to the world of men; but those merged in *tamas* go to hell, while those free from the qualities (*nirguṇa*) come to me alone.
One's own action is *sāttvika* when it is offered to Me or performed without desire for fruit;
it is *rājasa* when motivated by a desire for results; and it is *tāmasa* when it consists mostly of violence and the like. 23.

Knowledge that leads to liberation is characterized by goodness (sāttvika); that which is characterized by passion (rajas) is dualistic; knowledge pertaining to primordial nature (prakṛti) is characterized by darkness (tāmasa); and that which is established in Me is remembered as being beyond the qualities (nirguṇa). 24.
A forest is said to be sattvic habitation, a village is rajasic,
a gambling hall is tamasic, but my abode is beyond the gunas.
The agent who is free from attachment is considered *sāttvika*; the one blinded by passion is known as *rājasa*;
the one whose memory is lost is *tāmasa*; and the one devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) is he who takes refuge in me. 26.
Faith in the spiritual is sattvic; faith in ritual action is rajasic;
that which is in unrighteousness is tāmasi; but faith in service to Me is beyond the gunas. 27.
Food that is wholesome, pure, and not stale is declared to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
That which is dear to the senses is of the nature of passion (rājasa), and that which causes pain and is impure is of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). 28.
Happiness arising from the Self is characterized by goodness (sāttvika); that which arises from sense objects is characterized by passion (rājasa);
that which arises from delusion and dejection is characterized by darkness (tāmasa); but that which takes refuge in Me is beyond the gunas (nirguṇa). 29.
Substance, place, fruit, time, knowledge, and action are the causal factors; indeed, all—faith, state, form, completion, and the three qualities—are likewise [factors]. 30.
All states consisting of the qualities (guṇas) are presided over by the Puruṣa and the Unmanifest (avyakta).
These transmigrations of the person (puruṣa) are bound by the qualities and their actions. 31.
O gentle one, he by whom these qualities born of the mind have been conquered through the yoga of devotion, being established in me, attains to my own state of being. ||32||
Therefore, having obtained this [teaching] which arises from knowledge and realization, let the wise, having shaken off attachment to the qualities (guṇas), devote themselves to Me. 33.
Free from attachment, the wise sage, vigilant and with senses conquered, should worship Me; he should overcome passion and ignorance by cultivating goodness. 34.
One who is disciplined, tranquil in intellect, and free from worldly expectations shall conquer the quality of sattva;
being liberated from the gunas, the individual soul, having abandoned its individuality, attains Me. 35.
The living soul, when liberated from the individual self and from the qualities born of the latent impressions, becomes full through me alone as Brahman; it moves neither outside nor inside.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Qualities and the Qualityless," in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava, within the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the collection known as Pāramahaṃsyā Saṃhitā. ||25||
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
Having obtained this body characterized by Me, one should abide in My dharma.
One attains Me, the blissful Supreme Self, who abides within the self. ||1||
Liberated from the womb of the living being composed of the modes by means of steadfastness in knowledge, a person—
though existing amidst the modes which are seen as mere illusion and devoid of reality—
is no longer joined with those unreal modes. ||2||
One should never form an attachment to the wicked, who are gluttons for their genitals and bellies;
following them, one falls into blind darkness like a blind man following other blind men. //3//

The emperor Aila, of great renown, sang this verse while bewildered by separation from Urvaśī and despondent in his struggle against grief: 4. Even though I am devoted to you, I do not obtain you; alas, what is the use of this life? || 5 || 5. Even though I am devoted to you, I do not obtain you; alas, what is the use of this life? || 5 || 6. Even though I am devoted to you, I do not obtain you; alas, what is the use of this life? || 6 || 7. Even though I am devoted to you, I do not obtain you; alas, what is the use of this life? || 7 || 8. Even though I am devoted to you, I do not obtain you; alas, what is the use of this life? || 8 || 9. Even though I am devoted to you, I do not obtain you; alas, what is the use of this life? || 9 || 10. Even though I am devoted to you, I do not obtain you; alas, what is the use of this life? || 10 || 11. Even though I am devoted to you, I do not obtain you; alas, what is the use of this life? || 11 || 12.
