As she was departing, having abandoned him, the king, naked and like one insane, followed her wailing in distress, "O wife! O terrible one! Stay! ||5||

Unsatisfied with desires and indulging in trivial pleasures during the short nights of the rainy season, Urvashi, her mind captivated by him, knew not whether they were passing away or coming back. 6.
Aila said:
"Alas! How vast is my delusion, for my mind is clouded by passion; while holding the goddess by the neck, I did not perceive that these were fragments of my own life-span. (7)
"I do not know whether the sun has set or whether it has risen;
robbed of my senses, alas, many years and days have passed away. (8)
"Alas! What self-delusion is mine, by which I, a universal monarch and the crest-jewel of kings, have been turned by women into a pet deer! (9)
Having abandoned my lord along with his retinue like a blade of grass, I followed that woman as she departed—naked, weeping, and like one insane. ||10||
Whence could he have any majesty, or even power and lordship, he who followed a woman as she went away, having been kicked by her foot like a donkey? (11)
Of what use is knowledge, of what use is austerity, of what use is renunciation, or even sacred learning;
and of what use is solitude or silence for one whose mind has been stolen away by women? 12.
Fie on me, a fool who considers himself a scholar but is ignorant of his own true interest—me, who, having attained lordship, have been conquered by women like a bull or a donkey! (13)
Even after many years of serving me, Urvashi’s nectar of her lips does not satiate my innate passion, just as the sacrificial fire is never satiated by oblations. 14.
Who else indeed is capable of liberating the heart stolen by a harlot, except for the Lord Adhokṣaja, the Master who delights in the Self? 15.
Although I have been enlightened by the queen with her well-spoken words, O evil-minded one, the great delusion residing in my mind does not depart, for I have not conquered myself. (16)
What harm has this rope done to us, who perceive it as a snake?
It is only for one who does not know the true nature of the rope and whose senses are unsubdued that the notion "I am [the snake]" arises. ||17||

Where is this body, soiled with filth, consisting of foul odors and the like, and inherently impure; and where are qualities such as pleasantness? Indeed, this superimposition is created by ignorance. (18)

Is it one's own to one's parents, or to one's wife, or to one's master, or to fire, or to dogs and vultures? Is it one's own to oneself, or to one's friends? That which cannot be determined—[that is what is called wealth]. (19)
In that impure body, which is worthless and base, he becomes attached, thinking:
"Oh, how beautiful is the woman's face, with its fine nose and lovely smile! (20)
What difference is there between worms delighting in a collection of skin, flesh, blood, sinews, fat, marrow, and bone, and excrement, urine, and pus? (21)
Moreover, one who understands the true goal should not become attached to women or to those devoted to them;
for the mind becomes agitated through the union of the senses with their objects, and not otherwise.
From that which is unseen and unheard, no entity arises from another entity;
for one who does not engage the vital breaths, the mind becomes tranquil and still. ||23||
Therefore, attachment should not be formed toward women or those devoted to them by the senses;
for even the wise have no confidence in the group of six [internal enemies], so how much less those like me? 24.

The Blessed Lord said: Thus singing, that god among kings, having abandoned the world of Urvaśī, realized the Self within the Self and, with his delusion shaken off by knowledge, attained me and came to rest. ||25||
Therefore, having abandoned bad association, the wise person should attach himself to the virtuous;
for the virtuous sever one's mental attachment through their liberating discourses. 26.
The virtuous, free from expectations, with their minds fixed on Me, tranquil, seeing all equally,
devoid of "mine-ness," free from egoism, beyond the pairs of opposites, and without possessions— 27.
In those illustrious ones, O highly fortunate one, my beneficial discourses constantly arise; they purify the sins of men who take delight in them. 28.
Those who hear this, sing it, and rejoice in it with faith, being devoted to Me and full of trust, they find devotion unto Me. 29.
For the virtuous one who has attained devotion toward Me—the infinite Brahman whose nature is the experience of bliss—what else remains to be achieved? (30)
Just as cold, fear, and darkness depart from one who approaches the blessed fire, so too do they depart from one who serves the virtuous. ||31||
For those sinking and surfacing in the terrible ocean of worldly existence, the virtuous, peaceful knowers of Brahman are the supreme refuge, like a sturdy boat for those drowning in the waters. (32)
For food is the life-breath of living beings; I am the refuge for the afflicted;
dharma is the wealth of men after death; and the virtuous are the protection for those who fear in this world. 33.
The virtuous grant sight; the sun has risen abroad.
The virtuous are the deities, the virtuous are kinsmen, and the virtuous are my very self. 34.
Thereafter, Vaitasena likewise became indifferent to the world through Urvaśī; freed from attachment and finding delight in the Self, he wandered over this earth. ||35||

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Song of Aila," in the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, within the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
Uddhava said:
"O Lord, please explain the yoga of action (kriyā-yoga), which is the means of worshiping you."
O bull among the Sātvatas, because the Sātvatas worship you in such a manner...
The sages, the blessed Nārada, Vyāsa, and the teacher who is the son of Aṅgiras, repeatedly declare this to be the supreme good for men. ||2||
That which the unborn Blessed One spoke has issued forth from your lotus-like mouth;
and the Blessed Lord Bhava [spoke it] to his sons, headed by Bhṛgu, and to the Goddess.
O giver of honor, I consider this to be the most excellent among all blessings for all castes and stages of life, as well as for women and Śūdras. 4.
O lotus-petal-eyed one, O Lord of the Universe, tell this which liberates from the bonds of karma to one who is devoted and faithful. 5.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Uddhava, it is impossible to reach the end of the ritualistic section (Karmakāṇḍa), which is infinite and shoreless;
nevertheless, I shall describe it to you concisely, exactly as it is, in its proper sequence.
My sacrifice is threefold: Vedic, Tantric, and mixed. One should worship me according to whichever of these three methods one desires. ||7||
Now learn from me how a person, having attained the status of the twice-born according to his own scripture, should worship me with devotion and faith. (8)

In an image, on a sacrificial mound, in the fire, or in the sun, in water, or in the heart, a twice-born man, endowed with devotion, should worship me—his own guru—with material offerings and without guile. (9)
First, having cleansed one's teeth, one should perform a bath for the purification of the body;
this bath may be performed with both [water] and mantras, beginning with the taking up of earth.
Rites such as the twilight worship (sandhyopāsti) are not enjoined for me by the Veda;
yet, with a pure resolve, one should properly perform worship through them as a means of purifying one's actions.
An image is traditionally said to be of eight kinds: made of stone, wood, metal, plaster, painting, sand, mind, or gemstone. 12.

O Uddhava, the installation of the temple of the living soul is of two kinds: mobile and immobile; however, in the case of the immobile [installation], there is no need for the rites of dismissal or invocation during worship. (13)
If the ground is unstable, there may be mental visualization; however, on firm ground, both methods may be used.
Bathing is for a surface that cannot be smeared with clay, while elsewhere there is merely wiping clean.
For one who is free from deceit, my sacrifice is performed with well-known materials in images and the like;
for the devotee, however, it is indeed performed with whatever is obtained, and even through devotion within the heart.
O Uddhava, bathing and adorning are most dear when performed upon the image;
however, on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), it is the arrangement of the principles (tattva-vinyāsa), and in the fire, it is the oblation of clarified butter. 16.
Worship offered to the Sun is most dear to me; likewise, water—even if it be merely water—offered with faith by a devotee is most dear to me. ||17||
Even if it be abundant, that which is offered by one who is not devoted does not lead to my satisfaction—how much less so [the offerings of] perfume, incense, flowers, lamps, and food? 18.
Pure, having gathered the necessary materials, and having prepared a seat with darbha grass facing either east or north, he should sit and perform the worship, facing the image. ||19||

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), he should wipe my image—which has also been consecrated with nyāsa—with his hand; then he should duly prepare the water-pot and the vessel for sprinkling.
Having sprinkled the sacrificial ground,
the ritual materials, and himself with water, he should prepare three vessels with those respective materials and water.

The preceptor should consecrate three vessels intended for water for the feet, the guest-offering (argha), and water for sipping (ācamana) with the Heart-mantra, the Head-mantra, the Topknot-mantra, and the Gāyatrī. ||22||

When the body has been thoroughly purified by air and fire, one should meditate upon my supreme, subtle essence of life (jīvakalā) residing within the heart-lotus, which has been realized by the perfected ones at the conclusion of the primordial sound (nāda). ||23||

When the body is pervaded by that [consciousness] which has become one's own self, having worshipped it and become absorbed in it, one should invoke me and, having established me in the [limbs] beginning with the head, worship me with the limbs thus assigned. ||24||
One should provide the services beginning with water for the feet, water for sipping, and water for honoring;
and having prepared a seat for me with the nine attributes beginning with dharma.
Therein is an eight-petalled lotus, radiant with its pericarp and filaments;
for me, it serves the attainment of both goals through both the Vedas and the Tantras. ||26||

One should worship, in due order, the Sudarśana discus, the Pāñcajanya conch, the mace, the sword, the arrows, the bow, the plow, the club, the Kaustubha gem, the garland, and the Śrīvatsa mark. ||27||
Nanda, Sunanda, Garuḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and Caṇḍa;
Mahābala and Bala, as well as Kumuda and Kumudekṣaṇa. ||28||
One should worship Durgā, Vināyaka, Vyāsa, Viṣvaksena, the gurus, and the gods, facing them in their respective places with sprinkling and other rites. ||29||
When resources are available, one should always bathe [the deity] with waters scented with sandalwood, uśīra, camphor, saffron, and agallochum, while reciting mantras. ||30||
With the Svarṇagharma Anuvāka, the Mahāpuruṣavidyā, the Puruṣasūkta, and the Sāmans beginning with the Rājana, [he should worship]. ||31||
My devotee should lovingly adorn me with garments, sacred threads, ornaments, leaf-designs, garlands, perfumes, and ointments, as is appropriate. 32.
The worshipper should offer me with faith water for the feet, water for sipping, fragrance, flowers, unbroken grains, incense, lamps, and food offerings. ||33||
O Sati, one should prepare as an offering molasses, milk-rice with ghee, fried cakes, honey-cakes, sweetmeats, wheat-flour balls, curd, and soup.
Anointing with oil, massage, looking in a mirror, cleaning the teeth, ritual bathing, food and drink, song, dance, and so forth—these may take place on festival days or even daily. ||35||
Having established the fire in a pit prepared according to the rules, complete with its girdle,
trench, and altar, one should sweep the rising flames together around it with the hand.
Having spread the sacrificial grass and performed the preliminary rites according to the rule, one should sprinkle water around the fire;
then, having set down the ritual materials with the sprinkling-vessel and having sprinkled them, one should meditate upon me within the fire.
Resembling molten gold, with four arms shining with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, he is peaceful and clothed in the filaments of a lotus.
His crown, bracelets, waist-belt, and excellent armlets were quivering;
he had the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, the radiant Kaustubha gem, and wore a garland of forest flowers.
Meditating and having worshipped, he cast the pieces of wood smeared with the sacrificial oblation into the fire;
then, having offered the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) and the two libations (āghāra), he presented the oblation soaked in clarified butter.

The wise one should offer oblations with the root mantra sixteen times from each portion; then, according to the rule, he should perform the Sviṣṭakṛt offering for Dharma and the others with their respective mantras. 41.
Then, having worshipped and paid homage to the attendants, one should offer the oblation (bali);
one should mutter the root mantra while remembering Brahman, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa. 42.
Having offered water for sipping, one should set aside the remnants for Viṣvaksena;
then one should honor him with fragrant mouth-perfumes such as betel leaf and the like.
Singing, praising, dancing, enacting my deeds, causing my stories to be heard, and listening to them oneself—by doing these, one may become absorbed in me for even a moment. 44.
Having praised him with various hymns and praises, both those from the Purāṇas and those composed for the occasion, one should prostrate like a staff, saying, "O Blessed One, be gracious. ||45||
Placing my head at Your feet and clasping Your hands with my arms, O Lord, protect me who have sought refuge, for I am terrified of the ocean of the jaws of death. 46.
Thus, having respectfully placed this remnant given by me upon his head, he should perform the ritual dismissal;
if it is something to be dismissed, then that light should be dissolved back into the [supreme] Light. 47.
Whenever and wherever one has faith in an image or other such objects, there one should worship Me;
for I abide as the Self within all beings and as the Self of all. 48.
Thus, by means of the paths of ritual action and yoga—both Vedic and Tantric—a person worshipping me attains from me their desired perfection in both worlds. 49.
Having consecrated my image, one should cause a firm temple to be built, along with beautiful flower gardens intended for worship, processions, and festivals. (50)

Furthermore, by giving away fields, shops, cities, and villages for the sake of the continuous flow of worship and other rites on great festival days or even daily, one shall attain equality with me. 51.

Through consecration he attains equality with me by reaching the status of a sovereign; through a temple, the three worlds; and through worship and other rites, the realm of Brahmā—thus, by these three, he may attain my likeness. (52)
He alone attains Me through the yoga of devotion with complete detachment;
he who worships Me in this manner surely attains the yoga of devotion. 53.
He who seizes the means of subsistence given by himself or given by others to gods or Brahmins, is born as a consumer of excrement for ten million times ten thousand years. (54)
Furthermore, after death, the doer, the instigator, the driver, and even the one who approves of the actions share in the results; indeed, the fruit of those deeds becomes even greater.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava. ||27||
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
One should neither praise nor disparage the nature, character, or actions of others.
Beholding the universe as having a single essence through both Prakṛti and Puruṣa. ||1||
He who praises or blames the nature and actions of others quickly falls away from his own true purpose due to his attachment to what is unreal. (2)
When the Taijasa state is overcome by sleep, the individual soul (piṇḍastha) becomes unconscious;
likewise, the person who perceives manifold objects falls into illusion or death. ||3||
What is auspicious and what is inauspicious? How much is there of this unreal duality?
That which is uttered by speech and likewise meditated upon by the mind is false. (4)
For shadows, echoes, and reflections, though non-existent, perform functions;
likewise, entities such as the body and so forth grant fear until death. ||5||
The Self alone is this entire universe; the Lord creates it and is created;
the Soul of all protects it and is protected; the Sovereign is withdrawn and withdraws it.
Therefore, no state of being other than the Self has been established as distinct from it;
this threefold manifestation within the Self appears to be rootless.
Know this threefold world, composed of the qualities (guṇas), to be created by Māyā. (7)
Knowing this skill in knowledge and realization taught by me, he neither censures nor praises; he moves through the world like the sun. (8)

Having known through direct perception, inference, scripture, and self-realization that [the world] is unreal, being like something with a beginning and an end, one should wander here free from attachment. 9.
Uddhava said:

O Lord, transmigration belongs neither to the self nor to the body, for these two are the seer and the seen. To whom, then, does it belong that is perceived by one who perceives the non-self as the self?
The Self is imperishable, devoid of qualities, pure, self-luminous, and unobstructed;
since the body is like fire or like wood, whose is transmigration here in this world? (11)
The Blessed Lord said:

As long as there is contact of the self with the body, senses, and vital breaths, so long does worldly existence bear fruit for the undiscriminating person, even though it is ultimately meaningless. 12.
For even when the object does not exist, transmigratory existence does not cease for one who contemplates sense-objects, just as the arrival of misfortune occurs in a dream. ||13||
For just as sleep brings many misfortunes to one who has not awakened, that very same sleep does not lead to delusion for one who has awakened. ||14||
Grief, joy, fear, anger, greed, delusion, longing, and so forth, as well as birth and death, are seen to belong to the ego; they do not belong to the Self. 15.
The individual soul (jīva), who identifies with the body, senses, vital breath, and mind, is the inner self whose form consists of the modes and their activities;
celebrated by various names such as the "Thread" (sūtra) and the "Great One" (mahat), this transmigratory existence rushes forward, governed by time. ||16||
This manifold activity of mind, speech, breath, and bodily action is rootless;
having severed it with the sword of knowledge sharpened by meditation, the sage wanders the earth free from craving. 17.

Knowledge, discernment, scripture, austerity, direct perception, tradition, and inference—whatever exists at the beginning and the end of this world is that very same thing in the middle; it is both time and cause. 18.
Just as gold fashioned by itself before and after is the very same gold throughout all its golden forms, so am I in this world, though manifested through various designations in the midst of it. 19.
O limb, this consciousness consists of three states and possesses the three qualities; it is the cause, the effect, and the agent.
That alone which is the fourth, by means of which [consciousness] is connected through association and separated through distinction—that alone is the Truth. 20.
That which is not before, nor that which is after, and that which is in the middle—that is not a mere designation.
Whatever is real and well-known by another, it is my conviction that that very thing is what it is. 21.
That which appears though it does not exist—the transformative creation born of passion (rājasasarga)—is this;
therefore, Brahman, which is self-luminous, shines forth as a variegated manifestation consisting of the senses, their objects, and the transformations of the self. 22.

Thus, having clearly severed the doubt regarding the self through the means of discriminating Brahman and by being confident in censuring the views of others, one should desist, satisfied in one's own bliss, from all who lust after desires. 23.
The body is not the self; the senses are indeed the gods, for life is wind, water, and fire;
the mind is merely food, as are intellect, the quality of goodness (sattva), egoism, ether, earth, and the equilibrium of the elements. 24.

What quality could there be for me, whose abode is perfectly distinct from them, by means of the senses—which are composed of the qualities (guṇas) and themselves consist of the qualities—whether they are concentrated or distracted?
And what defect could there be when those dense clouds of the sun have arrived or departed? (25)

Just as the sky is not attached to the qualities of earth, water, fire, air, and ether, nor to the seasonal qualities that come and go, so too the Imperishable is beyond the impurities of goodness, passion, and ignorance, which are the causes of the ego-sense and of worldly transmigration. 26.

Nevertheless, attachment must be completely abandoned toward those qualities fashioned by illusion, until the impurity of the mind—the quality of passion—is cast out by means of firm yoga of devotion to Me. 27.

Just as a disease that is not properly treated repeatedly torments men as it breaks out again and again, so the mind—unripe through the karma of its latent tendencies—pierces the poor yogi with every attachment. 28.
Those practitioners of yoga who are hindered by human beings ordained as obstacles or by those sent by the gods,
resume their yoga practice once more through the power of their former habituation, and not because of the influence of ritual action.
A living being performs action and is acted upon by someone else until his fall, impelled by that force;
yet the wise man, even while remaining within primordial nature, is not affected therein, for his thirst has ceased through the experience of his own bliss. (30)

Whether standing, sitting, walking, lying down, urinating, or eating food—whether performing some other activity by its very nature—the one whose mind is fixed on the Self does not perceive the Self as being anything else. 31.

If he perceives something non-existent through the senses, or otherwise through various means of inference, the wise man does not regard it as a reality, just as one who has awakened does not regard a dream that vanishes upon rising. 32.
O dear one, that ignorance which was previously grasped as a manifold collection of qualities and actions, undifferentiated from the Self, ceases through discernment alone;
it is neither grasped nor is the Self abandoned by it. 33.

For just as the rising of the sun destroys the darkness of those with human vision but does not create it anew, so too may this skillful investigation of mine destroy the darkness of a person's intellect. 34.
He is self-luminous, unborn, immeasurable, of great majesty, and the experience of all;
He is the one without a second, beyond the reach of words, by whom as the Lord speech and the vital breaths move. 35.
Such is this self-delusion that conceptual construction relies upon a mere self, for it has no support other than the self which does not exist. (36)
That which is indeed graspable through forms, possessing five colors and uncontradicted—this eulogy of the "object," though devoid of actual meaning, is for those who fancy themselves wise. (37)
For the yogin whose yoga is unripened, while he is practicing, his body may be afflicted by obstacles that have arisen; in that case, this following rule is prescribed. ||38||

By means of yoga and concentration, some [obstacles] he should burn away; by means of postures combined with concentration, and by means of austerity, mantras, and medicinal herbs, he should burn away certain obstacles. (39)
By means of meditation upon Me, by the chanting of My names and so forth, or by following the Lord of Yoga, one may gradually destroy the bestowers of inauspiciousness. 40.
Some wise ones, having prepared this body well through various means while it is stable in its youth, then apply it toward spiritual accomplishment. 41.
For that is not a righteous act; it is indeed a fruitless exertion, because the body is finite, like the fruit of a tree. ||42||
If the body of one who constantly practices yoga were to attain perfection, even then a wise person devoted to Me should not abandon yoga out of faith in that. ||43||
A yogi who practices this yoga while relying upon me shall not be hindered by obstacles, being free from desire and experiencing his own bliss. 44.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Supreme Truth," in the dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Uddhava within the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the collection concerning the state of the Paramahaṃsas. ||28||
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter.
"I consider this practice of yoga to be very difficult to cross for one who has not disciplined the self. O Acyuta, tell me directly how a person may succeed easily. (1)
O lotus-eyed one, for the most part, yogis who strive to fix the mind falter due to a lack of concentration, being exhausted by the effort of restraining the mind. ||2||
Therefore, O lotus-eyed Lord of All, let the wise (haṃsas) take refuge in Your lotus feet, which yield bliss;
for these proud ones, obstructed by Your māyā, find no happiness through the rituals of yoga. ||3||

O Acyuta, what wonder is this on Your part—that You, who are free from all bonds, bestow Your own self-nature upon Your servants who have no other refuge? For You, whose footstool was pressed by the crowns of the illustrious lords of gods, chose to dwell together with the deer. ||4||
Who indeed would abandon You—the Lord who grants all goals to those who have taken refuge in Him, who knows their own deeds, and who is the beloved Self of all?
Or who would worship another for the sake of some trivial experience that leads only to forgetfulness; for what could possibly be lacking for us who delight in the dust of Your feet? ||5||
O Lord, even with a lifespan as long as that of Brahmā, the wise do not reach the limit of Your worship, for they remember the misdeeds committed even while You were their teacher;
You who, by shaking off the impurity within and without embodied beings, reveal Your own nature through the form of the preceptor and the Caitya. 6.
Śrī Śuka said:

Thus questioned by Uddhava, whose heart was deeply attached [to Him], the Lord of lords—who sports with the world through His own potencies and has assumed three forms—spoke with love and a charming smile. (7)
The Blessed Lord said:
"Behold, I shall declare to you my most auspicious duties, practicing which with faith a mortal conquers death, which is difficult to overcome. (8)
One should perform all actions for my sake, remembering me gradually, with mind and consciousness dedicated to me, and finding delight in the self through my dharma. 9.
One should resort to holy places frequented by my devotees and virtuous men, as well as those places where my devotees have practiced among gods, asuras, and humans. 10.
O Great King, he should cause separate great festivals for me to be held on the festival days with processions,
accompanied by songs, dances, and other displays of magnificence.
One whose mind is pure should perceive Me alone—unveiled both within and without—in all beings, and likewise perceive the Self within oneself, just as one perceives the sky. 12.
Thus, O one of great splendor, honoring all beings with the thought that they are my own self, he who relies solely on knowledge attains [liberation]. 13.
A wise person is considered to look with equanimity upon a Brahmin and a Pulkasa, a thief and one devoted to sacred knowledge, the sun and a spark, and one who is gentle and one who is cruel. (14)
For a man who constantly contemplates my nature among men, rivalry, envy, and contempt, along with egoism, indeed vanish before long. 15.
Casting aside smiles, his own gaze, and physical shame, he should prostrate himself like a staff upon the ground, even before a Cāṇḍāla, a cow, or a donkey. 16.
As long as my nature has not arisen within all beings, for that long one should worship in this manner through the activities of speech, mind, and body. ||17||
Perceiving through knowledge and the wisdom of the self that everything has Brahman as its essence, one should desist from all activity, freed from all doubt. 18.
For this is considered by me to be consistent with all ritual observances:
the state of being [absorbed] in me within all beings through the activities of mind, speech, and body. (19)
Indeed, O Uddhava, not even an atom of my dharma can perish at its commencement;
for it has been perfectly resolved by Me, being devoid of qualities and free from desire for rewards. 20.
Whatever dharma is prescribed for me, if it results in fruitlessness, that effort would be as useless as the exertion of a virtuous person out of fear or similar motives. (21)
This is the wisdom of the wise and the insight of the sagacious:
that by means of the mortal, which is untruth, one attains here the immortal, which is truth. 22.
This entire compendium of the discourse on Brahman has been declared to you according to the method of both summary and detail; it is difficult to comprehend even for the gods. 23.
You have repeatedly declared this knowledge, which is characterized by clear reasoning;
having understood this, a person whose doubts are destroyed shall be liberated. 24.
This well-secluded question of yours, even if held by me, leads one to attain the eternal secret of Brahman, the Supreme Brahman. ||25||
Whoever shall bestow this [teaching] in its entirety upon my devotees, to him—being a recipient of the gift of Brahman—I give myself by means of my own self. 26.
Whoever should study this supreme, pure, and holy [text], he shall be purified day by day, revealing Me through the lamp of knowledge. 27.
The man who, with faith and an undistracted mind, constantly hears this while offering supreme devotion to me, is not bound by his actions. (28)
O friend Uddhava, have you understood the Absolute Truth?
Has your delusion and this grief born of the mind departed from you? (29)
This should not be given by you to a hypocrite, an atheist, a rogue, one who does not wish to listen, one lacking devotion, or one who is ill-behaved. ||30||
One should speak to one who is free from these defects, who is devoted to Brahman, dear, virtuous, and pure; for Śūdras and women, there should be devotion [to such a teacher]. 31.
Having understood this, nothing remains for the seeker to know;
once one has drunk the nectar of immortality, nothing further remains to be drunk.
O dear one, whatever purpose there may be for men in knowledge, action, yoga, commerce, and the wielding of punishment— all that is found in me in my fourfold form.
When a mortal has renounced all actions, offered himself up, and desires to act for my sake, then,
attaining immortality, he indeed becomes fit for identity with my own self.
Śrī Śuka said:

Having thus been shown the path of yoga and having heard the words of Uttamaśloka, he stood with palms joined in reverence, his throat choked with love, and with eyes overflowing with tears, he said nothing at all. (35)

Stabilizing his agitated mind through fortitude and regarding him with great respect, O King, he spoke to that hero of the Yadus with palms joined in reverence, touching the lotus-feet of the Lord with his head. (36)
Uddhava said:
O Unborn One, the great darkness of delusion that had taken refuge within me has been dispelled by Your proximity;
for how could cold, darkness, or fear prevail today for one who has approached the sun? 37.

This lamp of knowledge has been bestowed upon me, your servant, by you, who are compassionate. O Grateful One, having abandoned your feet, what other refuge could one approach that is as dear to you? (38)

And my very firm bond of affection for the Daśārhas, Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, and Sātvatas has been severed by you, O Lord of the Daśārhas, who, through your own creative power (māyā), have employed the weapon of self-knowledge to increase the creation. 39.
Salutations be unto you, O Great Yogin; instruct me, who have sought refuge in you, so that there may be an unswerving devotion toward your lotus feet. 40.
The Blessed Lord said: Go, O Uddhava, as commanded by Me, to My hermitage named Badarī;
there, purified by bathing and sipping the water of the sacred ford at My feet. (41)
Having shaken off all impurities by the sight of the Alakanandā, O dear one, he dwelt wearing bark garments, subsisting on forest fare, happy and free from desire. ||42||
Enduring the pairs of opposites, of virtuous conduct, with senses restrained, tranquil, with a concentrated intellect, and endowed with both knowledge and realization. ||43||
Having learned from me what you have experienced as solitude, with speech and mind absorbed in me, be devoted to my dharma;
having transcended the three states of existence, you shall thereafter come to me. 44.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus addressed by Harimedha, Uddhava circumambulated him and, placing his head at his feet,
his mind moistened by a stream of tears, he drenched them— even though he was beyond the dualities— at the very outset of their meeting.

Distressed by the sorrow of separation from his beloved and unable to abandon him, for whom affection is so difficult to relinquish, he went with great difficulty, carrying the sandals of his lord upon his head; having offered his salutations, he departed again and again. (46)
Then, having placed Him within his heart, that great devotee went to Viśālā as instructed by the sole kinsman of the world; and from there, taking recourse to Hari, he attained His supreme goal. 47.

O Ānanda, whoever with true faith partakes of this nectar of knowledge, gathered from the ocean and spoken by Kṛṣṇa—whose feet are served by the masters of yoga—to that devotee of the Lord the world grants liberation. 48.
To destroy the fear of worldly existence, the author of the Vedas extracted the essence of knowledge and realization from them, just as a bee gathers the nectar of flowers;
he then caused his circle of disciples to drink that nectar of the Vedas like ambrosia from the ocean. I bow down to that primordial bull among men, known by the name Kṛṣṇa. 49.
Thus, in the glorious *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the great Purāṇa, in the *Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā*,
in the eleventh book, within the dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Uddhava, [this is] the narration of the easy means for attaining the supreme truth and Uddhava’s entry into Badarikāśrama.
The twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Nāma. ||29||
Now the thirtieth chapter.
The King said:
Then, when the illustrious Uddhava had departed for the forest, [the Lord spoke].
What did the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, do in Dvāravatī?
When his own lineage was overtaken by the curse of a Brahmin,
how did that bull among the Yādavas abandon his body, which was the beloved of all eyes?
Where women were unable to draw back their eyes once they were fixed upon it; where, having entered the ears, it did not depart from them;

which, when attached to the souls of the virtuous, produces delight in their speech—what indeed could poets have been proud of, seeing that even they attained equality with it when they beheld it mounted on the chariot of Arjuna in battle? (3)
The sage said:
Having seen great portents arisen in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space,
Kṛṣṇa spoke this to the Yadus as they were seated in the Sudharmā assembly hall.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O best of the Yadus, these terrible and great portents at Dvārakā are the banners of Death;
we must not remain here for even a moment."
"Let the women, the children, and the elderly go from here to Śaṅkhoddhāra;
we shall go to Prabhāsa, where the Sarasvatī flows westward. (6)
Having been consecrated there, pure, fasting, and well-composed,
we shall worship the deities with baths, ointments, and offerings.
Having performed the rites of auspiciousness, we [honored] the highly fortunate Brahmins with cows, land, gold, garments, elephants, horses, chariots, and dwellings. (8)
For this is the ritual that wards off misfortune and is the supreme path to auspiciousness;
it consists of the worship of gods, the twice-born, and cows, and the cultivation of supreme compassion toward all living beings. (9)
Having heard this from the enemy of Madhu, all the elders of the Yadu clan said,
"So be it," and having crossed over by means of boats, they proceeded to Prabhāsa by chariots.
In that regard, the Blessed One instructed that the Yādavas, out of devotion and fear of others, performed everything that increases all forms of welfare. ||11||
Then, their intellects led astray by fate, they drank the intoxicating liquor *maireyaka* at that great drinking bout— a substance by which the mind is utterly corrupted.
A truly great conflict arose among those heroes who were intoxicated by their great prowess, whose minds were arrogant, and who were utterly deluded by the illusion of Kṛṣṇa. 13.
Enraged by fury, those assailants fought on the shore with bows, swords, maces, clubs, and spears. ||14||
Chariots, elephants, donkeys, camels, cattle, buffaloes, and even men—with their banners fluttering—encountered one another along with mules;
utterly intoxicated, they struck each other like wild elephants in a forest with their tusks. ||15||
Pradyumna and Sāmba, filled with martial pride in battle; Akrūra and Bhoja, Aniruddha and Sātyaki;
Subhadra and Saṃgrāmajit, both most formidable; Gada and Sumitra, and Suratha—all these met one another. ||16||

And others indeed—Niśaṭha, Ulmuka, and the rest, including Sahasrajit, Śatajit, Bhānu, and their leaders—having encountered one another and blinded by intoxication, struck each other, utterly deluded by Mukunda. ||17||

The Dāśārhas, Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, Bhojas, Sātvatas, Madhus, Arbudas, Māthuras, Śūrasenas, Visarjanas, Kukuras, and Kuntayas—having thus mutually abandoned their affection for one another, they departed. || 18 ||
Sons fought with fathers and brothers, as well as with sisters' sons, daughters' sons, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles;
friends with friends, well-wishers with well-wishers, and kinsmen, being utterly deluded, slaughtered their very own kinsmen. 19.
When the arrows were exhausted, the bows broken,
and the weapons depleted, they seized *erakā* grass and struck with their fists.
Those iron clubs, indeed like unto thunderbolts, were grasped by their fists;
though restrained by Kṛṣṇa, they struck his enemies, and he likewise struck them with those very weapons. ||21||
Considering Balabhadra to be their adversary and being deluded, O King, they set their minds on killing him; thus, as desperadoes, they fell into calamity.
Then those two, also enraged, O descendant of Kuru,
raised their fists of *erakā* grass like iron clubs and struck one another in battle as they grew old.
Afflicted by the curse of Brahmā and enveloped by the illusion of Kṛṣṇa, their very selves were led to destruction by rivalry and anger, just as a forest is consumed by a fire of bamboo. 24.
When all his own kinsmen had thus perished, Keśava considered that the burden of the earth had been removed, leaving nothing remaining behind.
Rāma, having resorted to human effort through yoga at the shore of the ocean, abandoned that mortal world by uniting his self within the Self. 26.
Having beheld Rāma’s departure, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī,
sat down upon the surface of the earth, having silently approached a peepal tree.
Bearing a four-armed form, radiant with its own splendor, it made the quarters of the sky clear, like a smokeless fire. ||28||
Marked with the Śrīvatsa, dark as a rain cloud, possessing the luster of refined gold, and beautifully draped in a pair of silken garments, he was most auspicious. ||29||
His lotus-face was graced with a beautiful smile and adorned with dark locks of hair; his eyes were as delightful as white lotuses, and he wore shimmering earrings shaped like sea-monsters.
He was resplendent with a waist-thread, a sacred thread, a crown, bracelets, and armlets;
with necklaces, anklets, and hand-marks, and with the Kaustubha gem.
His limbs were encircled by a forest garland, and his own weapons stood before him in embodied form;
he sat with his right foot placed upon his broad thigh, his complexion as red as a lotus.
The hunter Jarā, whose iron club was shattered into fragments by [the arrow], pierced that foot—which had the appearance of a deer's mouth—mistaking it for a deer. ||33||
Seeing that four-armed Person, he who had committed the sin, terrified, fell with his head at the feet of the enemy of the Asuras. ||34||
"O Madhusūdana, this was done by me, a sinner, out of ignorance;
O sinless one of excellent fame, you ought to forgive this transgression of mine. (35)
O Viṣṇu, O Lord, I have committed an evil deed against You, whose remembrance destroys the darkness of ignorance for human beings—so they say. 36.
Therefore, O Vaikuṇṭha, quickly slay me, the sinful deer-hunter, so that I may never again commit such a transgression against the virtuous. (37)
Viriñca, Rudra, and others—his sons who are the lords of speech—do not understand this self-manifested yoga of Yours;
their vision being obscured by Your Māyā, how can we, who have resorted to the unreal, truly describe that which belongs to You? ||38||
The Blessed Lord said: "Do not fear, O Jarā; arise, for this desire has indeed been fulfilled by me.
Depart, permitted by me, to heaven, the abode of those who have performed meritorious deeds. (39)
Thus instructed by the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, who possesses a body at will, he circumambulated him three times, bowed to him, and departed for heaven in his celestial chariot. 40.
Seeking the path of Kṛṣṇa, Dāruka approached him;
having caught the fragrance of the Tulasī breeze, he proceeded toward Him. 41.

Seeing her husband there at the foot of the Ashvattha tree, his banner already raised, surrounded by weapons of fierce luster, he—his soul drenched in affection and his eyes filled with tears—leaped down from his chariot and fell at his feet. 42.
O Lord, for me who does not behold Your lotus feet, my vision has perished and entered into darkness;
I know not the directions and find no peace, like one at night when the moon has vanished. 43.
While the charioteer was thus speaking, O king of kings, the chariot marked with the emblem of Garuḍa leapt into the sky along with its horses and banner, even as they looked on. 44.
The divine weapons of Viṣṇu followed him;
then Janārdana, his soul filled with great wonder at that, spoke to his charioteer.
"Go to Dvāravatī, O Sūta, and tell my kinsmen of our mutual destruction;
report Saṃkarṣaṇa’s departure to his relatives, and speak of my own condition. (46)
And you, along with your kinsmen, must not remain in Dvārakā;
for the ocean will submerge the city of the Yadus once it has been abandoned by me. (47)
"Taking each your own possessions and our parents as well,
all of you, protected by Arjuna, shall go to Indraprastha."
But you, abiding in my dharma, established in knowledge and equanimous, having understood this construction of my māyā, attain peace. 49.
Having been addressed thus, he circumambulated him and paid homage again and again;
placing his feet upon his head, he departed for the city with a heavy heart.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Destruction of the Yadu Clan," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the great Purāṇa, in the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||30||
Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
Śrī Śuka said: Then Brahmā arrived there, as did Bhava together with Bhavānī.
The gods, headed by Mahendra, along with the sages and the lords of the progenitors.
The Pitṛs, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Mahoragas, Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Kiṃnaras, Apsarases, and the twice-born Brahmins. ||2||
Desirous of seeing the Blessed One’s parinirvāṇa, they were intensely eager,
singing and chanting of the deeds and the birth of Śauri.
Filled with supreme devotion, O King, they showered rains of flowers from rows of celestial chariots, making the sky dense with them. ||4||
Beholding the Grandfather, the omnipresent Lord,
the manifestation of his own self, joined his own self within himself and closed his lotus-eyes.
Having incinerated his own body— which was a delight to the world— by means of the fiery concentration (dhāraṇā) and meditation (dhyāna), which are auspicious,
he entered his own abode through that yogic concentration.
In heaven the drums resounded and flowers fell from the sky;
Truth, Dharma, Fortitude, Fame, and Prosperity followed him from the earth. (7)
The gods and others, headed by Brahmā, did not perceive Kṛṣṇa as he entered his own abode; yet, seeing him whose movement was unperceived, they were utterly amazed. ||8||
Just as the path of a lightning flash departing through the sky after leaving behind a mass of clouds cannot be perceived by mortals, so too the path of Kṛṣṇa cannot be perceived by the gods. 9.
But Brahmā, Rudra, and the others, having witnessed that yogic power of Hari, were filled with wonder; praising it, they then departed for their respective worlds. ||10||
O King, know that the birth, death, and activities of embodied beings belonging to another are but a deceptive display of Māyā, like that of an actor.
Having created this universe by His own power, entered it, sported within it, and finally withdrawn it, He remains at rest through His own majesty. ||11||

That lord of the earth, who—being a mere mortal—brought back the son of his preceptor from the realm of Yama and you yourself when consumed by the supreme weapon, and who conquered even the Lord who is the end-maker of Death; would he not surely protect his own subjects by destroying the hunter along with his body? (12)

Nevertheless, although He is the sole cause of the maintenance and origination of all things, He who possesses infinite power does not wish to lead this remaining body [of His] away from here, as if demonstrating to mortals the path of one who remains in well-being. (13)
Whoever, having risen at dawn, recites with devotion and self-restraint this supreme path of Kṛṣṇa, attains that very same unsurpassed state. 14.
Dāruka, having arrived at Dvārakā, fell at the feet of Vasudeva and Ugrasena and bathed them with tears shed for Kṛṣṇa. 15.
O King, he related the complete destruction of the Vṛṣṇis;
hearing that, the people became agitated in heart and were overwhelmed by grief. ||16||
There they went in haste, overwhelmed by the separation from Kṛṣṇa, to where their kinsmen lay lifeless, their faces covered as they were being slain. ||17||
Devakī, Rohiṇī, and Vasudeva likewise, beholding their two sons Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, lost their composure, being afflicted by grief. 18.
There, afflicted by the separation from the Blessed One, they gave up their lives;
embracing their husbands, O dear one, the women ascended the funeral pyre.

The wives of Rāma embraced that body and entered the fire; the wives of Vasudeva, including Pradyumna and the other daughters-in-law of Hari, as well as the wives of Kṛṣṇa headed by Rukmiṇī, who were absorbed in him, likewise entered the fire. ||20||
Arjuna, distressed by separation from his dearest friend Kṛṣṇa, consoled himself with the well-spoken verses sung by Kṛṣṇa. 21.
Arjuna performed the funeral rites for his kinsmen who had lost their lineage and were slain in battle,
according to the rules and in proper succession.
O great king, once Dvārakā had been abandoned by Hari, the ocean submerged it in an instant,
except for the glorious abode of the Blessed One.
The Blessed Lord Madhusūdana is eternally present there;
by remembering him, all inauspiciousness is removed, and he is the source of all auspiciousness. 24.
Taking with him the women, children, and the elderly who remained after the slaughter, Dhanañjaya established them in Indraprastha and there consecrated Vajra as king.
O King, having heard of the slaughter of their friend by Arjuna, your grandfathers,
having made you the upholder of the lineage, all departed upon the great path.
The mortal who recites with faith these deeds and the birth of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, is liberated from all sins. ||27||

Thus, by hearing and chanting of the most peaceful heroic deeds and childhood exploits of the Blessed Lord Hari—whether heard elsewhere or here—a person attains supreme devotion toward the state of the Paramahaṃsas. 28.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Clubs," in the Eleventh Book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā. ||31||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Song of Uddhava."
